## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}

\end{marginfigure}
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}
::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_stack.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Machine Learning Systems Architecture Stack"}

*Architecture stack focus for this chapter.*

:::

_Why does moving data cost more than computing it?_

Arithmetic is inexpensive relative to data movement. In the time required to fetch a single scalar operand from off-chip DRAM, modern arithmetic units can execute dozens to hundreds of floating-point operations, and that DRAM access consumes on the order of a hundred times more energy than the computation itself. This imbalance, the memory wall, means specialized accelerators are not merely faster arithmetic engines. Rather, their microarchitectures are designed to stage, amortize, and hide data movement through wide spatial interconnects, deep on-chip memory hierarchies, and specialized execution pipelines. When general-purpose processor scaling faltered, hardware specialization enabled machine learning models to continue scaling by turning transistor budgets into high-throughput tensor datapaths. Delivered performance, however, depends on whether a model's tensor access patterns match the data paths of the underlying silicon. Hardware selection cannot be reduced to comparing peak FLOP/s: two accelerators with identical theoretical compute ratings often deliver radically different throughput on real workloads because one saturates its functional units while the other starves for data. A recommendation model dominated by sparse embedding lookups stresses memory bandwidth and interconnect latency, demanding a different memory architecture than a dense transformer training run bounded by matrix multiply-accumulate throughput. If an operation is bandwidth bound, reducing theoretical operation count yields zero speedup because arithmetic is not the binding constraint. Matching workload characteristics to architectural dataflows determines whether an accelerator operates near its hardware ceiling or languishes at a fraction of its advertised peak. In D·A·M terms, the accelerator makes the machine constraint concrete, governing which algorithms and model architectures remain practical in production.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

- Explain hardware acceleration as tensor-workload specialization and why Amdahl's law bounds its end-to-end speedup
- Compare Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, SIMD/SIMT units, and sparse execution for ML compute primitives
- Diagnose memory-wall bottlenecks using bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device transfer, and energy-movement costs
- Calculate arithmetic intensity and execution-path roofline ceilings, then use profiling to diagnose compute or memory limits
- Select dataflow, tiling, and mapping strategies that maximize reuse under memory-capacity constraints
- Analyze compiler and runtime optimizations that fuse kernels, plan memory, and schedule accelerators
- Evaluate accelerator choices across throughput, latency, power, cost, and deployment-context constraints

:::

## Anatomy of an Accelerator {#sec-hardware-acceleration-ai-hardware-acceleration-fundamentals-9b28}

```{python}
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *

from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_int,
    fmt,
    fmt_qty_int,
    check,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_flop_rate,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_energy,
    fmt_count,
    fmt_params,
    fmt_carbon_intensity,
    fmt_compute_efficiency,
    fmt_multiple_range,
)

class HwAccelSetup:
    """H100 peak FP16/BF16 throughput vs. the registry reference CPU for the opening callout."""

    # LOAD
    gap = Scenarios.H100OverReferenceCpu  # H100 FP16 peak against the 1-2 TFLOP/s reference-CPU range

    # EXECUTE
    cpu_gap_min = gap.ratio_low
    cpu_gap_max = gap.ratio_high

    # GUARD
    check(480 <= cpu_gap_min <= 510, f"Unexpected lower CPU gap: {cpu_gap_min:.1f}x")
    check(960 <= cpu_gap_max <= 1020, f"Unexpected upper CPU gap: {cpu_gap_max:.1f}x")

    # OUTPUT
    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    cpu_gap_range_mult_str = fmt_multiple_range(round(cpu_gap_min, -1), round(cpu_gap_max, -1), precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hw_acceleration_dam_locator.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="D·A·M taxonomy triangle with three vertices labeled D, A, and M connected by edges. The M (Machine) vertex is filled in solid color; the D and A vertices are gray, marking the Machine axis."}

*Hardware acceleration turns on the machine axis.*
:::

@Sec-model-compression closed on a deployment profile for ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 (@tbl-resnet50-int8-profile): a model four times smaller whose large-batch throughput rises severalfold on the reference H100 while its batch-one latency barely moves. Data selection reduced the iron law's Data factor ($\text{Samples/Task}$) and compression reduced the Algorithm factor ($\text{FLOPs/Sample}$) and byte traffic ($\DataVolume$), but whether either saving reaches the wall clock is decided by the Machine factor ($\text{Seconds/FLOP}$). This chapter supplies the machine side of that profile. It explains why the same INT8 weights run faster on one execution path than on another, and why the hardware, not the model, determines how much of every compression saving survives execution. The explanation starts with the memory wall: arithmetic is cheap relative to data movement, so specialized hardware matters less because it raises compute throughput than because it organizes memory, dataflow, and parallelism so that its arithmetic units stay fed.

One workload runs through the chapter. ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 carries the book's compute-bound regime (@tbl-lighthouse-examples): its convolutions reuse each weight across many image positions, so on a data-center accelerator most of its time can go to arithmetic rather than to moving bytes. It reappears at every level of the machine, from the matrix units that execute its convolutions to the compiler that lowers its graph, and each time the question is what the INT8 path changes. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at a time supplies the single contrast. It carries the bandwidth-bound regime: every generated token streams all of the model's weights from memory for about two operations per parameter, so the machine that keeps ResNet-50 busy spends most of a decode step waiting for bytes. MobileNetV2, whose depthwise layers trade arithmetic for a small parameter footprint, and keyword spotting (KWS), the power-bound lighthouse, return where the chapter reaches phone-class and embedded chips. DLRM appears where its embedding lookups, the capacity-bound regime, break the regular access patterns that accelerators assume. The reference machine is the NVIDIA H100, the data-center accelerator this book uses for training and serving examples; its numbers are one generation's instance of limits that every generation obeys.

::: {#dfn-hw-acceleration-hardware-acceleration .callout-definition title="Hardware acceleration"}

***Hardware acceleration***\index{Hardware acceleration!definition} is the practice of mapping work from general-purpose execution onto specialized processors or functional units optimized for a narrower operation class. For ML workloads, that specialization commonly trades some programmability for the compute density $(\PeakRate)$ and performance-per-watt gains that regular tensor operations can exploit.

1.  **Significance**: An H100 GPU delivers `{python} HwAccelSetup.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` for dense FP16/BF16 matrix multiplication; against this chapter's illustrative 1–2 TFLOP/s reference-CPU baseline, this is a `{python} HwAccelSetup.cpu_gap_range_mult_str` gap. Its 80 billion transistors devote far more silicon to parallel arithmetic than to branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and large caches [@choquette2023].
2.  **Distinction**: A general-purpose CPU is designed for flexible execution, low-latency control, and varied workloads. An accelerator instead concentrates resources on a narrower operation class, so it achieves its gains only when the workload exposes the supported operations and enough parallel work to keep its arithmetic units busy.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that an accelerator's advertised peak throughput is the throughput a workload receives. Delivered performance is bounded above by the lower of the compute ceiling and what memory bandwidth can feed (the roofline constraint, developed later in this chapter). A low-arithmetic-intensity kernel can therefore sit at a small fraction of peak FLOP/s no matter how fast the silicon is rated, because it starves for data rather than for arithmetic.

:::

The anatomy of an accelerator\index{Accelerator!anatomy} is the arrangement of parts that every machine learning accelerator shares: arithmetic units built for tensor operations, on-chip memory that holds operands next to those units, a wide path to off-chip memory, and a host interface through which work arrives. Every inference and every training step on such a machine is a stream of operand movements that ends in multiply-accumulate operations, and the anatomy decides how far each operand travels before it is used. A matrix unit that can retire thousands of multiply-accumulates per cycle sits idle whenever its next operands are still in flight, and an off-chip access can take many processor cycles and cost orders of magnitude more energy than the low-precision operation it feeds. The arithmetic units are the easy part of the design; the rest of the anatomy exists to keep them fed.

The definition becomes concrete in the generic chip of @fig-accelerator-anatomy, which serves as this chapter's map. External high-bandwidth memory (HBM) feeds shared on-chip storage (an L2 cache), which distributes operands into rows of processing elements\index{Processing element!accelerator building block}, each equipped with a private scratchpad or cache, a matrix unit, a vector unit, and a special function unit. A host interface connects the chip to the CPU that issues its work.

::: {#fig-accelerator-anatomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Anatomy of a Modern AI Accelerator**: This generic schematic combines common components rather than depicting one product. A host interface connects the accelerator to a CPU, a high-bandwidth device-memory interface feeds shared on-chip storage, and processing elements contain matrix, vector, and special-function units with local memory. Real accelerators differ in which units they provide and whether storage is hardware-managed cache or software-managed scratchpad." fig-alt="Generic schematic of an AI accelerator chip linked by a host interface to a host CPU and by a memory interface to high-bandwidth memory. Inside the chip, rows of processing elements surround shared on-chip storage. An enlarged processing element contains an L1 cache or scratchpad, a tensor core, a vector unit, and a special function unit (SFU). A separate dashed link connects host DRAM to the host CPU."}

Within each processing element, specialized units partition execution across distinct mathematical primitives: dedicated matrix units (Tensor Cores)\index{Tensor Core!matrix multiplication} execute dense matrix multiplication, vector units\index{Vector Unit!element-wise operations} evaluate element-wise arithmetic, and special function units (SFUs)\index{Special Function Unit!activation functions} approximate transcendental operations such as activations and exponentials. Their number, grouping, and names vary by vendor; some designs arrange them into an explicit 2D systolic grid, and others distribute matrix engines among wide parallel cores.

The memory hierarchy amortizes the cost of data transport across tiers. High-bandwidth memory\index{HBM!throughput requirements} provides off-chip capacity and throughput, while shared on-chip storage and per-element caches or scratchpads cut off-chip traffic. Because moving a tensor tile across the package boundary costs orders of magnitude more energy than keeping it on chip, compilers and kernels must coordinate tile capacity, reuse, and prefetching to keep operands staged locally. More HBM bandwidth raises the off-chip ceiling, but without local reuse the execution units still stall. The system assumptions appendix (@sec-appdx-system-assumptions) collects reference specifications for the accelerators this book uses, including the H100.

The host interface links the accelerator to the host CPU, which coordinates execution graphs, asynchronous I/O, and fallback operations while the accelerator executes dispatched kernels. Direct-memory-access engines can overlap host-device transfers with execution, but an operator unsupported by the accelerator backend may require a CPU round-trip. An operator outside the matrix-unit instruction set may instead use vector or other device kernels. These execution boundaries help set the effective speedup envelope. Kernel execution time matters little if transfers, launches, and synchronization dominate end-to-end latency. The three parts of the figure (the processing elements, the memory tiers, and the host link) are the parts this chapter takes apart in turn.

The anatomy embodies the chapter's central engineering trade-off. General-purpose processors allocate silicon area to complex control logic, speculative execution, branch prediction, and multi-level cache hierarchies to handle arbitrary control flow. An accelerator redirects that transistor budget toward dense arithmetic arrays, dedicated register files, and high-bandwidth memory paths tailored to a narrower workload class. When the software path exposes sufficient tensor parallelism, this specialization yields order-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency and throughput per watt. Silicon built for a narrow class of dense tensor operations pays off only because, as the bitter lesson predicts, the general methods that win by exploiting computation keep reducing to those same operations at ever larger scale. The dependence also runs the other way, because scale keeps winning only while accelerators keep lowering the time and energy of each additional operation, so the hardware this chapter studies is part of what sustains the bitter lesson itself.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The bitter lesson, the observation that general methods exploiting computation win as computation grows, is established in @sec-introduction-bitter-lesson-79c7.
:::

Hardware alone cannot achieve these gains. Algorithms must structure operations to expose data reuse and regular memory access, while silicon architectures must allocate physical units to the mathematical primitives and numeric precisions that algorithms actually execute. That mutual dependence motivates a complementary principle: hardware-software co-design.

::: {#dfn-hw-acceleration-hardware-software-co-design .callout-definition title="Hardware-software co-design"}

***Hardware-Software Co-design***\index{Hardware-Software Co-design!definition} is an ML accelerator development method that crosses conventional abstraction boundaries, allowing algorithm constraints to inform silicon design and hardware capabilities to shape algorithm formulation.

1.  **Significance**: On a supported tensor-core path, 8-bit integer (INT8) quantization can deliver multi-fold throughput gains because hardware executes lower-precision operations more densely and moves fewer bytes than an FP32 path; the exact gain depends on the architecture and workload [@NVIDIA2020; @dally2021; @dally2023].
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike layered abstraction (where software calls a hardware API without knowing the silicon details), co-design exposes hardware constraints directly to algorithm and compiler authors: data alignment requirements, precision formats, and memory access patterns all become visible inputs to global cross-layer optimization.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that co-design is a one-time hardware design choice. In practice, the supported features continue to evolve: NVIDIA Tensor Cores began with FP16 matrix multiplication, later generations added TF32 and broader integer support, and Ampere added acceleration for 2:4 structured sparsity [@nvidia_tensors_fp16_2017; @NVIDIA2020].

:::

Co-design explains why model compression techniques deliver real speedups. Quantization shows why converting FP32 to INT8\index{Quantization!INT8 co-design} accelerates execution on supported hardware: reduced precision cuts memory traffic, while specialized arithmetic units execute more low-precision operations per cycle than FP32 equivalents [@NVIDIA2020]. Structured pruning\index{Structured pruning!hardware alignment} improves performance when it produces smaller dense shapes or a sparsity pattern recognized by silicon, whereas arbitrary unstructured sparsity incurs metadata handling and non-coalesced memory accesses that often erase theoretical gains. Evaluating accelerator performance requires tracing this path from workload to silicon: compute primitives, memory hierarchies, roofline diagnosis, mapping and dataflow, and compiler scheduling. The recurring question is why algorithmic improvements frequently fail to deliver proportional end-to-end speedups. Amdahl's law (principle \ref{pri-amdahl}) already answered it for model-side optimizations, since whatever an optimization leaves untouched caps the overall gain. The same bound governs hardware. The theorem below applies the principle to an accelerator, and the only new quantity is the gain, which becomes the accelerator's path gain $\AcceleratorGain$.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Quantization and its effect on weight payload, memory traffic, and compute cost are established in @sec-model-compression-quantization-precision-cd46.
:::

::: {#thrm-hw-acceleration-fundamental-limit-acceleration-amdahls-law .callout-theorem title="The fundamental limit of acceleration (Amdahl's law)"}

Hardware acceleration *does not speed up the entire system*; it speeds only the baseline-time fraction using the accelerated path. For that fraction $\ParallelFraction$ and path gain $\AcceleratorGain$, **Amdahl's law**\index{Amdahl's law!definition}\index{Parallel Computing!Amdahl's Law} [@amdahl1967] gives the bound in @eq-amdahl.
$$ \text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1 - \ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\AcceleratorGain}} $$ {#eq-amdahl}

*   **Accelerated fraction**\index{Parallel fraction!accelerated path} ($\ParallelFraction$): Share of baseline time receiving the stated gain, often in matrix multiplication or another supported kernel.
*   **Accelerator gain**\index{Accelerator gain!definition} ($\AcceleratorGain$): The raw speed advantage of the GPU or Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) over the CPU for the accelerated portion of the workload.
*   **Unaccelerated fraction**\index{Serial fraction!Amdahl bottleneck} ($1-\ParallelFraction$): Work outside the chosen path, such as data loading, host overhead, unsupported operators, and kernel launch latency\index{Kernel Launch Latency!serial overhead}.

**Pitfall**: *Unaccelerated work caps total speedup.* If 10 percent of baseline time is unaffected ($\ParallelFraction=0.9$), even infinite path gain ($\AcceleratorGain=\infty$) yields at most 10$\times$ overall. Once the accelerated component is fast enough, unaffected work dominates.

:::

Hardware acceleration targets specific terms in the iron law of ML systems\index{Iron law of ML systems!hardware acceleration}, which decomposes end-to-end time into data movement $(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)$, computation $(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))$, and fixed latency $(\Latency)$. Data selection reduced the number of samples processed ($\text{Samples/Task}$, shrinking both $\Operations$ and input traffic $\DataVolume$), and model compression reduced the operations and bytes per sample ($\text{FLOPs/Sample}$ and weight traffic $\DataVolume$). Hardware acceleration instead reduces the realized time per operation ($\text{Seconds/FLOP}$) by improving $\PeakRate$, $\EfficiencyHw$, and $\Bandwidth$. Which of these physical terms an upgrade actually improves determines its accelerated fraction under Amdahl's law.[^fn-amdahls-law-acceleration]

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The decomposition of execution time into data, compute, and latency terms is established in @sec-introduction-iron-law-ml-systems-c32a.
:::

[^fn-amdahls-law-acceleration]: **Amdahl's law**\index{Amdahl's law!acceleration ceiling}: Maps onto the iron law only after the proposed change is specified. If a faster tensor unit reduces the computation term $(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))$ but leaves data transfer and fixed latency unchanged, those unaffected terms bound total speedup. A different accelerator or memory system may improve bandwidth as well. The unaccelerated fraction is therefore defined by the intervention, not by a permanent classification of each term as serial.

This dynamic explains why hardware upgrades frequently fail to produce proportional end-to-end speedups. @Fig-iron-law-heatmap maps system speedup across accelerator gain ($\AcceleratorGain$) and accelerated fraction ($\ParallelFraction$), charting where those returns diminish\index{Amdahl's law!diminishing returns}. Where the unaccelerated fraction $1-\ParallelFraction$ remains substantial, the white contour curves flatten horizontally into the unaccelerated-bound regime, bounding total speedup at the $1/(1-\ParallelFraction)$ asymptote regardless of how far $\AcceleratorGain$ scales along the horizontal axis. Because $\ParallelFraction$ differs substantially across workload archetypes running on identical hardware, a workload's vertical position on this map determines whether an accelerator investment pays off or stalls on non-matrix operations.

::: {#fig-iron-law-heatmap fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Iron Law Heatmap**: Total system speedup as a function of accelerator gain ($\AcceleratorGain$) and accelerated fraction ($\ParallelFraction$). High speedup appears only near the top-right corner, where both accelerator gain and accelerated fraction are high. At $\ParallelFraction=0.9$, for example, even an infinite gain on the accelerated path cannot exceed 10$\times$ end-to-end speedup. Contours span roughly 1$\times$–200$\times$ speedup." fig-alt="Heatmap of speedup vs. accelerator gain and accelerated fraction. High speedup in red and orange appears near the top-right corner where the accelerated fraction is near 1.0 and accelerator gain is high; lower-fraction regions remain blue. White contour lines labeled 2x to 50x follow the lower bands, a colorbar at the right labels every band from 1x to 500x, and text labels mark a High Accelerated Fraction region above and an Unaccelerated Bound region below."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IRON LAW HEATMAP (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-iron-law-heatmap—Amdahl's Law and Acceleration Wall
# │
# │ Goal: Visualize speedup = 1/((1-p)+p/S) as function of S and p; show
# │       diminishing returns when parallel fraction is low.
# │ Show: Contour heatmap; High Accelerated Fraction vs Unaccelerated Bound regions.
# │ How: meshgrid S, P; contourf with LogNorm; book_style.setup_plot().
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Visualize speedup = 1/((1-p)+p/G_accel) as function of accelerator gain and p; show
import sys
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style
from mlsysim.physics import calc_amdahls_speedup

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(5.8, 4.2))

# =============================================================================
# PLOT: The Iron Law Heatmap
# =============================================================================
g_accel_vals = np.logspace(0, 3, 100)
p_vals = np.linspace(0.8, 0.999, 100)
g_accel_grid, p_grid = np.meshgrid(g_accel_vals, p_vals)
overall_speedup = np.vectorize(calc_amdahls_speedup)(p_grid, g_accel_grid)

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
levels = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500]
norm = mcolors.LogNorm(vmin=1, vmax=500)

cf = ax.contourf(g_accel_grid, p_grid, overall_speedup, levels=levels, cmap='RdYlBu_r', norm=norm, alpha=0.8)
# Inline labels only where contours have room; the 100x and 200x contours crowd
# into the top sliver of the linear f axis, so the colorbar labels every band.
# The labeled levels get their own contour set: clabel(levels=..., manual=...)
# on a larger set raises IndexError in matplotlib 3.8 to 3.10.
ax.contour(g_accel_grid, p_grid, overall_speedup, levels=[levels[0]] + levels[6:], colors='white', linewidths=0.8, alpha=0.6)
cs = ax.contour(g_accel_grid, p_grid, overall_speedup, levels=levels[1:6], colors='white', linewidths=0.8, alpha=0.6)
ax.clabel(
    cs,
    inline=1,
    fontsize=9,
    fmt='%gx',
    colors='black',
    manual=[(2.43, 0.85), (9, 0.9), (31, 0.93), (700, 0.951), (150, 0.9866)],
)
cbar = fig.colorbar(cf, ax=ax, ticks=levels, pad=0.02, fraction=0.05)
cbar.ax.set_yticklabels([f"{v:g}×" for v in levels])
cbar.set_label("Overall speedup")

ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel(r'Accelerator gain ($G_{\mathrm{accel}}$)')
ax.set_ylabel(r'Accelerated fraction ($f_{\mathrm{parallel}}$)')

ax.text(
    100,
    0.975,
    "High Accelerated Fraction",
    color='black',
    ha='center',
    va='top',
    fontweight='bold',
    fontsize=9,
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)
ax.text(
    100,
    0.82,
    "Unaccelerated Bound",
    color='white',
    ha='center',
    va='bottom',
    fontweight='bold',
    fontsize=9,
    bbox=dict(facecolor='black', alpha=0.6, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)
plt.show()
plt.close()

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

:::

::: {#chk-hw-acceleration-parallelism-gate .callout-checkpoint title="The parallelism gate"}

These checks turn Amdahl's bound into a hardware-selection test.

**Amdahl's reality**

- [ ] **Serial bottlenecks**: use Amdahl's bound to explain why a 1,000$\times$ faster GPU may only speed up training by 5$\times$ when data loading is slow.
- [ ] **Speedup ceiling**: for $\ParallelFraction=0.95$ and $\AcceleratorGain=100$, estimate total speedup and compare it with the infinite-accelerator ceiling.
- [ ] **Workload variation**: what baseline profiling would establish the ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50!compute-bound workload} and MobileNet accelerated fractions for a proposed hardware change? Explain how those fractions would determine which benefits more.

:::

The serial bottleneck becomes concrete on real hardware, where the same accelerator that nears its parallel ceiling on one workload can stall on another. The comparison below uses the INT8 (8-bit integer) path, whose advantage over FP32 or FP16 has two sources. Each operand occupies a half or a quarter of the bytes, and an 8-bit multiplier occupies far less silicon area than a floating-point one, so the same die holds more multiply-accumulate (MAC) units. Two workloads on an NVIDIA H100 with different unaccelerated fractions show how that fraction governs whether this peak INT8 advantage becomes realized speedup. A second look at the decode case then separates that limit from a different one, bandwidth-boundedness.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Order-of-magnitude throughput, bandwidth, and capacity for each accelerator class are collected for reference in @sec-appdx-machine-foundations-ai-hardware-cheat-sheet-modern-reference-4dc1.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: amdahl-h_h100-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AMDAHL'S LAW ON H100
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Amdahl's Law on H100" lighthouse callout
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the limits of parallel speedup on H100.
# │ Show: Why ResNet achieves 20× speedup while GPT-2 is capped at 5×.
# │ How: Apply Amdahl's Law with different parallelizable fractions (95% vs 80%).
# │      Then re-evaluate GPT-2 decode with a bandwidth-set path gain, to keep
# │      memory-boundedness (shrinks G_accel) distinct from the serial fraction.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_ops_rate, fmt_ratio, check

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class AmdahlH100:
    """
    Namespace for Amdahl's Law on H100.
    Scenario: Comparing speedup for a 5% vs 20% unaccelerated fraction (ResNet vs GPT-2).
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # H100 INT8 peak against an assumed 8 TOPS server CPU; 95% (ResNet-50) and
    # 80% (GPT-2 decode) of baseline time on the accelerated path.
    resnet = Scenarios.ResNet50InferenceH100OverServerCpu
    gpt2 = Scenarios.Gpt2DecodeH100OverServerCpu
    gpt2_bw = Scenarios.Gpt2DecodeH100OverServerCpuBandwidth  # path gain set by bandwidth
    cpu_int8_tops = resnet.baseline_rate  # scenario assumption: baseline server-CPU INT8 throughput
    p_resnet = resnet.fraction
    p_gpt2 = gpt2.fraction

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Amdahl's Law: Speedup = 1 / ((1-p) + (p/G_accel))
    hw_speedup_factor = resnet.gain
    speedup_resnet = resnet.speedup
    speedup_gpt2 = gpt2.speedup

    # Step 1: Theoretical ceiling (if accelerator gain tends to infinity)
    ceiling_gpt2 = gpt2.ceiling

    # Step 2: Decode is memory bound, so its path gain is the bandwidth ratio
    bw_gain = gpt2_bw.gain
    speedup_gpt2_bw = gpt2_bw.speedup

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(speedup_resnet >= speedup_gpt2 * 3, f"ResNet speedup ({speedup_resnet:.1f}x) should be much higher than GPT-2 ({speedup_gpt2:.1f}x).")
    check(speedup_gpt2 <= ceiling_gpt2, "Speedup cannot exceed theoretical ceiling.")
    check(bw_gain < hw_speedup_factor, "Bandwidth gain should be well below the INT8 compute ratio.")
    check(speedup_gpt2_bw < speedup_gpt2, "A smaller path gain must lower the bound.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Hardware context
    h100_int8_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["int8"], unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=False)
    cpu_int8_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(cpu_int8_tops, unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=False)
    hw_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(hw_speedup_factor), precision=0, commas=False)
    hw_speedup_factor_str = fmt_int(hw_speedup_factor, commas=False)

    # ResNet
    p_resnet_str = fmt(p_resnet, precision=2, commas=False)
    p_resnet_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_resnet, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    serial_resnet_str = fmt(1 - p_resnet, precision=2, commas=False)
    serial_resnet_pct_str = fmt_percent(1 - p_resnet, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    p_resnet_over_accel_str = fmt_ratio(p_resnet / hw_speedup_factor, precision=4, commas=False)
    amdahl_resnet_str = fmt(speedup_resnet, precision=1, commas=False)
    amdahl_resnet_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup_resnet, precision=1, commas=False)

    # GPT-2
    p_gpt2_str = fmt(p_gpt2, precision=2, commas=False)
    serial_gpt2_str = fmt(1 - p_gpt2, precision=2, commas=False)
    serial_gpt2_pct_str = fmt_percent(1 - p_gpt2, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    p_gpt2_over_accel_str = fmt_ratio(p_gpt2 / hw_speedup_factor, precision=4, commas=False)
    amdahl_gpt2_str = fmt(speedup_gpt2, precision=1, commas=False)
    amdahl_gpt2_ceiling_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ceiling_gpt2, precision=0, commas=False)
    amdahl_gpt2_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup_gpt2, precision=1, commas=False)
    bw_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(bw_gain), precision=0, commas=False)
    amdahl_gpt2_bw_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup_gpt2_bw, precision=1, commas=False)

    resnet_speedup_eq_math = fmt_math(
        rf"\text{{Speedup}} = \frac{{1}}{{(1-{p_resnet_str}) + \frac{{{p_resnet_str}}}{{{hw_speedup_factor_str}}}}} "
        rf"= \frac{{1}}{{{serial_resnet_str} + {p_resnet_over_accel_str}}} "
        rf"\approx {amdahl_resnet_str}\times"
    )
    gpt2_speedup_eq_math = fmt_math(
        rf"\text{{Speedup}} = \frac{{1}}{{(1-{p_gpt2_str}) + \frac{{{p_gpt2_str}}}{{{hw_speedup_factor_str}}}}} "
        rf"= \frac{{1}}{{{serial_gpt2_str} + {p_gpt2_over_accel_str}}} "
        rf"\approx {amdahl_gpt2_str}\times"
    )
```

::: {#lhs-amdahl-h_h100 .callout-lighthouse title="An illustrative Amdahl budget on H100"}

**Illustrative ResNet-50 inference on NVIDIA H100**:

- Assume H100 provides $\AcceleratorGain$ = `{python} AmdahlH100.hw_speedup_mult_str` on matrix multiplication relative to a server CPU without matrix extensions (`{python} AmdahlH100.h100_int8_tops_str` INT8 vs. ~`{python} AmdahlH100.cpu_int8_tops_str`) [@choquette2023]. The CPU's INT8 rate is a scenario assumption for this budget, not the FP32 peak of the reference CPU used elsewhere in the chapter.
- Assume $\ParallelFraction$ = `{python} AmdahlH100.p_resnet_str`: `{python} AmdahlH100.p_resnet_pct_str` of baseline time receives that gain, while `{python} AmdahlH100.serial_resnet_pct_str` remains in data loading, preprocessing, postprocessing, and other work.
$$
\text{`{python} AmdahlH100.resnet_speedup_eq_math`}
$$
The `{python} AmdahlH100.hw_speedup_mult_str` path gain produces only `{python} AmdahlH100.amdahl_resnet_speedup_mult_str` end-to-end speedup because the `{python} AmdahlH100.serial_resnet_pct_str` unaffected fraction sets the ceiling.

**Contrast with GPT-2 (autoregressive)**:

- For GPT-2 token generation, assume $\ParallelFraction$ = `{python} AmdahlH100.p_gpt2_str`; the remaining `{python} AmdahlH100.serial_gpt2_pct_str` includes host overhead, sampling, and decoding work outside the accelerated matrix path.
$$
\text{`{python} AmdahlH100.gpt2_speedup_eq_math`}
$$
Less token-generation time receives the assumed gain, so even an infinite path gain yields at most $1/(1-\ParallelFraction)$ = `{python} AmdahlH100.amdahl_gpt2_ceiling_speedup_mult_str`.

This calculation still overstates the decode path gain. Decode is bandwidth bound, so its accelerated path runs at the rate weights stream from memory rather than at the INT8 TOPS rate. The relevant ratio is the H100's memory bandwidth over the reference CPU socket's, `{python} AmdahlH100.bw_gain_mult_str` (a different path from the host-DRAM link used below). INT8 helps decode on either machine by halving the bytes each weight occupies relative to FP16, not by multiplying faster. With that gain the bound falls from `{python} AmdahlH100.amdahl_gpt2_speedup_mult_str` to `{python} AmdahlH100.amdahl_gpt2_bw_speedup_mult_str`, barely moving, because the unaccelerated fraction already dominates. Two distinct limits are at work. Bandwidth-boundedness shrinks $\AcceleratorGain$, whereas the unaccelerated fraction caps what any $\AcceleratorGain$ can deliver. Serving optimizations attack both. Batching raises the work done per weight byte fetched. Speculative decoding, developed in @sec-model-serving, lets a small draft model propose several tokens that the full model then verifies in one step, reducing the number of sequential full-model steps.

:::

Whether an operation is limited by compute rate or by data movement dictates both hardware selection and software optimization. Under the arithmetic intensity law (principle \ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}), upgrading to an accelerator with $10\times$ higher peak compute yields negligible speedup if data delivery is the binding bottleneck. The roofline model\index{Roofline model!hardware diagnosis}, previewed in @sec-ml-systems-matching-workloads-hardware-bf91, makes this diagnosis [@williams2009]. It compares an operation's arithmetic intensity\index{Arithmetic intensity!roofline diagnostic}, the ratio of operations to bytes of memory traffic (FLOP/byte), with the hardware's ridge point. An operation below the ridge is bandwidth bound, the regime the roofline literature calls *memory bound*; an operation above it is compute bound. GPT-2 decode and ResNet-50 sit on opposite sides of that line, a difference the Amdahl budget above already registered in the decode path gain. @Sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff turns the classification into numbers once the compute units and memory systems that set the two ceilings have been examined.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The arithmetic-intensity spectrum that separates the workload signatures of the major architectures is established in @sec-network-architectures-understanding-arithmetic-intensity-ade5.
:::

The chapter builds the machine from the bottom up (@tbl-hw-acceleration-chapter-spine). Compute primitives and compute units supply the arithmetic side of the anatomy, ending with the INT8 and sparse paths that ResNet-50's profile depends on, and memory systems supply the other side, from registers to host memory. Performance bounds then combine the two into the roofline's ceilings and show which ResNet-50 layers clear the H100's ridge at FP16 and which fall below it at INT8; this is the chapter's midpoint, marked by a checkpoint. The second half asks how software reaches those ceilings, through hardware mapping and then the compilers and runtimes that make its choices automatically. Three shorter sections widen the view to work beyond one accelerator, heterogeneous systems-on-chip, and the choice of an accelerator for a workload and a budget.

| **Section**                  | **Part of the accelerator**       | **Question it answers**                                               | **ResNet-50 INT8 thread**                             |
|:-----------------------------|:----------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| **Hardware Specialization**  | The whole chip                    | Why silicon is specialized for tensor work, and what a byte costs     | Why its convolutions justify dedicated matrix silicon |
| **Compute Primitives**       | Operations the hardware executes  | Which operation classes earn dedicated units                          | Its convolutions lower to matrix multiplication       |
| **Compute Units**            | Vector, matrix, and special units | How each unit executes its primitive, including INT8 and sparse paths | The INT8 tensor path and its arithmetic floor         |
| **Memory Systems**           | Registers through host memory     | Where operands live and what each tier costs                          | One activation tile's trip from HBM to registers      |
| **Performance Bounds**       | Compute and bandwidth ceilings    | Which ceiling binds a given kernel                                    | Which layers clear the FP16 and INT8 ridge points     |
| **Hardware Mapping**         | Placement, dataflow, and tiling   | Which schedule captures the available reuse                           | Weight-stationary tiles and fused epilogues           |
| **Compilers and Runtimes**   | Software that lowers the graph    | Who makes the mapping decisions, and when                             | Naive versus compiled latency                         |
| **Beyond One Accelerator**   | Links between accelerators        | What changes when one accelerator is not enough                       | Awareness only; ResNet-50 fits one accelerator        |
| **Heterogeneous SoC Design** | Phone and embedded chips          | How shared memory and power budgets change the mapping                | MobileNetV2 and KWS take over                         |
| **Choosing an Accelerator**  | The complete system               | Which machine fits a workload, a latency target, and a budget         | Energy and cost per request                           |

: **Chapter Map**: Each section supplies one part of the accelerator's anatomy and follows the chapter's INT8 ResNet-50 workload into it; the first five sections build the machine and its ceilings, and the remaining sections ask how software and system choices reach them. {#tbl-hw-acceleration-chapter-spine tbl-colwidths="[22,22,32,24]"}

The first stage of the accelerator's anatomy begins with a simpler question: why build specialized silicon for tensor math at all, rather than running those operations on general-purpose processors?

## Hardware Specialization {#sec-hardware-acceleration-evolution-hardware-specialization-fdb7}

General-purpose processors dedicate substantial silicon area and power to instruction fetch, branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and cache coherence, machinery built for arbitrary control flow that yields poor arithmetic density on regular, dense linear algebra. When Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit (TPU v1) into production data centers alongside contemporary CPUs and NVIDIA K80 GPUs, stripping away that general-purpose control machinery in favor of a dedicated matrix array produced an immediate efficiency jump (example \ref{exmp-hw-acceleration-tpuv1-vs-k80-efficiency-shock}). Whenever an algorithmic pattern becomes sufficiently dominant and structured, specialized hardware\index{Hardware specialization!evolution} outperforms general-purpose platforms by replacing dynamic control hardware with dense arithmetic arrays and software-managed data movement.

::: {#exmp-hw-acceleration-tpuv1-vs-k80-efficiency-shock .callout-example title="The TPU v1 vs. K80 efficiency gap"}

**Scenario**: In 2015, Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit (TPU v1) into production data centers, comparing its throughput and energy efficiency against general-purpose NVIDIA K80 GPUs [@jouppi2017].

**Diagnosis**: The K80 was a programmable GPU designed to support a broader mix of graphics and compute workloads. The TPU v1 domain-specific architecture (DSA) made a narrower, inference-focused design choice, pairing a large 8-bit systolic matrix unit with software-managed memory and simpler control.

**Systems lesson**: On the six Google inference workloads and contemporary CPU/GPU baselines evaluated in the TPU paper, tailoring silicon to the dominant matrix operations delivered 15–30$\times$ higher throughput and 30–80$\times$ better performance per watt [@jouppi2017]. Those ratios describe the evaluated systems, not every workload.

:::

In D·A·M terms, this efficiency gain stems from tailoring machine resources to algorithmic structure. The TPU[^fn-tpu-google-origin] replaced hardware caches with software-managed buffers and routed data directly between neighboring arithmetic units, raising data reuse and cutting off-chip traffic. The cost is rigidity. Irregular memory access, dynamic control flow, or an unsupported numeric precision stalls a fixed-function data path and leaves expensive silicon idle. Every modern ML accelerator, from DianNao-class designs [@chen2014diannao] to GPUs with Tensor Cores, strikes its own balance between specialization and flexibility, following a pattern that began decades before deep learning.

[^fn-tpu-google-origin]: **TPU (tensor processing unit)**\index{TPU!origin}: The first TPU made a deliberately narrow design choice, centering the design on a single $256{\times}256$ systolic array for 8-bit matrix multiplication and avoiding much of the control machinery required by a general-purpose core [@jouppi2017]. That trade buys high compute density on dense matrix multiplication at the cost of flexibility. Irregular or branch-heavy code remains a poor fit, and compiler tiling, padding, and layer dimensions determine how fully the array is used.

### Specialized computing {#sec-hardware-acceleration-specialized-computing-22ce}

On a late-1970s microprocessor without floating-point hardware, a single 32-bit floating-point multiply\index{Floating-point unit!precision bottleneck} required a software routine of dozens of integer shift-and-add instructions, turning scientific and signal-processing loops into an instruction-fetch bottleneck. Hardware specialization emerges whenever one computational pattern becomes a bottleneck that general-purpose processors cannot scale past. The Intel 8087\index{Intel 8087!floating-point coprocessor}\index{Floating-point unit!history} coprocessor (1980) executed floating-point operations directly in hardware [@palmer1980intel8087], and the Intel 486DX (1989) later moved the floating-point unit onto the CPU die itself [@patterson2017hardware]. That cycle—specializing silicon to relieve an acute bottleneck and integrating it once the capability proves universal—recurs in every later era, and so does its limit. Dedicated silicon removes the instruction overhead around a dominant operation, but the overall gain is bounded by how much of the run time that operation occupies.

Graphics supplied the second lesson, throughput over latency. A CPU spends most of its silicon on control logic, branch prediction, and caches that minimize the latency of a single instruction stream, which buys nothing when identical arithmetic must be applied to millions of independent pixels. GPUs\index{GPU!history} reallocated that silicon to dense arrays of arithmetic units, and when unified shader architectures (2006) replaced separate vertex and pixel pipelines with arrays of identical programmable cores, the GPU became a general-purpose parallel processor [@owens2008]. Digital signal processors\index{Digital signal processing!multiply-accumulate units} such as Texas Instruments' TMS32010 (1983) contributed the memory organization. To meet hard real-time deadlines, they replaced caches, whose misses introduce variable latency, with software-managed scratchpads feeding dedicated MAC data paths [@lyons2011understanding]. ML accelerators inherit both lessons.

The payoff arrived in 2012, when AlexNet\index{AlexNet!GPU deep learning era} [@krizhevsky2012imagenet] won the ImageNet competition after training on two consumer GPUs, the co-design result examined in @sec-introduction-deep-learning-era-infrastructure-bottleneck-2f02. Its dense 2D convolutions mapped directly onto thousands of GPU arithmetic lanes. In D·A·M terms, the machine constraint had dictated which algorithms were feasible, and aligning the algorithm's parallel structure with throughput-oriented hardware lifted it.

Across five eras from the 1980s to the 2020s (@fig-timeline), specialization moved from discrete coprocessors such as the Intel 8087 FPU and TMS32010 DSP through graphics engines and dedicated media codecs to deep-learning tensor arrays and wafer-scale hardware. Each era's specialized unit targets a different bottleneck, yet the principles modern accelerators depend on (dedicating silicon to the dominant operation, staging operands in local memory, and minimizing off-chip data movement) were all in place before deep learning arrived.

::: {#fig-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Hardware Specialization Timeline**: Computing architectures evolve through recurring cycles of specialization and integration across five eras. Each era introduces domain-specific hardware to resolve an important memory or arithmetic bottleneck, from off-chip FPUs to GPUs, codecs, and TPU/Tensor Core array units. Many of these capabilities later appear alongside CPUs in broader systems, even when the specialized units remain distinct." fig-alt="Five-column timeline from the 1980s through the 2020s. The columns list floating-point and signal processing (Intel 8087, TMS32010 DSP), 3D graphics and multimedia (early GPUs, GeForce 256), real-time media and network processing (H.264 and MP3 codecs, IXP2800), deep-learning tensor operations (Google TPU v1 and NVIDIA Tensor Cores), and application-specific acceleration (AI engines, SmartNICs, and multi-chip and wafer-scale systems)."}

### Domain-specific architectures {#sec-hardware-acceleration-emergence-domainspecific-architectures-e56e}

A general-purpose CPU core spends most of its energy on instruction fetch and decode, branch prediction, speculative execution, and cache coherence rather than arithmetic: executing one scalar instruction can burn hundreds of picojoules of control overhead just to perform a floating-point operation that costs a few picojoules. For decades, Moore's law\index{Moore's law!slowdown}[^fn-moores-law-scaling] [@moore1998] and Dennard scaling\index{Dennard Scaling!end of} [@dennard1974] hid that overhead by letting operating voltage fall as transistors shrank, so clock frequencies rose at constant power density. When leakage current halted voltage scaling in the mid-2000s, frequencies stalled against the power wall of @sec-ml-systems-deployment-spectrum-71be. Adding more general-purpose cores then ran into Amdahl's law and **dark silicon**\index{Dark Silicon!specialization driver}, the thermal limit under which only a fraction of a chip's transistors can switch at full speed simultaneously [@esmaeilzadeh2011]. As @hennessy2019 argued in their Turing Lecture, the way past this wall is **domain-specific architectures (DSAs)**\index{DSA!definition}\index{DSA!scaling law breakdown}\index{Domain-Specific Architecture|see{DSA}},[^fn-dsa-domain-efficiency] hardware that gives up general-purpose control machinery to spend its power budget directly on the operations a target domain performs.

A DSA wins by specializing every layer of the machine around the workload's invariants. Its data path\index{Data path!customization} is custom-built. Matrix units in AI accelerators are often **systolic arrays**\index{Systolic array!definition}, grid-like networks of processing elements that compute and forward data directly to neighboring units. A value fetched once from on-chip memory is therefore reused across an entire row or column of multiply-accumulate operations instead of returning to a register file after each use. Its memory hierarchy\index{Memory hierarchy!domain-specific} follows the workload's reuse pattern, with software-managed scratchpads and prefetching\index{Prefetching!accelerator optimization} replacing hardware-managed caches for deterministic tensor streams. Its instruction set encodes coarse tensor operations, so one macro-instruction configures thousands of arithmetic units. The same recipe produced smartphone video codecs, genomics aligners, and cryptographic application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)\index{ASIC!flexibility trade-off} wherever a kernel stabilized [@sullivan2012; @turakhia2018darwin; @bedford_taylor2017].

The pressure to specialize has grown because model demand has outrun single-device hardware scaling. The measured trend is the historical training-compute curve charted in @sec-introduction, whose fitted doubling time runs from 3.4 to about 6 months depending on the window, far faster than the roughly two-year doubling of transistor density [@amodei2018ai; @epochai2024compute]. No single chip closes a gap that compounds at that rate; parallelism and co-design must close the rest.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The measured growth of training compute and its doubling time are established in @sec-introduction-efficiency-framework-8dd4.
:::

[^fn-moores-law-scaling]: **Moore's law**\index{Moore's law!ML systems consequence}: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation, revised in 1975, that the number of transistors per chip doubles roughly every two years [@moore1998]. It describes density, not performance; performance tracked density only while Dennard scaling held.

[^fn-dsa-domain-efficiency]: **DSA (domain-specific architecture)**\index{DSA!efficiency trade-off}: A DSA that excels at dense matrix multiplication may perform worse than a CPU on irregular workloads such as graph traversal, so its gain on the target domain must justify the software, compiler, and ecosystem cost of a narrower machine [@hennessy2019; @patterson2017hardware].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cpu-ml-inefficiency
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CPU ML INEFFICIENCY STATISTICS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Machine Learning Hardware Specialization" section
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the inefficiency of general-purpose CPUs for ML.
# │ Show: An illustrative CPU utilization scenario alongside accelerator baselines.
# │ How: Compute delivered GFLOP/s at the upper end of an assumed utilization range.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_ops_rate

class CpuMlInefficiency:
    """CPU vs accelerator efficiency gap for ML workloads."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    cpu_utilization_min_value = 5  # illustrative % of peak
    cpu_utilization_max_value = 10  # illustrative % of peak
    cpu_peak_flops = Hardware.Cloud.ReferenceCPU.compute.peak_flops

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    cpu_delivered_flops = cpu_peak_flops * (cpu_utilization_max_value / 100)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(round(cpu_delivered_flops.to(GFLOP / second).magnitude) == 100, f"Delivered CPU GFLOP/s mismatch: {cpu_delivered_flops}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    cpu_utilization_min_str = fmt_percent(round(cpu_utilization_min_value / 100, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    cpu_utilization_max_str = fmt_percent(round(cpu_utilization_max_value / 100, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    cpu_gflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(cpu_delivered_flops, unit=GFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)

    # A100/V100/Mobile specs for footnote comparison
    a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    v100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(Hardware.Cloud.V100.compute.peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    a100_tf32_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.precision_flops['tf32'], unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    mobile_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(Hardware.Mobile.iPhone15Pro.compute.peak_flops, unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=False)
```

### Machine learning hardware specialization {#sec-hardware-acceleration-machine-learning-hardware-specialization-09c5}

That compounding gap between model demand and transistor scaling turned into an operational crisis at Google in 2013, when an internal projection showed that three minutes of daily voice search per user would require doubling the company's global CPU fleet just to serve neural-network inference (example \ref{exmp-hw-acceleration-google-tpu-voice-search}), the projection that launched the TPU v1 program introduced at the start of this section. Many important neural-network workloads concentrate their arithmetic in regular tensor operations, such as dense matrix multiplications and convolutions, with substantial data parallelism, predictable reuse, and tolerance for reduced precision. Other ML operations remain irregular, bandwidth bound, or too small to fill a wide engine, so an accelerator need not speed up every part of a model. Hardware built to exploit the regular portion forms the class of ML accelerators.

::: {#exmp-hw-acceleration-google-tpu-voice-search .callout-example title="The TPU capacity cliff"}

**Scenario**: Google projected in 2013 that user adoption of voice-search speech recognition (3 minutes/day/user) would require doubling global data center capacity to run CPU-based neural network inference [@jouppi2017].

**Diagnosis**: General-purpose CPU server capacity was economically unable to absorb the exponential growth in inference FLOPs, threatening a capital infrastructure bottleneck.

**Systems lesson**: Custom hardware acceleration becomes a candidate when workload volume makes the existing fleet uneconomical. Workload reuse, supported operations, development cost, and server total cost of ownership determine whether a custom ASIC is preferable to software changes or other hardware.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: ml-accelerator-callout-calc
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_multiple

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class MlAcceleratorCallout:
    """H100 throughput and bandwidth against the host DRAM path for the ML accelerator callout."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_peak_flops = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.peak_flops
    h100_bandwidth = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth
    host_dram_bandwidth = Hardware.Tech.Storage.HostDram.bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    hbm_vs_host_dram = (h100_bandwidth / host_dram_bandwidth).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(h100_peak_flops.to(TFLOP / second).magnitude - 989.0) < 1.0, "H100 peak FLOP/s drifted from 989 TFLOP/s")
    check(abs(h100_bandwidth.to(TB / second).magnitude - 3.35) < 0.05, "H100 memory bandwidth drifted from 3.35 TB/s")
    check(abs(hbm_vs_host_dram - 16.75) < 0.1, "H100 HBM vs host DRAM bandwidth ratio drifted from 16.75x")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bandwidth, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(host_dram_bandwidth, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    hbm_vs_host_dram_mult_str = fmt_multiple(hbm_vs_host_dram, precision=1, commas=False)
```

The fleet projection exposed how little of a CPU's rated throughput survives on dense tensor layers. Take the chapter's reference CPU, the low end of the 1–2 TFLOP/s baseline used in the definition of hardware acceleration, and assume it sustains `{python} CpuMlInefficiency.cpu_utilization_min_str`–`{python} CpuMlInefficiency.cpu_utilization_max_str` of its peak on a neural network workload. The upper endpoint then delivers approximately `{python} CpuMlInefficiency.cpu_gflop_per_s_str` (billions of floating-point operations per second). CPUs optimize for single-thread performance and irregular memory access, whereas neural networks require extensive parallelism and predictable data streams, and a single layer that touches gigabytes of parameters overwhelms cache hierarchies designed for smaller working sets.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: energy-gap-anchor-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ENERGY GAP ANCHOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The chapter's single canonical movement-vs-arithmetic energy ratio
# │
# │ Goal: State one DRAM-vs-arithmetic ratio and reuse it everywhere.
# │ Show: A 32-bit DRAM access vs. one FP32 multiply (Horowitz 45 nm), the same
# │       pair @tbl-energy-movement-cost normalizes to.
# │ How: Divide registry per-event energies.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import pJ, flop
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_energy, fmt_multiple

class EnergyGapAnchor:
    """Canonical DRAM-access vs. FP32-multiply energy ratio for this chapter."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    dram_access = Hardware.Tech.Memory.DRAM.energy_per_access
    fp32_mul = Hardware.Tech.Op.FlopFp32.energy

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    dram_vs_fp32 = dram_access.to(pJ).magnitude / fp32_mul.to(pJ / flop).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(100 < dram_vs_fp32 < 1000, "Prose calls the gap roughly two orders of magnitude.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    dram_pj_str = fmt_energy(dram_access, unit=pJ, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp32_mul_pj_str = fmt_energy(fp32_mul * flop, unit=pJ, precision=1, commas=False)
    dram_vs_fp32_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(dram_vs_fp32), precision=0, commas=False)
```

The deeper mismatch is energy\index{Energy!data movement cost}. Per event, accessing a 32-bit value from DRAM costs about `{python} EnergyGapAnchor.dram_pj_str` in the 45 nm estimates of @horowitz2014, roughly `{python} EnergyGapAnchor.dram_vs_fp32_mult_str` the `{python} EnergyGapAnchor.fp32_mul_pj_str` of one FP32 multiply, the same ratio @tbl-energy-movement-cost reported for the data pipeline. The roughly 145-fold gap quoted with the iron law in @sec-introduction-iron-law-ml-systems-c32a comes from the same table but compared one DRAM byte, a quarter of this 32-bit access, with one FP16 operation. Exact values vary by technology node and design, but a gap of two orders of magnitude, the energy-movement principle (\ref{pri-energy-movement}), makes data movement a primary optimization target [@sze2017]. Purpose-built accelerators such as TPUs sustain high utilization on dense kernels because systolic arrays and similar structures maximize data reuse while minimizing movement.

Data access can dominate the energy budget of a memory-intensive kernel.[^fn-von-neumann-bottleneck] On a logarithmic scale, representative 45 nm operation energies span more than four orders of magnitude, from an INT8 addition ($0.03\text{ pJ}$) and an FP32 multiply ($3.7\text{ pJ}$) to an off-chip DRAM fetch ($640\text{ pJ}$) (@fig-energy-hierarchy). This ladder is the chapter's single reference for what moving a value costs; later sections cite it rather than restate it.

[^fn-von-neumann-bottleneck]: **Von Neumann bottleneck**\index{Von Neumann bottleneck!ML accelerator constraint}: Separating storage from compute requires instructions and data to cross interfaces rather than remain in local registers. The exact cost of each crossing changes with technology and operation, but locality remains a first-order design concern.

::: {#fig-energy-hierarchy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Energy Hierarchy**: Representative 45 nm energy estimates on a logarithmic scale from @horowitz2014. An off-chip DRAM access costs about 173$\times$ an FP32 multiply and about 128$\times$ a read from an 8 KB SRAM array in this model; a small, register-adjacent L1 access (about 0.5 pJ in the registry used elsewhere in this chapter) is cheaper still. The values are not universal device specifications; they illustrate why reuse in registers and SRAM can matter more than reducing arithmetic count alone." fig-alt="Log-scale horizontal bar chart of representative 45-nanometer energy estimates. INT8 addition is 0.03 pJ, FP32 addition is 0.9 pJ, FP32 multiplication is 3.7 pJ, an 8 KB SRAM read is 5 pJ, and a DRAM read is 640 pJ. An arrow from the SRAM bar to the DRAM bar marks an approximately 128-fold difference."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ENERGY HIERARCHY (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-energy-hierarchy—Horowitz Numbers and Von Neumann bottleneck
# │
# │ Goal: Visualize energy cost per operation (INT8 add to DRAM read); show
# │       ~128× gap between an 8 KB SRAM read and DRAM that drives locality optimization.
# │ Show: Horizontal bar chart; log scale; "~128× Cost" annotation.
# │ How: Hardware.Tech.Op / Hardware.Tech.Memory (Horowitz 2014, 45 nm); barh.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Visualize energy cost per operation (INT8 add to DRAM read); show
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 4.5))

# =============================================================================
# DATA: Horowitz Numbers (Hardware.Tech, 45 nm)
# =============================================================================

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.core.units import pJ, flop

_op, _mem = Hardware.Tech.Op, Hardware.Tech.Memory
ENERGY_DATA = [
    ('INT8 Add', _op.AddInt8.energy.to(pJ / flop).magnitude),
    ('FP32 Add', _op.AddFp32.energy.to(pJ / flop).magnitude),
    ('FP32 Mult', _op.FlopFp32.energy.to(pJ / flop).magnitude),
    ('SRAM Read (8 KB)', _mem.SRAM_8KB.energy_per_access.to(pJ).magnitude),
    ('DRAM Read', _mem.DRAM.energy_per_access.to(pJ).magnitude),
]
ops = [name for name, _ in ENERGY_DATA]
energy = [e for _, e in ENERGY_DATA]
sram_pj, dram_pj = energy[3], energy[4]

# =============================================================================
# PLOT: The Energy Hierarchy
# =============================================================================
colors = [COLORS['GreenLine'], COLORS['BlueLine'], COLORS['BlueLine'], COLORS['OrangeLine'], COLORS['RedLine']]
y_pos = np.arange(len(ops))

ax.barh(y_pos, energy, color=colors, alpha=0.8)
ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
ax.set_yticklabels(ops)
ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Energy per Operation (picojoules) [Log Scale]')
ax.set_xlim(0.01, 2100)

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for i, v in enumerate(energy):
    ax.text(
        v * 1.1,
        i,
        f"{v:g} pJ",
        va='center',
        fontsize=9,
        fontweight='bold',
        color=COLORS['primary'],
        bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
    )

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.annotate("", xy=(dram_pj, 3), xytext=(20, 3), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=1.5))
ax.text(
    115,
    3.12,
    f"~{dram_pj / sram_pj:.0f}× Cost (The Memory Wall)",
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    ha='center',
    va='bottom',
    fontsize=9,
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

Training and inference\index{Training vs. Inference!accelerator design} load an accelerator differently. Training computes gradients, typically in mixed precision with lower-precision tensor operations and higher-precision accumulation\index{FP16!training precision}\index{FP32!gradient computation} [@micikevicius2017mixed], and backpropagation\index{Backpropagation!memory requirements} retains or recomputes activations, raising memory demand. Inference requires only the forward path and may use INT8 or INT4 when the model and kernels support it. The service objective, whether tail latency, throughput, cost, or energy, then decides which accelerator fits.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The activation memory that backpropagation must retain is established in @sec-model-training-activation-memory-requirements-f44c.
:::

::: {#dfn-hw-acceleration-ml-accelerator .callout-definition title="ML accelerator"}

***Machine Learning Accelerators***\index{ML Accelerator!definition}\index{Accelerator!ML} are processors or specialized units designed primarily for common neural-network tensor operations and dataflows. They pursue high $\PeakRate$ and data reuse on matching workloads by devoting more resources to arithmetic and local data movement than a general-purpose execution path can.

1.  **Significance**: An ML accelerator's defining feature is not raw arithmetic alone but a balanced path that supplies operands and retains reusable values nearby. The H100 provides `{python} MlAcceleratorCallout.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` of device-memory bandwidth, about `{python} MlAcceleratorCallout.hbm_vs_host_dram_mult_str` the illustrative `{python} MlAcceleratorCallout.host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str` host-DRAM path used here [@choquette2023]. This is a ceiling comparison, not a guarantee: sufficient arithmetic intensity, concurrency, and reuse are still required to approach its `{python} MlAcceleratorCallout.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` dense FP16/BF16 peak.
2.  **Distinction**: The gains are conditional on operation support, parallel work, regular data access, and a software stack that selects the intended path. An ML accelerator can be orders of magnitude faster than a reference CPU on large dense matrix multiplication, yet lose much of that advantage on small, irregular, synchronization-heavy, or control-heavy workloads. Transfers and unsupported operators can dominate even when the accelerated kernel itself is fast.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that ML accelerators always accelerate ML. Approaching peak throughput requires a compatible precision, operation shape, layout, and enough parallel work to keep the relevant units busy, and memory and interconnect paths must sustain that work. A batch-1 autoregressive request may therefore use only a small fraction of a large training accelerator's arithmetic capacity even though the same device performs well on batched prefill or training.

:::

Deployment context decides which constraint binds. In data centers it is often time-to-result for training large models. An NVIDIA H100\index{NVIDIA!H100} trades hundreds of watts of power for high throughput [@choquette2023], and Google's TPU v4\index{TPU!data center integration} makes a similar trade through systolic arrays and high-bandwidth memory [@jouppi2023]; whether either lowers total cost depends on utilization, rental price, workload scaling, and the electricity rate.

At the edge, the priority shifts toward energy per inference and hard latency or power limits. A smartphone camera or always-on audio path inside a few-watt budget cannot adopt a data center memory system, so edge architectures reduce movement through local scratchpads, tight integration, and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. Because the binding constraint differs by setting, no single architecture dominates, yet the memory wall governs both. Data center chips buy capacity and bandwidth with HBM, while edge chips depend on proximity and reuse.

::: {#chk-hw-acceleration-accelerator-gate .callout-checkpoint title="The accelerator gate"}

The energy hierarchy decides when specialization pays.

**Energy hierarchy**

- [ ] **Data movement cost**: explain why a DRAM access costs about two orders of magnitude more energy than the FP32 multiply that consumes its operand?
- [ ] **Architectural response**: why would keeping and reusing operands near arithmetic units reduce movement energy? Use this prediction when the following sections develop systolic arrays and Tensor Cores.

**Selection logic**\index{Selection logic!definition}

- [ ] **Training vs. inference**: how do training and inference objectives affect precision, memory capacity, bandwidth, and latency requirements? Explain why both phases can need high memory bandwidth.

:::

### The integration bottleneck {#sec-hardware-acceleration-integration-bottleneck-ai-needs-specialized-hardware-0b41}

Packing thousands of multiply-accumulate units onto a die buys nothing if those units spend most cycles stalled waiting for operands to cross the memory hierarchy. Once specialized arrays make arithmetic cheap and abundant [@palmer1980intel8087; @sze2017; @jouppi2017], the dominant hardware difficulty shifts from computing products to feeding the units that compute them. This **integration bottleneck**\index{Integration bottleneck!data movement cost} is the memory wall seen from inside the accelerator: transporting operands and results through the memory hierarchy quickly and efficiently enough to keep thousands of parallel compute units busy. Specialized silicon delivers its performance-per-watt advantage only when the workload's demand concentrates into regular operations that align with the hardware's data paths.

Neural-network kernels make this integration bottleneck tractable because their arithmetic, dataflow, and numerical requirements reinforce one another. Large matrix multiplications and convolutions expose abundant data parallelism that dense processing-element arrays can execute concurrently. Because static or compiled tensor graphs move those operands along predictable paths, compilers can tile and stage transfers into local scratchpads[^fn-scratchpad-sram-memory] instead of relying exclusively on hardware-managed caches. Those staged operands also tolerate reduced precision\index{Quantization!reduced precision tolerance}, allowing supported 8-bit or 4-bit paths to pack more values into each scratchpad and multiply them more densely [@dally2021; @dally2023]. Workloads dominated by dynamic control flow, large embedding tables, small tensors, variable shapes, or strict precision requirements break these assumptions and remain bound by memory latency and irregular access.

[^fn-scratchpad-sram-memory]: **Scratchpad memory**\index{Scratchpad memory!ML advantage}: When a compiler can determine a tensor kernel's access pattern, it can explicitly stage tiles in fast, software-controlled local memory. This avoids some tag, replacement, and coherence machinery, but transfers, synchronization, banking, and capacity must be scheduled correctly. Scratchpads complement rather than universally replace caches because irregular or shared data may still benefit from hardware management. Google's TPU v1, for example, used a 24 MB software-managed Unified Buffer for intermediate activations, while weights and instructions used other paths [@jouppi2017].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: hw-acceleration-hbm-vs-gddr

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HBM VS GDDR6X BANDWIDTH GAP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: footnote fn-hbm-bandwidth-cost in the integration-bottleneck
# │          discussion — quantifies the HBM-over-GDDR6X bandwidth advantage.
# │
# │ Goal: Anchor the HBM vs GDDR6X comparison to registry values instead of
# │       hand-typed ranges (the old 500–700 GB/s GDDR6X figure contradicted
# │       the registry's 760 GB/s).
# │ Show: Device-level HBM range (A100 HBM2e to H100 HBM3), GDDR6X tech-class
# │       bandwidth, and the computed advantage multiple.
# │ How: Read Hardware.Cloud.A100/H100 memory bandwidth and
# │      Hardware.Tech.Memory.GDDR6X.bandwidth; form range and ratio.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty_range, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_multiple_range, check

class HbmVsGddr:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gddr6x_bw = Hardware.Tech.Memory.GDDR6X.bandwidth
    hbm_low = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.bandwidth  # HBM2e device anchor
    hbm_high = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth  # HBM3 device anchor

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    gap_low = (hbm_low / gddr6x_bw).to("").magnitude
    gap_high = (hbm_high / gddr6x_bw).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(2.0 < gap_low < gap_high < 5.0, f"HBM-over-GDDR6X advantage should span roughly 2-5x, got {gap_low:.1f}-{gap_high:.1f}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    hbm_bw_range_str = fmt_qty_range(hbm_low, hbm_high, TB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    gddr6x_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(gddr6x_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    gap_mult_range_str = fmt_multiple_range(gap_low, gap_high, precision=1, commas=False)
```

Because off-chip DRAM transfers\index{DRAM!energy cost} carry that `{python} EnergyGapAnchor.dram_vs_fp32_mult_str` energy penalty over an FP32 multiply, accelerator architects allocate silicon area and thermal budgets to stacked HBM, wide on-chip SRAM, and software-managed scratchpads\index{Scratchpad Memory!accelerator design} rather than packing in additional floating-point logic.[^fn-hbm-bandwidth-cost] Those are the memory tiers drawn in @fig-accelerator-anatomy, and they occupy as much of the design as the arithmetic units they feed.

[^fn-hbm-bandwidth-cost]: **HBM**\index{HBM!bandwidth-cost trade-off}: The A100 and H100 generations provide `{python} HbmVsGddr.hbm_bw_range_str` of device-memory bandwidth through stacked memory and wide interfaces, compared with `{python} HbmVsGddr.gddr6x_bw_str` for the GDDR6X reference used here [@NVIDIA2020; @choquette2023]. Raising the bandwidth ceiling can move some kernels toward the compute-bound side of the roofline, but only if their access pattern and arithmetic intensity can use it. HBM also increases packaging and system cost, so its value depends on the workload's bandwidth demand.

The specialization evident in processing elements, vector pipelines, and tiered scratchpads reflects the computational profile of neural networks, which repeatedly invoke a compact set of linear-algebraic and element-wise primitives. Within the D·A·M framework, an algorithmic change produces a wall-clock speedup only when its computational structure and memory access pattern map onto these primitives; one that cuts theoretical operations without aligning with the hardware's data paths leaves compute units starved. The next section identifies those primitives, beginning with the multiply-accumulate that carries nearly all of ResNet-50's arithmetic.

## Compute Primitives {#sec-hardware-acceleration-ai-compute-primitives-2c99}

A single forward pass through a neural network layer can issue millions or billions of MAC operations\index{NN!dominant MAC pattern}, and executing them one scalar instruction at a time would swamp the processor in instruction-fetch and register-access overhead. Across fully connected, convolutional, and attention layers, learned linear transformations reduce to these repeated MACs, whose regular tensor structure exposes the parallel work and operand reuse that hardware specialization requires. MACs do not dominate every model or phase (normalization, routing, indexing, communication, and element-wise operations can become limiting), but they account for much of the peak arithmetic capacity in modern ML accelerators. Whether they dominate elapsed time still depends on tensor shape, data movement, and the surrounding operators.

The hardware units that exploit these patterns are **AI compute primitives**\index{AI compute primitive!definition}: specialized functional blocks, each optimized for a particular class of operation. Three primitives are especially common in accelerators, each targeting a distinct computational pattern found in neural networks; at the framework level, a single declarative statement encapsulates thousands of their arithmetic operations (@lst-dense_layer_def).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: weight-matrix-calc
from mlsysim import MFLOP, flop
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_flops, fmt_time, check
```
