```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: systolic-ops-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SYSTOLIC ARRAY OPERATIONS PER CYCLE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Prose describing systolic array dimensions and throughput
# │
# │ Goal: Calculate the peak throughput of a systolic array.
# │ Show: That a 128×128 array achieves over 16,000 MACs per cycle.
# │ How: Multiply array dimensions to derive total processing element count.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt, fmt_count

class SystolicOpsCalc:
    """Peak MAC throughput of the canonical 128×128 systolic array."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    tpuv4 = Hardware.Cloud.TPUv4  # each matrix unit is a 128 x 128 systolic array
    systolic_dim_value = tpuv4.compute.systolic_array_dim
    tpuv4_bw = tpuv4.memory.bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    systolic_ops_value = tpuv4.compute.systolic_macs_per_cycle

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(systolic_ops_value == 16384, f"Systolic ops mismatch: {systolic_ops_value}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    systolic_dim_str = fmt(systolic_dim_value, precision=0, commas=False)
    systolic_ops_str = fmt_count(systolic_ops_value, label="operation")
    tpuv4_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(tpuv4_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=True)
```

A `{python} SystolicOpsCalc.systolic_dim_str` $\times$ `{python} SystolicOpsCalc.systolic_dim_str` systolic array capable of `{python} SystolicOpsCalc.systolic_ops_str` per cycle requires a continuous operand stream to maintain utilization. On-chip buffers feed activations and weights to the array edges and are replenished from off-chip memory as needed; reuse within the array avoids fetching every operand from HBM each cycle. The TPU v4's `{python} SystolicOpsCalc.tpuv4_bw_gb_per_s_str` HBM2 bandwidth helps sustain this stream, but off-chip bandwidth can still limit models whose working sets and reuse patterns exceed on-chip capacity.

::: {#psp-hw-acceleration-matching-architecture-workload .callout-perspective title="Matching architecture to workload"}

**Challenge**: Systolic arrays must choose which operand to keep stationary in processing-element registers (weights, inputs, or partial sums), and that choice hard-codes the hardware's preference for certain model types. @Sec-hardware-acceleration-dataflow-optimization-strategies-ce52 develops the three options as a general mapping decision.

No single accelerator architecture suits every workload. A chip optimized for weight-stationary dataflow (like early TPUs) excels at convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where filter weights are small and reused across many image patches. That same architecture stalls on large language model (LLM) autoregressive inference at batch size 1, where the entire weight matrix must be read from off-chip memory once per generated token with zero batch reuse. No choice of stationary operand recovers reuse that does not exist; the levers are batching, lower-precision weights, and memory bandwidth.

:::

### Numerics and sparsity on the datapath {#sec-hardware-acceleration-numerics-ai-acceleration-f7be}

Storing weights in INT8 or pruning half of them to zero shrinks a checkpoint on disk. If the accelerator lacks a datapath that multiplies narrow integers or skips zero weights in silicon, however, the runtime must unpack those weights back to dense floating point and executes no faster than the baseline. Number formats and structured sparsity patterns were defined in @sec-model-compression; what turns them into wall-clock speedups—including the ResNet-50 INT8 profile—is the hardware datapath that executes them. Systolic arrays and Tensor Cores often provision higher multiply-accumulate capacity for narrower formats such as FP16, BF16, INT8, and FP8, while halving or quartering the bytes moved per value relative to FP32. That speedup is not automatic: it requires a supported kernel, matching input and accumulation formats, and enough parallel work to keep the narrower datapath full without hitting another bottleneck.

#### Precision trade-offs {#sec-hardware-acceleration-precision-tradeoffs-8fa8}

Lower precision\index{Precision!hardware design parameter} is not free, for the range-and-precision reasons that forced loss scaling in mixed-precision training and that @sec-model-compression-numerical-format-comparison-8fa2 compared format by format. FP16 trades dynamic range for significand bits, BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range at the cost of precision, and INT8 has no exponent at all, so its usable range depends on scale, zero-point, and clipping choices. For the hardware designer, those numerical properties set the silicon cost of each datapath. A narrower format needs a smaller multiplier and moves fewer bytes, but accumulation usually stays wider, as the FP32 accumulator of the Tensor Core instruction in @lst-tensor_core_op shows, so part of the area saved in the multipliers is spent keeping sums accurate.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The software side of mixed-precision training, including loss scaling, is established in @sec-model-training-mixedprecision-training-9218.
:::

Precision support is integrated into execution units and memory paths. SIMD and SIMT lanes may support several scalar formats, while Tensor Cores (@sec-hardware-acceleration-tensor-cores-771f) and systolic units (@sec-hardware-acceleration-systolic-arrays-6fa8) expose architecture-specific input and accumulation combinations. Changing storage alone may reduce bytes without producing the advertised arithmetic speedup, because the model must select a kernel that uses the efficient path. Converting FP32 weights to INT8 cuts weight traffic by 4$\times$. Whether that moves a kernel from bandwidth bound to compute bound depends on the operation's original arithmetic intensity, the ridge point of the accelerator's INT8 path, and the overhead of quantization and dequantization (@eq-dequantize). Tiling and dataflow, not precision itself, determine reuse, while conversion, scaling, or fallback overhead can offset part of the gain. A format is useful only when the kernel and numerical policy can employ it safely.

#### Mixed-precision computing {#sec-hardware-acceleration-mixedprecision-computing-656f}

Modern AI accelerators support mixed-precision execution\index{Mixed-Precision Computing!training and inference}, in which different stages of one computation use different numerical formats. The training recipe (FP16 or BF16 multiplications with FP32 accumulation) [@micikevicius2017mixed; @mellempudi2019mixed] is developed in @sec-model-training-mixedprecision-training-9218, and the inference recipe (INT8 or INT4 weights with selected activations kept wider) in @sec-model-compression-quantization-precision-cd46. The hardware's part is to execute several formats side by side, with an accumulator wide enough for each.

The shift toward precision diversity is evident in the evolution of AI hardware. Early architectures such as NVIDIA Volta provided Tensor Core support only for FP16, whereas later architectures, including Turing and Ampere, added integer formats and then TF32, a hybrid between FP32 and FP16, alongside BF16 [@nvidia_tf32; @nvidia2017gpu; @nvidia2018t4; @NVIDIA2020]. The generation-by-generation list of supported formats belongs with the other dated specifications in @sec-appdx-system-assumptions; the durable observation is the direction of the trend, toward more formats, each narrower than the last.

The precision format used in hardware design has cascading implications across the entire system. Reducing an operand from FP32 to FP16 halves its value bytes. When those values dominate traffic, the reduction can substantially lower movement energy; the full energy budget still includes access counts, arithmetic, and other device activity [@horowitz2014]. Simultaneously, Tensor Cores and systolic arrays can pack more lower-precision multiply-accumulate units into the same silicon area, raising peak throughput [@dally2021; @dally2023]. Lower-precision integer arithmetic also consumes less energy than FP32 in representative technology studies [@horowitz2014], and the inference-focused TPU v1 was built around 8-bit multiply units [@jouppi2017]. Reduced precision can therefore cut value traffic *and* raise the supported compute ceiling at the same time.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ B200 FP4 PEAK THROUGHPUT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: FP8 and FP4 paragraph in
# │          @sec-hardware-acceleration-numerics-ai-acceleration-f7be.
# │
# │ Goal: Surface the H100 FP16 and FP8 peaks and NVIDIA's headline B200 FP4
# │       peak throughput (dense + sparse).
# │ Show: ~9 PFLOP/s dense / ~18 PFLOP/s sparse in FP4 per chip.
# │ How: Read Hardware.Cloud.B200.compute.precision_flops["fp4"] from constants and double
# │      for the sparse case per the constants-file comment.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_percent

class B200FP4Specs:
    """H100 FP16/FP8 peaks and B200 FP4 peak throughput (dense and sparse)."""

    h100_fp16 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    h100_fp8 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["fp8"]
    dense_flops = Hardware.Cloud.B200.compute.precision_flops["fp4"]
    sparse_flops = 2 * dense_flops
    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_fp16, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_fp8_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_fp8, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=True)
    dense_pflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(dense_flops, unit=PFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    sparse_pflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(sparse_flops, unit=PFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Each narrower format raises the arithmetic ceiling again. The H100 advertises `{python} B200FP4Specs.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` on its dense FP16 tensor path and `{python} B200FP4Specs.h100_fp8_tflop_per_s_str` on its FP8 path, an 8-bit floating-point format introduced for training and inference [@choquette2023; @blankevoort2022; @micikevicius2022fp8]. NVIDIA's Blackwell (B200) architecture extends this trajectory with an FP4 tensor datapath (a 4-bit floating-point format that, unlike INT4, spends some of its four bits on an exponent and so trades uniform spacing for range). The datapath is rated at up to `{python} B200FP4Specs.dense_pflop_per_s_str` dense or `{python} B200FP4Specs.sparse_pflop_per_s_str` sparse peak throughput per chip [@nvidia2024blackwell]. Reaching those theoretical ceilings requires numerical representations, kernel implementations, and sparsity patterns that align exactly with the specialized hardware paths. Narrower numerical formats expand the available design space, but numerical stability and dynamic range requirements dictate whether a workload can safely use FP4.

#### N:M structured sparsity mechanics {#sec-hardware-acceleration-nm-structured-sparsity-mechanics-9a71}

The sparse rating in that comparison depends on one more datapath feature, one that skips zeros only when they follow a fixed pattern. While unstructured pruning reduces model parameter counts, it rarely translates to hardware speedup\index{Sparsity!hardware speedup requirement} because arbitrary nonzero placements destroy memory locality. Hardware accelerators resolve this with N:M structured sparsity\index{Sparsity!N:M structured pattern},[^fn-sparsity-nm-regularity] the pruning constraint from model compression that keeps exactly $\StructuredSparsityNonzeroCount$ of every $\StructuredSparsityGroupSize$ contiguous values along the reduction dimension nonzero, so memory access stays uniform and indexing predictable across parallel execution units.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The N:M and 2:4 structured sparsity patterns and their compressed storage are established in @sec-model-compression-structured-pruning-9692.
:::

[^fn-sparsity-nm-regularity]: **N:M structured sparsity**\index{Structured sparsity!N:M pattern}: The 2:4 ratio (50 percent density) used by NVIDIA's Ampere Sparse Tensor Cores is a hardware-friendly compromise: every contiguous four-value group retains two nonzero values, preserving regular indexing while halving the dense value payload [@NVIDIA2020]. At 2:4, the metadata overhead is compact enough to store alongside the weights without overwhelming the memory-traffic savings, which is the constraint that makes the advertised 2$\times$ tensor-math throughput path plausible when kernels and model weights satisfy the pattern.

Parallel hardware needs this regularity because of how sparse matrices are encoded. Classical formats such as Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) and Block Compressed Sparse Row (BSR) rely on auxiliary index arrays to locate nonzero entries, and the corresponding activation gathers can touch scattered addresses, reducing useful bytes per memory transaction. Varying numbers of nonzeros across rows also create load imbalance and divergent execution. Block sparsity groups retained values into larger dense tiles to restore regularity, at the cost of a more restrictive pruning pattern. In the block formats, a short list of nonzero block indices tells the hardware which tiles to fetch, so zero blocks are never read. Whether an indexed format saves bytes or time at a given sparsity, its break-even point, is derived in @sec-model-compression-sparse-break-even-7e4a. The datapath question here is how regular the retained values must be for parallel hardware to use them.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The CSR storage format is collected for reference in @sec-appdx-algorithm-foundations-sparse-matrix-formats-0bd0.
:::

NVIDIA's Sparse Tensor Cores\index{Sparse Tensor Core!2:4 constraint} implement the 2:4 instance of the N:M pattern\index{Sparsity!structured, 2:4 hardware support} [@NVIDIA2020; @nvidia_cusparse_block]. Their input is the compressed 2:4 encoding, the two retained values of each group plus a 4-bit metadata tag (2 bits per value) recording their original positions. During execution, the memory hierarchy transfers only the compressed weights and their metadata, halving the weight-value payload while adding metadata traffic; total transferred bytes therefore fall by less than half before other overheads. Inside the Sparse Tensor Core datapath, the 4-bit metadata steers an internal multiplexer network that selects the matching two values from an uncompressed four-element activation vector. These selected activations and the two nonzero weights are then routed into a half-sized dot-product multiplier tree. Because the hardware computes only on the nonzeros while streaming compressed weights, this design doubles the peak arithmetic instruction throughput. The result is an advertised 2$\times$ tensor-math speedup over dense operations when weights are fine-tuned to satisfy the pattern (@fig-2-4-gemm).

::: {#fig-2-4-gemm data-explore="original-v1-2-4-gemm" data-explore-key="vol1:fig-2-4-gemm" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**2:4 Structured Sparsity GEMM**: Left: standard dense matrix multiplication on Tensor Cores using full 8-element rows. Right: 2:4 sparse multiplication retains two nonzeros in every group of four and uses compact indices to select matching elements from the dense right-hand matrix. A supported sparse inner loop can halve the multiplied values, although metadata handling and the rest of the execution path determine end-to-end speedup. Source: PyTorch blog [@pytorch_sparsity_blog]." fig-alt="Side-by-side comparison of dense and 2:4 sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores. Left shows an 8-element dense row multiplication. Right shows a sparse row with two retained values per group of four and compact indices selecting matching elements from the dense right-hand matrix."}


:::

The 2:4 pattern saves about half of the weight bytes and half of the multiplies, minus the metadata, so the reduced weight payload can lower traffic across HBM and on-chip SRAM. A roofline comparison must use consistent accounting: useful dense-equivalent operations can stay fixed while bytes decrease, whereas the count of physically executed sparse operations also decreases. Metadata and activation traffic remain in either traffic budget. Narrower values and skipped zeros therefore help when they reduce the bytes moved and keep the matrix engines fed. The ResNet-50 INT8 profile collects that benefit only on an execution path that supports both its format and its shapes. How fast such a path can possibly run follows from one division.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: resnet-arithmetic-floor-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESNET-50 ARITHMETIC FLOOR ON THE H100 INT8 PATH
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Closing paragraph of
# │          @sec-hardware-acceleration-compute-units-execution-models-f406.
# │
# │ Goal: Make the microsecond-scale arithmetic floor reproducible.
# │ Show: ResNet-50 inference operations divided by the H100 INT8 tensor peak,
# │       and the same division at the FP16 peak for contrast.
# │ How: Registry operation count over registry peak rates.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_flops, fmt_time, fmt_ops_rate, fmt_flop_rate

class ResnetArithmeticFloor:
    """Peak-rate lower bound on one ResNet-50 inference on an H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_flops = Models.Vision.ResNet50.inference_flops
    h100_int8 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["int8"]
    h100_fp16 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    floor_int8 = Scenarios.ResNet50Batch1H100Int8PeakRate.result.latency_compute.to(microsecond)
    floor_fp16 = Scenarios.ResNet50Batch1H100Fp16PeakRate.result.latency_compute.to(microsecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(1 < floor_int8.magnitude < 10, f"ResNet-50 H100 INT8 floor should be a few microseconds, got {floor_int8}")
    check(floor_fp16 > floor_int8, "The FP16 floor must exceed the INT8 floor.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_gflop_str = fmt_flops(resnet_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    h100_int8_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(h100_int8, unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=True)
    floor_int8_us_str = fmt_time(round(floor_int8.magnitude) * microsecond, unit=microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    floor_fp16_us_str = fmt_time(round(floor_fp16.magnitude) * microsecond, unit=microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Dividing a model's total operation count by peak arithmetic throughput produces an idealized lower bound on execution time, not a realistic inference latency. On the H100's INT8 tensor path, dividing ResNet-50's `{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.resnet_gflop_str` per inference by the `{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.h100_int8_tops_str` peak yields a floor of about `{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.floor_int8_us_str`, against `{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.floor_fp16_us_str` at the FP16 peak. Real single-image ResNet-50 inference takes far longer than either floor. Part of that gap is kernel launch, synchronization, and host overhead that no roofline captures; part is memory traffic in low-intensity layers, because bandwidth has improved more slowly than tensor arithmetic throughput. That imbalance decides whether the advertised INT8 peak delivers high sustained utilization or sits largely idle on a given workload [@horowitz2014; @gholami2024]. Closing the gap requires the other half of the anatomy, the memory hierarchy that supplies the compute units.

## Memory Systems {#sec-hardware-acceleration-ai-memory-systems-0057}

That gap between a `{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.floor_int8_us_str` arithmetic floor and real inference latency opens whenever the memory subsystem cannot deliver weights and activations fast enough to keep the compute units busy. Modern accelerators provide hundreds of teraflops (or even petaflops) on low-precision tensor datapaths [@NVIDIA2020; @choquette2023; @nvidia2024blackwell], yet their arithmetic pipelines idle as soon as memory traffic saturates the bus. This is the memory wall\index{AI memory systems!bandwidth bottleneck}, the growing divergence between arithmetic capability and memory bandwidth, seen from inside the accelerator.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The memory wall, the widening gap between compute growth and memory bandwidth growth, is established in @sec-ml-systems-deployment-spectrum-71be.
:::

Because deep neural networks manipulate millions or billions of parameters across high-dimensional activation tensors, performance is frequently dictated by data movement rather than raw arithmetic capacity. Accelerators combat this memory wall through tiered storage hierarchies, software-managed scratchpads, high-bandwidth 3D stacked memory, and architectural dataflow strategies designed to maximize spatial and temporal reuse. For the chapter's ResNet-50 workload the question becomes where each activation tile lives between the moment one convolution writes it and the moment the next consumes it, and what each tier on that path costs in time and energy.

### The AI memory wall {#sec-hardware-acceleration-understanding-ai-memory-wall-3ea9}

Upgrading to an accelerator with twice the peak FLOP/s yields zero speedup when a workload's weights and activations already saturate memory bandwidth, pinning execution time at $\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}$. On an accelerator the **AI memory wall**\index{Memory wall!AI accelerators} is chiefly this bandwidth ceiling, set by the parameter volumes and activation tensors of deep learning rather than by the single-access latency gap of the classic CPU formulation. Adding more memory capacity does not remove it either, because a model that fits comfortably in device memory still waits on the rate at which its bytes reach the compute units of @sec-hardware-acceleration-compute-units-execution-models-f406. The energy side of the wall was set out with the energy ladder in @sec-hardware-acceleration-machine-learning-hardware-specialization-09c5: an off-chip DRAM access costs about `{python} EnergyGapAnchor.dram_vs_fp32_mult_str` the energy of the FP32 multiply that consumes its operand (@fig-energy-hierarchy). The memory wall adds the time side of the same imbalance, which grows with every hardware generation.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: memory-wall-h100-specs-calc
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_bandwidth, fmt_flop_rate

class MemoryWallH100Specs:
    """H100 peak throughput and bandwidth for the memory-wall scaling prose."""

    h100_peak_flops = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.peak_flops
    h100_bandwidth = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth

    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_fp8_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["fp8"], unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=True)
    h100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bandwidth, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
```

#### Quantifying the compute-memory performance gap {#sec-hardware-acceleration-quantifying-computememory-performance-gap-1526}

Over the past two decades, peak computational capabilities have grown substantially faster than DRAM bandwidth\index{Memory Bandwidth!scaling trends} [@gholami2024]. This divergence stems from physical scaling constraints: while transistor scaling and dense systolic arrays multiply arithmetic throughput, memory bandwidth remains bounded by pin counts, package-substrate routing density, and interface signaling power. Representative high-end accelerators can deliver on the order of $10^3$ TFLOP/s of peak tensor throughput (for example, NVIDIA H100 delivering `{python} MemoryWallH100Specs.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` in FP16 or `{python} MemoryWallH100Specs.h100_fp8_tflop_per_s_str` in dense FP8) while providing approximately `{python} MemoryWallH100Specs.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` of memory bandwidth [@choquette2023]. This implies that on the order of $10^2$ FLOP of work per byte moved is required to fully use the compute, a threshold @sec-hardware-acceleration-hardware-balance calls the ridge point and that exceeds the arithmetic intensity of many practical neural network workloads.

When a workload's arithmetic intensity falls below this threshold, data transfer ($\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}$) sets the larger of the two modeled time bounds. Accelerators attempt to tolerate memory latency (typically hundreds of clock cycles for off-chip DRAM) by maintaining thousands of concurrent execution threads and switching between active warps while memory requests remain in flight. However, when memory bandwidth saturates or when register pressure limits occupancy, the scheduler runs out of independent instructions to issue. Compute pipelines then stall, leaving high-throughput tensor cores idle while waiting for operands. Simultaneously, wide off-chip memory buses that cross capacitive printed circuit board traces and PHY interfaces consume a substantial fraction of the chip's thermal design power (TDP), which directly constrains the energy budget available for arithmetic logic [@horowitz2014; @sze2017].

The time gap and the energy ladder describe the same pressure from two sides: each byte fetched from DRAM costs more time relative to the arithmetic it feeds with every generation, on top of its energy cost. The TPU v1's performance-per-watt advantage (example \ref{exmp-hw-acceleration-tpuv1-vs-k80-efficiency-shock}) came largely from minimizing that off-chip movement through systolic arrays and large on-chip SRAM [@jouppi2017]. Whether a model can exploit such a design depends on the pattern of its memory accesses, which differs sharply among parameters, activations, and optimizer state.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEMORY WALL TREND (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-memory-wall and the paragraph that introduces it.
# │
# │ Goal: Compare growth in dense model parameters with growth in per-device
# │       accelerator memory bandwidth since 2014.
# │ Show: ~3,900× dense-parameter growth (VGG-16 to PaLM) against
# │       ~33× per-device bandwidth growth (one K80 GPU to B200).
# │ How: Registry parameters, bandwidths, and release years; growth indices
# │      relative to the 2014 baselines. The MoE model is plotted at total
# │      parameters but excluded from the trend and the headline multiple.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_multiple

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class MemoryWallTrend:
    """Dense model-size growth vs per-device memory-bandwidth growth since 2014."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    growth = Scenarios.DenseParametersVsBandwidthSince2014
    # Figure labels, in the scenario's accelerator and model order.
    chip_labels = [
        "NVIDIA K80 (one GPU)",
        "Google TPU v2",
        "NVIDIA V100",
        "NVIDIA A100",
        "Google TPU v4",
        "NVIDIA H100",
        "AMD MI300X",
        "Google TPU v6e",
        "AMD MI325X",
        "NVIDIA B200",
    ]
    dense_labels = ["AlexNet", "VGG-16", "ResNet-50", "BERT-Large", "GPT-3", "PaLM", "Llama 3.1 405B"]
    moe_labels = ["DeepSeek-V3"]
    chips = list(zip(chip_labels, growth.accelerators))
    dense_models = list(zip(dense_labels, growth.dense_models))
    moe_models = list(zip(moe_labels, growth.sparse_models))
    baseline_chip = growth.baseline_accelerator
    baseline_model = growth.baseline_model

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    chip_names = [n for n, _ in chips]
    chip_years = [h.release_year for _, h in chips]
    chip_bw_gbs = [h.memory.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude for _, h in chips]
    chip_index = growth.bandwidth_index
    dense_names = [n for n, _ in dense_models]
    dense_years = [m.release_year for _, m in dense_models]
    dense_params = [m.parameters.to("count").magnitude for _, m in dense_models]
    dense_index = growth.dense_index
    moe_names = [n for n, _ in moe_models]
    moe_years = [m.release_year for _, m in moe_models]
    moe_params = [m.parameters.to("count").magnitude for _, m in moe_models]
    moe_index = growth.sparse_index
    bandwidth_growth = growth.bandwidth_growth
    model_growth = growth.parameter_growth

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(baseline_chip.release_year == 2014 and baseline_model.release_year == 2014, "Both growth indices are relative to 2014.")
    check(len(chips) == len(growth.accelerators) and len(dense_models) == len(growth.dense_models), "One label per series entry.")
    check(25 <= bandwidth_growth <= 40, f"Expected ~33x per-device bandwidth growth, got {bandwidth_growth:.1f}.")
    check(3000 <= model_growth <= 4500, f"Expected ~3,900x dense-parameter growth, got {model_growth:.0f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    bandwidth_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(bandwidth_growth), precision=0)
    model_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(model_growth, -2), precision=0, commas=True)
```

Hardware balance is the supply side of the memory wall; model size is the demand side. The structural widening between model footprints and available memory bandwidth is what turns the iron law's memory term into the binding constraint across generations. Parameter count is a capacity quantity. In low-batch dense decoding with weights streamed from device memory, weight traffic per generated token grows with the parameter count. Sparse expert models read selected experts rather than every stored parameter, so their total parameter counts do not directly specify per-token traffic. @Fig-memory-wall plots this logarithmic divergence relative to 2014. It contrasts the roughly `{python} MemoryWallTrend.model_growth_mult_str` increase in dense model parameters (filled red points) against the `{python} MemoryWallTrend.bandwidth_growth_mult_str` increase in per-device accelerator memory bandwidth (blue points). The contrast isolates the widening shaded memory-wall gap [@krizhevsky2012imagenet; @simonyan2014very; @brown2020language; @chowdhery2022palm; @dubey2024llama]. DeepSeek-V3 appears as an open marker at its total parameter count and is left out of the trend for exactly that reason [@deepseek2025v3]. Even high-bandwidth accelerators such as NVIDIA B200 and AMD MI300X/MI325X cannot close this growth-rate gap through bandwidth scaling alone [@nvidia2024blackwell; @amd2023mi300x]. Parameter counts for proprietary systems such as GPT-4 and Gemini are not officially disclosed, so they are not plotted as factual data points.

::: {#fig-memory-wall fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Model Size vs. Hardware Bandwidth**: Both series are the base-10 logarithm of growth relative to 2014 (VGG-16 for parameters, one GPU of the dual-GPU K80 board for bandwidth), so each unit on the vertical axis is a tenfold increase. Over the plotted decade dense parameter counts grow roughly `{python} MemoryWallTrend.model_growth_mult_str` against per-device bandwidth's `{python} MemoryWallTrend.bandwidth_growth_mult_str`. The open marker is a sparse expert model plotted at total parameters and excluded from the fit. The shaded band is a gap between logarithms rather than a difference, so its width reads as a ratio, and the fitted trends describe the decade's average rates; the dense frontier has been flat since 2022. Method after @gholami2024." fig-alt="Scatter plot with two fitted trend lines from 2012 to 2024. The vertical axis is base-10 logarithm of growth relative to 2014, running from about negative one to four. Red model-size points rise to about 3.5 and blue bandwidth points to about 1.5, with one open red marker for DeepSeek-V3 above the red trend and a gray band shaded between the two trend lines from 2016 onward, labeled in bold as the AI memory wall."}

### Memory access patterns in ML workloads {#sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-access-patterns-ml-workloads-a960}

In dense FP16 autoregressive generation at batch size 1, streaming a model's weights from device memory for each generated token yields roughly 1 FLOP/byte on the matrix-vector work, starving compute units before activations or gradients ever enter the picture. Across training and inference, parameters, activations, and optimizer states compete for that same memory bandwidth in distinct ways. Model parameters (weights and biases) can span hundreds of billions of values [@brown2020language] that must stream from memory whenever batch reuse is low. Intermediate activations produced at each layer must also be buffered for subsequent operations, and during training those forward activations must either stay in memory until backpropagation consumes them or be recomputed on the backward pass. Training then compounds the traffic with gradients and optimizer state. Backpropagation writes a gradient for every parameter, and adaptive optimizers such as Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) read and write multi-word momentum states on every step, multiplying the bytes moved per parameter update [@narayanan2021; @kwon2019].

The physical cost of this data movement depends on where each tensor resides in the memory hierarchy. While an on-chip register access completes in a single clock cycle at sub-picojoule energy, a dependent off-chip DRAM fetch can expose hundreds of cycles of latency and expends orders of magnitude more energy. Independent requests can overlap that latency, subject to available concurrency and bandwidth. Tracing a single tensor of the chapter's ResNet-50 workload through the memory tiers during an inference pass makes this disparity concrete (lighthouse \ref{lhs-hw-acceleration-life-tensor-resnet50}).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tensor-lifecycle-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TENSOR LIFECYCLE: A RESNET-50 ACTIVATION MAP ON THE H100
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: lighthouse \ref{lhs-hw-acceleration-life-tensor-resnet50} in
# │          @sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-access-patterns-ml-workloads-a960.
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the physical costs of the memory hierarchy on the
# │       chapter's running workload.
# │ Show: Size of one stage-2 activation map at INT8 and FP16, which H100 tiers
# │       can hold it, and the latency and energy of each tier.
# │ How: ResNet-50 stage-2 shape; H100 capacities and Hopper latencies from the
# │      registry; 45 nm DRAM energy per byte.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_energy, fmt_memory, fmt_time, fmt_ops_rate, fmt_memory_capacity

class TensorLifecycleCalc:
    """Memory-hierarchy costs for one ResNet-50 stage-2 activation map on an H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    stage2 = Scenarios.ResNet50Stage2ConvBatch32  # 56 x 56 x 64 output map, batch 32, FP16
    stage2_int8 = Scenarios.ResNet50Stage2ConvBatch32Int8
    map_read = Scenarios.ResNet50Stage2MapInt8ReadOnce  # one INT8 map read once from DRAM
    map_h = stage2.height  # ResNet-50 stage-2 spatial size
    map_c = stage2.out_channels  # ResNet-50 stage-2 bottleneck channels
    batch = stage2.batch_size  # same batch as the roofline analysis
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    dram_energy_per_byte = map_read.energy_per_byte
    reg_energy_per_access = Hardware.Tech.Memory.Register.energy_per_access

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    map_int8 = stage2_int8.activation_bytes
    map_fp16 = stage2.activation_bytes
    batch_map_int8 = stage2_int8.batch_output_bytes
    smem = h100.memory.shared_memory_per_sm
    l2 = h100.memory.l2_cache
    stream_time = (map_int8 / h100.memory.bandwidth).to(nanosecond)
    map_dram_energy = map_read.energy.to(microjoule)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(map_int8 < smem < map_fp16, "One INT8 stage-2 map must fit one SM's shared memory; the FP16 map must not.")
    check(batch_map_int8 < l2, "A batch-32 INT8 stage-2 map must fit in the H100 L2 cache.")
    check(
        stream_time < Hardware.Tech.Memory.HopperGlobalMemory.latency,
        "Streaming one map at full bandwidth must take less than one HBM access latency.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    map_dims_math = fmt_math(rf"{map_h}{{\times}}{map_h}")
    map_c_str = fmt_int(map_c, commas=False)
    batch_str = fmt_int(batch, commas=False)
    map_int8_kb_str = fmt_memory(round(map_int8.to(KB).magnitude) * KB, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    map_fp16_kb_str = fmt_memory(round(map_fp16.to(KB).magnitude) * KB, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    batch_map_mb_str = fmt_memory(batch_map_int8, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    smem_kb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(smem, unit=KiB, precision=0, commas=False)
    l2_mb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(l2, unit=MiB, precision=0, commas=False)
    latency_hbm_ns_str = fmt_time(
        round(Hardware.Tech.Memory.HopperGlobalMemory.latency.to(nanosecond).magnitude) * nanosecond, unit=nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False
    )
    latency_l2_ns_str = fmt_time(
        round(Hardware.Tech.Memory.HopperL2.latency.to(nanosecond).magnitude) * nanosecond, unit=nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False
    )
    latency_smem_ns_str = fmt_time(
        round(Hardware.Tech.Memory.HopperSharedMemory.latency.to(nanosecond).magnitude) * nanosecond, unit=nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False
    )
    stream_ns_str = fmt_time(round(stream_time.magnitude) * nanosecond, unit=nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    dram_energy_pj_byte_str = fmt_energy(dram_energy_per_byte * byte, unit=pJ, precision=0, commas=False)
    map_dram_energy_uj_str = fmt_energy(map_dram_energy, unit=microjoule, precision=1, commas=False)
    reg_energy_pj_str = fmt_energy(reg_energy_per_access, unit=pJ, precision=1, commas=False)
    h100_int8_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(h100.compute.precision_flops["int8"], unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=True)
```

::: {#lhs-hw-acceleration-life-tensor-resnet50 .callout-lighthouse title="Life of a tensor: A ResNet-50 activation map"}

Follow one activation map of the chapter's ResNet-50 workload, the output of a stage-2 convolution (`{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.map_dims_math` positions by `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.map_c_str` channels), on its way to the next convolution's Tensor Cores on an H100:

1.  **HBM**: The previous kernel wrote the map here.
    *   **Size**: `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.map_int8_kb_str` per image at INT8 and `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.map_fp16_kb_str` at FP16; a batch of `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.batch_str` holds `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.batch_map_mb_str` at INT8.
    *   **Latency**: A dependent off-chip request takes about `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.latency_hbm_ns_str`, while streaming one image's map at full bandwidth would take only about `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.stream_ns_str`, so the kernel must keep many requests in flight to approach the bandwidth ceiling.
    *   **Energy**: About `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.dram_energy_pj_byte_str` per byte in the 45 nm estimates used throughout the chapter, or about `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.map_dram_energy_uj_str` to read one image's map once.
2.  **L2 cache**: The H100 shares `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.l2_mb_str` of L2 across its streaming multiprocessors (SMs), enough to hold the whole batch's map at INT8 if the next kernel consumes it soon after the previous one wrote it.
    *   **Latency**: About `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.latency_l2_ns_str` on Hopper.
3.  **Shared memory**: One SM stages a tile of the map in its `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.smem_kb_str` of software-managed shared memory. A whole image's map fits at INT8 but not at FP16, so the INT8 format changes which tier can hold it.
    *   **Latency**: About `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.latency_smem_ns_str` on Hopper.
4.  **Registers**: The Tensor Core reads its operands here.
    *   **Latency**: A small number of cycles, depending on the instruction.
    *   **Energy**: About `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.reg_energy_pj_str` per access, more than three orders of magnitude below an off-chip access.
    *   **Device arithmetic peak**: `{python} TensorLifecycleCalc.h100_int8_tops_str` on the H100 INT8 tensor path, the rate these registers must sustain, not a register-transfer rate.

**Systems insight**: Latency and energy per access rise from registers to HBM. The working set's location, access count, reuse, and dependencies determine the memory contribution to time and energy; arithmetic adds its own cost. The bandwidth term of the roofline is whichever link of this ladder the working set must cross; HBM-to-L2 is one possible limiting link, not the only one.

:::

The boundary between bandwidth-bound and compute-bound execution emerges directly from the balance between data transfer time and arithmetic execution time. Consider a workload that requires data volume $\DataVolume$ (bytes) across available memory bandwidth $\Bandwidth$ (bytes/s). It executes $\Operations$ floating-point operations on hardware with peak throughput $\PeakRate$ (FLOP/s) at realized hardware utilization $\EfficiencyHw$. The respective execution times are the iron law's data and compute terms:
\begin{gather*}
\IronlawTermTimesMemory = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}
\\
\IronlawTermTimesCompute = \frac{O}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}
\end{gather*}

In a strictly sequential model without overlap, $\IronLawMemoryTime > \IronLawComputeTime$ identifies bandwidth-bound execution. When hardware overlaps memory transfers with computation, the larger term sets the theoretical lower bound on execution time. In practice, however, data dependencies, memory controller queueing, and partial pipeline overlap dictate how much arithmetic hardware remains idle while waiting for operands.

#### Irregular memory access {#sec-hardware-acceleration-irregular-memory-access-c6ec}

Production machine learning workloads combine regular dense matrix kernels with irregular memory access patterns\index{Memory Access!irregular patterns} that defeat conventional caching and prefetching hardware. While dense operations like general matrix multiply (GEMM) and convolution stream contiguous blocks that map cleanly onto hardware caches and systolic arrays, irregular operations rely on indirect, sparse, or input-dependent memory addresses. @Tbl-traditional-vs-ml-mem contrasts these two memory regimes across access geometry, cache locality, and hardware pressure.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}
```

| Feature                                  | **Regular dense kernels**                               | **Irregular ML components**                          |
|:-----------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Access pattern**                       | Contiguous or tiled                                     | Indirect, scattered, or input-dependent              |
| **Cache locality**\index{Cache locality} | Often high after tiling                                 | Often lower and workload-dependent                   |
| **Data reuse**\index{Data reuse}         | Structured across tiles or batches                      | Sparse or dynamic, depending on the operator         |
| Dependencies                             | Static loop nests                                       | Input-dependent routing or variable shapes           |
| Examples                                 | GEMM, convolution, dense attention                      | Embedding lookup, unstructured sparsity, MoE routing |
| **Primary pressure**                     | Compute or bandwidth, depending on arithmetic intensity | Latency, bandwidth, metadata, and load imbalance     |
| **Energy consequence**                   | Depends on reuse and memory tier                        | Extra movement and metadata can increase energy      |

: **Regular and Irregular Memory Access**: Regular dense kernels expose tileable reuse and predictable addresses, whereas irregular ML components rely more on indirect or input-dependent access, weakening caching and prefetching and adding metadata or load-balance overhead. A single model may contain both regimes. {#tbl-traditional-vs-ml-mem tbl-colwidths="[20,32,48]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

Within a single neural network, memory access behavior varies sharply across layer types. Convolutional layers have high spatial locality and register reuse as small weight kernels slide across input feature maps. Fully connected layers and dense attention, by contrast, execute regular matrix multiplications whose large parameter matrices or key-value caches can exceed on-chip SRAM capacity and become bandwidth bound when operational reuse is low. Variable sequence lengths complicate memory buffer allocation, yet the attention operations within each sequence remain regular, contiguous matrix multiplies.

True memory irregularity arises instead from unstructured sparsity,[^fn-sparsity-memory-access] embedding lookups, and dynamic token routing. Unstructured sparsity stores nonzero weights or activations in compressed formats (such as CSR or COO) that require pointer indirection to decode operand coordinates. Embedding tables break sequential transfers in a different way: sparse categorical IDs select arbitrary rows from tables spanning tens of gigabytes in DRAM, turning reads into uncoalesced, scattered fetches. DLRM, the book's capacity-bound lighthouse, is the extreme case. Its embedding tables exceed one accelerator's memory, and each lookup fetches a short row from an address known only when the input arrives, which defeats both caches and prefetchers. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)\index{MoE!dynamic computation paths} models introduce a third irregularity at the routing layer, where gates direct tokens to different expert networks based on input context. Although deterministic for a given input, token assignments vary across batches, disrupting prefetch pipelines and unbalancing execution queues across parallel cores.

[^fn-sparsity-memory-access]: [offset=-17mm] **Sparsity and memory irregularity**\index{Sparsity!memory access irregularity}: Unstructured sparse formats commonly gather nonzero elements through indirect addressing, which can weaken sequential access and make metadata overhead significant. Structured sparsity preserves hardware-friendly blocks, so its access behavior differs from arbitrary pruning. Without suitable kernels or hardware support, an unstructured sparse model can run slower than its dense counterpart despite performing fewer arithmetic operations.

Irregularity degrades performance through distinct mechanisms, and treating them as one memory problem can point to the wrong optimization. Scattered addresses may turn one logical access into several memory transactions, so each fetched cache line carries few useful payload bytes. Indirection can also serialize address generation: the system must fetch an index or pointer before it knows which payload to request, limiting memory-level parallelism even when aggregate bandwidth remains available. Input-dependent routing creates a third failure mode when some processing elements receive longer queues than others; completion time follows the slowest queue while neighboring units idle. Variable-sized allocations may fragment capacity, but fragmentation is neither necessary nor sufficient for irregular access. A sequential stream can saturate bandwidth without being irregular, whereas a dependent lookup chain can stall far below peak bandwidth.

The paired address strips in @fig-irregular-address-transactions isolate spatial utilization from address dependence. The example counts traffic at a declared sector interface, so it does not infer physical DRAM traffic from logical addresses alone.

With a cold cache, no reuse, and requests merged within each sector, adjacent requests fetch one sector while scattered requests fetch four for the same useful payload. The separate dependency chain shows why a payload read may have to wait even when bandwidth is available." fig-alt="Two strips of sixteen word cells show four adjacent requested addresses within one sector and four scattered requested addresses in separate sectors. Packing requests into fewer sectors reduces surplus bytes at that interface. It does not remove the dependency in the lower panel: the payload request still waits until the index or pointer returns its address. Increasing bandwidth and exposing independent requests therefore address different limits.

Diagnosis should therefore begin with the mechanism that prevents forward progress. A low ratio of useful payload bytes to transferred bytes indicates poor spatial utilization or coalescing. Long memory stalls alongside unused bandwidth indicate dependent misses or too few concurrent requests to hide latency. Uneven queue depths or per-route work reveal load imbalance rather than a cache-capacity problem. Cache hit rate alone cannot distinguish these cases because a miss can waste bandwidth, expose latency, or both. Each diagnosis implies a different remedy: packing or blocking improves spatial utilization, reordering and prefetching expose concurrent requests, structured sparse formats reduce indexing overhead, and routing or partitioning balances work. The memory hierarchy determines the cost of the remaining accesses, while dataflow and tensor-layout choices determine how much irregularity software can remove before execution reaches the hardware.

The optimization order follows that diagnosis. Representation comes first when the format is under system control because a block-structured sparse format or grouped routing can remove indirection before a kernel executes. Request organization comes next: accesses issued together should target adjacent addresses, and enough independent requests must remain in flight to hide unavoidable latency. Additional cache capacity or bandwidth helps only when profiling shows that the regularized request stream still exhausts that resource. More bandwidth cannot resolve a serial pointer dependency, and more capacity cannot rebalance skewed work. The objective is to expose as much regular structure as possible while confining unavoidable irregularity to the smallest portion of execution.

Software can mitigate irregular access by regularizing tensor layouts, enforcing structured sparsity, and sorting dynamic routes into uniform batches. Yet software restructuring cannot eliminate the physical penalty of data movement: whether a memory request is contiguous or scattered, every transferred byte must cross physical wires governed by finite bandwidth, propagation latency, and energy dissipation. Bounding these physical costs requires organizing storage into cascading hardware tiers. Rather than treating memory as a uniform pool, accelerator architectures deploy multilevel memory hierarchies that trade off capacity against latency and energy at every tier.

### Memory hierarchy {#sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-hierarchy-1839}

No single storage technology can simultaneously satisfy the multi-terabyte-per-second bandwidth required by dense execution units and the tens of gigabytes of capacity required to hold modern model parameters. Accelerators resolve this tension through multilevel memory hierarchies\index{Memory hierarchy!speed-capacity trade-off}. Rather than treating memory as a monolithic address space, the machine organizes storage into distinct physical tiers, each optimized for a specific balance of capacity, access latency, bandwidth, and energy dissipation.

At the apex of the hierarchy, register files\index{Register!fastest memory} and on-chip SRAM caches supply operands to arithmetic units with sub-nanosecond latency and single-digit picojoule energy costs, but their capacity is strictly limited by silicon die area. At the base, nonvolatile flash storage holds hundreds of gigabytes of model checkpoints and training datasets, but requires milliseconds or microseconds to access. Between these boundaries, software-managed scratchpads stage active tensor tiles, while device-local DRAM (such as HBM or GDDR) provides the primary working memory for parameters and activations.

This organization establishes an inverse relationship across tiers: as storage capacity expands and physical distance from arithmetic units grows, bandwidth falls, latency lengthens by orders of magnitude, and energy consumption per bit escalates. @Tbl-memory-hierarchy compares these tiers across latency, bandwidth, capacity, and functional roles in deep learning workloads.

| Memory Level                                     | **Relative latency**                |      Bandwidth      | **Relative capacity** | **Example Use in Deep Learning**                                 |
|:-------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------|:-------------------:|:----------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Registers                                        | Lowest                              |       Highest       | Tiny                  | Storing operands for immediate computation                       |
| **L1/L2 Cache (SRAM)**\index{SRAM!on-chip cache} | Very low                            |         High        | Small                 | Caching frequently accessed activations and small weight blocks  |
| **Scratchpad memory**\index{Scratchpad memory}   | Very low                            |         High        | Small to medium       | Software-managed storage for intermediate computations           |
| **Device DRAM (HBM, GDDR, or LPDDR)**            | High                                | Moderate--Very High | Large                 | Storing model parameters and activations that do not fit on-chip |
| **Host DRAM (typically DDR)**                    | High locally; transfer adds latency |       Moderate      | Large to very large   | Staging or offloading data outside accelerator memory            |
| **Flash Storage (SSD/NVMe)**                     | Very high                           |         Low         | Very large            | Storing pretrained models and checkpoints for later loading      |

: **Memory Hierarchy Trade-Offs**: AI accelerators use a multilevel memory hierarchy to balance performance and capacity. Each level provides distinct latency, bandwidth, and capacity characteristics that dictate how neural network components (weights, activations, and intermediate results) should be allocated to minimize bottlenecks and maximize throughput. Relative labels describe the typical ordering; exact values depend on architecture. @Sec-appdx-machine-foundations-latencies-every-programmer-know-e89f supplies registry-backed reference latencies. {#tbl-memory-hierarchy tbl-colwidths="[22,17,14,12,35]"}

A recurring systems question is why accelerators cannot bypass on-chip SRAM entirely and stream all operands directly from high-capacity off-chip DRAM. A dependent DRAM request exposes the full access latency. Many independent requests can hide that latency, but their sustained operand supply remains limited by off-chip bandwidth; on-chip staging also enables reuse.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: speed-of-light-limit-calc
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.core.units import millimeter
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_area

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class SpeedOfLightLimitCalc:
    """Chip-area reference for the signal-propagation callout."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_die_area = Hardware.Cloud.H100.die_area

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(800 <= h100_die_area.to(millimeter**2).magnitude <= 830, "H100 die area should stay near 814 mm^2.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_die_area_mm2_str = fmt_area(h100_die_area, unit=millimeter**2, commas=False)
```

::: {#nbk-hw-acceleration-speed-light-limit .callout-notebook title="Why HBM cannot feed the array directly"}

**Problem**: Why is on-chip SRAM necessary instead of fetching all data from HBM?

**Math**:

1.  **Clock cycle**: At 2 GHz, $1/(2\text{ GHz}) = 500\text{ ps}$.
2.  **DRAM access**: Off-chip HBM sits millimeters away on the package, but row activation, DRAM-array latency, serialization, protocol traversal, and queuing add up to 100+ cycles per access.
3.  **Distance, for comparison**: On an H100-class `{python} SpeedOfLightLimitCalc.h100_die_area_mm2_str` die, signals travel ~20 mm; at $\approx 0.5\VacuumLightSpeed$, $20\text{ mm}/(0.5\VacuumLightSpeed) \approx 130\text{ ps}$, less than one cycle.

**Systems insight**: The propagation estimate alone does not explain the DRAM access cost, and it omits real interconnect delay from wiring and routing. Independent requests can overlap the 100-plus-cycle access path; a dependent request cannot. Registers and SRAM supply operands at the rate the array needs while reusing values that would otherwise cross HBM repeatedly. Transformer tiling addresses both operand supply and reuse, whereas streaming a growing KV cache can still limit inference when its required traffic exceeds the available bandwidth.

:::

#### On-chip memory {#sec-hardware-acceleration-onchip-memory-72d1}

The **on-chip memory**\index{On-chip memory!definition} subsystem integrates registers, Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) caches\index{SRAM!on-chip fast memory}, and software-managed scratchpads directly on the accelerator die. Register files provide the immediate operand and accumulator storage needed by execution pipelines. Modern accelerators provision substantial register capacity in aggregate across the chip, but partition this pool dynamically among concurrent threads or warps. Increasing per-thread register allocation allows individual threads to retain larger matrix tiles, but limits the total number of concurrently scheduled warps, reducing the hardware's ability to hide memory latency. Conversely, underallocating registers forces the compiler to spill values to off-chip memory, converting single-cycle register accesses into multi-cycle stalls. Efficient kernel design balances register allocation to maintain maximum occupancy while keeping hot operands resident.

Hardware-managed L1 and L2 caches provide fast buffering for frequently referenced data using automatic tag checking and hardware eviction policies. However, automatic caches are poorly suited for streaming multi-gigabyte tensor operations: scanning through large activation tensors can evict reusable weight tiles before arithmetic units can reuse them. Furthermore, specialized execution pipelines impose strict layout and data-type constraints that general caches cannot satisfy automatically. As illustrated in example \ref{exmp-hw-acceleration-tensor-core-contract}, hardware matrix engines require specific alignments and memory layouts; a mismatch may require padding, conversion, or a different kernel whose efficiency must be checked.

::: {#exmp-hw-acceleration-tensor-core-contract .callout-example title="Tensor Cores that never engage"}

**Scenario**: An engineering team migrates a transformer workload to NVIDIA A100 GPUs expecting automatic Tensor Core acceleration, but profiling reveals Tensor Cores remain idle [@NVIDIA2020].

**Diagnosis**: The workload used shapes and data types that selected less efficient kernels rather than the intended Tensor Core path.

**Systems lesson**: Specialized paths have operator, precision, layout, and shape requirements. Libraries can often handle nonaligned dimensions through padding or alternative kernels, but reaching high utilization requires verifying which path was actually selected.

:::

To avoid the eviction overhead and unpredictability of automatic caches, AI accelerators incorporate scratchpad memory\index{Scratchpad Memory!software-managed storage}. Unlike hardware caches, scratchpads are software-managed SRAM structures mapped directly into the core's address space without tag directories or hardware replacement logic. The compiler or programmer explicitly controls when tensor tiles are loaded from external DRAM, how long they reside on-chip, and when updated values are written back. In convolutional models, scratchpads retain input feature maps and weight kernels across sliding receptive windows, eliminating redundant DRAM reads [@chen2017]. On NVIDIA GPUs, scratchpad memory is exposed as *shared memory*: a fast, programmer-controlled SRAM bank shared across all threads within a thread block. Custom kernels written in CUDA or Triton manage shared memory explicitly. FlashAttention demonstrates the power of this mechanism. Rather than materializing the full $\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength$ attention score matrix in off-chip HBM, the kernel tiles queries, keys, and values through shared memory and updates softmax statistics online [@dao2022]. The speedup stems entirely from eliminating high-latency HBM round trips rather than reducing arithmetic operations; in fact, the algorithm recomputes intermediate attention values during the backward pass to avoid storing them to off-chip memory.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ FlashAttention as an IO-aware attention kernel for training is established in @sec-model-training-flash-attention-ioaware-attention-optimization-3da0.
:::

#### Off-chip memory {#sec-hardware-acceleration-offchip-memory-ecdb}

When tensor working sets exceed on-chip SRAM capacity, operands and parameters reside in device-local DRAM. Rather than sequential hierarchy levels, HBM\index{HBM!3D die stacking}, Graphics DDR (GDDR)\index{GDDR!off-chip DRAM variant}, and Low-Power DDR (LPDDR)\index{LPDDR!low-power DRAM variant} represent alternative memory architectures engineered for distinct cost, bandwidth, and power envelopes. High-performance accelerators use HBM, which stacks DRAM dies vertically using through-silicon vias (TSVs) and interfaces with the accelerator die across a wide silicon interposer (e.g., 1,024 to 8,192 bits). This wide bus delivers multi-terabyte-per-second bandwidth at lower clock frequencies and lower energy per bit than conventional DRAM, but requires complex 2.5D packaging. Where silicon interposers are cost-prohibitive, accelerators adopt GDDR, which uses narrower buses (e.g., 256 to 384 bits) driven at high pin speeds across standard circuit boards. Mobile and embedded accelerators use LPDDR, trading raw bandwidth for low operating voltage and reduced standby power.

When parameter and activation footprints exceed device-local DRAM capacity, the system must offload state to host DRAM (typically standard DDR). Accessing host memory requires crossing an I/O interconnect such as PCIe or a coherent fabric like NVLink or Compute Express Link (CXL). Because PCIe bandwidth (tens of gigabytes per second) is one to two orders of magnitude lower than accelerator DRAM bandwidth, unmanaged offloading stalls arithmetic execution. Efficient runtimes mitigate this penalty by overlapping asynchronous direct memory access (DMA) copies with kernel execution, prefetching upcoming layer parameters while current layers compute.

At the base of the hierarchy, nonvolatile flash storage and solid-state drives (SSDs) provide persistent, multi-terabyte capacity for datasets and training checkpoints [@narayanan2021]. With read latencies measured in tens of microseconds and bus bandwidths capped at single-digit gigabytes per second, flash devices cannot participate directly in kernel execution. Checkpointing and data-loading pipelines treat flash storage as an asynchronous streaming source, staging batches through host DRAM into accelerator memory before computation begins.

The physical tiers of the memory hierarchy establish the latency floors and capacity ceilings of the accelerator, but advertised memory bandwidth\index{Memory Bandwidth!achievable vs. peak} is only a ceiling within them. Achievable bandwidth depends on access pattern, batching, locality, and the host interface that feeds the accelerator. Peak figures assume continuous, stride-1 coalesced access across all memory channels. Real neural network workloads deviate substantially from this ideal: transformer attention, convolution, and fully connected layers realize distinct fractions of peak bandwidth because their memory access strides, tiling dimensions, and operational reuse differ. A sufficiently large, coalesced weight stream can approach peak bandwidth even at small batch size. Batching instead reuses each loaded weight across more samples, raising arithmetic intensity as analyzed under the roofline model in @sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff. Small or irregular kernels may lack enough concurrent accesses to approach the bandwidth ceiling, making memory latency and available parallelism part of the diagnosis.

### Host-accelerator communication {#sec-hardware-acceleration-hostaccelerator-communication-bb7a}

An accelerator rated for hundreds of teraflops sits idle if its input tensors are still crawling across a host PCIe bus an order of magnitude slower than its on-package HBM. In discrete accelerator systems, the host CPU and the accelerator operate as separate computational domains joined by a peripheral bus. The host manages storage I/O, network streams, and runtime orchestration in system DRAM, while the accelerator executes dense mathematical kernels over device memory (HBM or GDDR). Because those two memories occupy separate physical address spaces, computation cannot begin until tensors cross the host-accelerator interconnect\index{Host-Accelerator Communication!transfer bottleneck}, making peripheral bus bandwidth and launch latency a hard gate on end-to-end speedup.

@Fig-host-accelerator-data-movement sequences the four-stage execution trace across host and device lifelines. Step 1 copies input data across PCIe to device memory via DMA\index{DMA!computation overlap}. Step 2 dispatches kernel instructions from the CPU. Step 3 executes parallel core compute with local writeback. Step 4 copies results back to host memory. In a naive synchronous execution model, every transfer step sits directly on the critical path, stalling either the host or the accelerator until each memory transaction finishes.

::: {#fig-host-accelerator-data-movement fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Host-Accelerator Data Transfer Sequence**: Four-step execution flow between CPU host and GPU device: (1) copying input data over PCIe, (2) issuing kernel instructions, (3) GPU compute, and (4) transferring results back to host memory. Low PCIe bandwidth and host dispatch latencies can easily dominate runtime unless kernel compute time exceeds data transfer overhead." fig-alt="Four-step data flow diagram: (1) copy data from main memory to GPU memory, (2) CPU instructs GPU, (3) GPU executes in parallel, (4) results copy back to main memory."}
