```{.tikz}
\draw[Line,-latex]($(B2)!0.37!(2B2)$)--
node[above,text=black,pos=0.26]{Instruct the processing (2)}
($(B4)!0.37!(2B4)$);
%
\draw[Line,-latex]($(B4)!0.75!(2B4)$)--
node[above,text=black,pos=0.5]{Store results}
($(B3)!0.75!(2B3)$);
\draw[Line,-latex]($(B3)!0.85!(2B3)$)--
node[above,text=black,pos=0.25]{Copy the result (4)}
($(B1)!0.85!(2B1)$);
%
\draw[Line,-latex]($(B4)!0.57!(2B4)$)
to [out=10,in=350,distance=42]
node[above,text=black,pos=0.1,fill=white]{Execute parallel in each core (3)}
($(B4)!0.62!(2B4)$);
\end{tikzpicture}

```

:::

The end-to-end latency of a kernel launch decomposes into transfer time, queue dispatch overhead, and arithmetic execution time. When tensor transfers are small or frequent, the fixed overhead of driver submission and bus round trips dominates runtime. When transfers are large, the low bandwidth of PCIe relative to on-package HBM creates a sustained I/O bottleneck. In D·A·M terms, the Machine boundary between host and accelerator forces the Algorithm to maximize arithmetic reuse on the device once tensors arrive.

#### Node-level interconnect topology {#sec-hardware-acceleration-nodelevel-interconnect-topology-b45b}

Within a single machine, how bits move between GPUs and the CPU sets the next ceiling. In the 1–8 GPU regime, scaling is achieved through high-speed intra-node interconnects such as NVLink\index{NVLink!intra-node scaling} and host-to-device PCIe\index{PCIe!host-to-device transfers} transfers that mitigate the memory wall. These links form a **bandwidth taper**\index{Bandwidth taper!interconnect hierarchy}: data-movement speed falls at each step away from the compute units, from on-package HBM through the GPU-to-GPU NVLink bridge down to the host PCIe link. The PCIe step is much slower than the accelerator-local memory and inter-GPU fabric, so any data path that touches the CPU can become a performance hazard. Keeping accelerator-to-accelerator traffic off that link is the reason NVLink\index{NVLink!PCIe bottleneck} exists [@NVIDIA2020nvlink]. A typical AI server is therefore not a flat mesh of connected devices, and optimizing data movement starts from its physical topology.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: interconnect-bandwidth
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INTERCONNECT BANDWIDTH SPECS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Node-Level Interconnect Topology" prose
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the bandwidth hierarchy across system interconnects.
# │ Show: The 30-100× slowdown when data moves from local NVLink to PCIe or Network.
# │ How: List bandwidth constants for NVLink, PCIe, and InfiniBand.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_bandwidth

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class InterconnectHierarchy:
    """
    Namespace for Interconnect Bandwidth Hierarchy.
    Scenario: The bandwidth taper from Chip -> Node -> Cluster.
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Device
    hbm_bw = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.bandwidth

    # Chip-to-Chip
    nvlink_a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100.nvlink.bandwidth
    nvlink_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth

    # Host-to-Device
    pcie_gen4 = Hardware.Cloud.A100.interconnect.bandwidth

    # Node-to-Node (Network)
    ib_hdr_gbps = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_HDR.bandwidth.to(Gbps).magnitude
    ib_hdr_bw = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_HDR.bandwidth

    ib_ndr_gbps = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth.to(Gbps).magnitude

    # Bandwidth-taper equation constants (H100-class)
    taper_hbm = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth
    taper_nvlink = nvlink_h100
    taper_pcie = Hardware.Cloud.H100.interconnect.bandwidth
    taper_net = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    # The "bandwidth taper" must hold: HBM > NVLink > PCIe > Network
    check(hbm_bw > nvlink_h100 > pcie_gen4 > ib_hdr_bw, "Bandwidth hierarchy violated. HBM > NVLink > PCIe > Network")
    check(taper_hbm > taper_nvlink > taper_pcie > taper_net, "bandwidth taper HBM > NVLink > PCIe > Network must hold")
    check(taper_pcie / taper_net < 2, "PCIe and the NIC are comparable, so the equation uses > rather than >> for that step")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    nvlink_a100_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink_a100, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink_h100, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)

    # Bandwidth-taper equation — one consistent chip (H100-class) so HBM, NVLink,
    # PCIe (Gen5), and the NDR network link cannot mix incompatible generations.
    taper_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\begin{{aligned}} \text{{HBM ({taper_hbm.to(GB/second).magnitude:.0f} GB/s)}} &\gg \text{{NVLink ({taper_nvlink.to(GB/second).magnitude:.0f} GB/s)}} \\ &\gg \text{{PCIe ({taper_pcie.to(GB/second).magnitude:.0f} GB/s)}} > \text{{Network ({taper_net.to(GB/second).magnitude:.0f} GB/s)}} \end{{aligned}}"
    )
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_hw_acceleration_margin_002.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical log-scale ladder of violet bandwidth bars, widest at top: HBM, then NVLink, then PCIe, down to a narrow network bar at the bottom."}

*Bandwidth tapers steeply as data moves farther from the accelerator.*
:::

Within a multi-accelerator server node, two interconnect tiers define this bandwidth taper below device memory:

1. **Device-device interconnect (NVLink/Infinity Fabric)**: Modern multi-GPU nodes use specialized high-speed bridges like NVLink[^fn-nvlink-interconnect-bandwidth]\index{NVLink!GPU interconnect}\index{GPU Interconnect!switching fabric}\index{Infinity Fabric!AMD interconnect} to connect accelerators directly, bypassing the host CPU. Bandwidth ranges from `{python} InterconnectHierarchy.nvlink_a100_gb_per_s_str` to `{python} InterconnectHierarchy.nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str` per GPU [@NVIDIA2020nvlink; @choquette2023]. This link matters whenever tensors must move between accelerators within one server, including model partitioning, activation exchange, and gradient synchronization during training. The architectural principle is the boundary: traffic that stays on the accelerator fabric is far cheaper than traffic that falls back through the host.
2. **Host-device interconnect (PCIe)**: The link between the CPU and the accelerator. Bandwidth ranges from 32 to 64 GB/s (PCIe Gen4/Gen5)\index{PCIe!host-device interconnect}\index{PCIe!bandwidth generations}. Host-staged training data can bottleneck here, although resident data, direct storage or network I/O, and coherent accelerator links can use other paths. Multi-GPU servers may also provide multiple PCIe links rather than a single shared 64 GB/s path.

[^fn-nvlink-interconnect-bandwidth]: **NVLink (NVIDIA Link)**\index{NVLink!definition}: This direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect exists to keep accelerator-to-accelerator traffic off PCIe when tensors must move inside a server. Its 600--900 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth is roughly 300--450 GB/s per direction under balanced full-duplex traffic, several times the directional bandwidth of a standard PCIe link, so workloads with frequent cross-device tensor movement can remain in the fast part of the bandwidth taper [@NVIDIA2020nvlink; @choquette2023]. Training algorithms determine how much tensor traffic must cross this link; the hardware fact needed here is the bandwidth gap. \index{NVLink!training scaling}

A third tier, the network link from one server to others, continues the taper beyond the node (@sec-hardware-acceleration-multichip-scaling-c649). Together the levels produce a characteristic bandwidth taper:

`{python} InterconnectHierarchy.taper_eq_math`

System efficiency depends on keeping tensors on the highest-bandwidth links available. Because PCIe and network links offer orders of magnitude less bandwidth and higher latency than on-package memory, placement and scheduling must minimize crossings across these boundaries.

#### Transfer optimization {#sec-hardware-acceleration-transfer-optimization-85a8}

The standard remedy for transfer overhead is the asynchronous pipeline of @sec-ml-frameworks-device-memory-management-9404. Batches staged in pinned (page-locked) host memory are copied by dedicated DMA engines while the accelerator computes on the previous batch. This double buffering conceals transfer latency behind arithmetic runtime whenever computation time exceeds transfer time ($\IronLawComputeTime \ge \BatchTransferTime$). When compute duration is too short to amortize the transfer, execution remains bus bound and the compute units stall.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The feeding problem, in which data delivery fails to keep pace with compute throughput, is established in @sec-data-engineering-feeding-problem.
:::

Unified Memory\index{Unified Memory!single address space} takes the opposite approach, presenting a single virtual address space that spans host DRAM and device HBM while the driver migrates pages on demand whenever either processor touches an address. On-demand migration removes staging code at the cost of predictability, because each page fault stalls execution and scattered accesses can thrash pages across the PCIe bus. High-throughput production workloads therefore rely on explicit, pipelined DMA transfers and reserve Unified Memory for prototyping or for applications where programmer productivity outweighs sustained hardware utilization. Once tensors reside on the accelerator, the model's own architecture determines whether weights, activations, or lookup tables dominate the device memory hierarchy.

### Model memory pressure {#sec-hardware-acceleration-model-memory-pressure-f95e}

An optimization that relieves memory pressure for one model family can leave another untouched: caching weights helps nothing when ResNet-50's early convolutions spill large activation maps to DRAM, and spatial activation tiling helps nothing when GPT-2 decode streams gigabytes of weights for a single token. Model architecture determines which memory term binds\index{Model Memory Pressure!architecture-specific}. The architectural reasons each family stresses memory as it does were traced in @sec-network-architectures-understanding-arithmetic-intensity-ade5; the hardware consequence differs by family, and the lighthouse models of @tbl-lighthouse-examples cover the cases.

Dense layers, the multilayer perceptron (MLP) blocks that every family contains, are bound by weight traffic at small batch. At batch size $\BatchSize= 1$, each parameter loaded from off-chip memory serves a single multiply-accumulate operation (often $\le 1\text{ FLOP/byte}$), so execution sits on the bandwidth slope; batching reuses each loaded weight across $\BatchSize$ inputs and moves the layer toward the compute ceiling. Dense weight matrices regularly exceed the tens of megabytes of on-chip SRAM, so parameters reside in HBM and stream through tiles that the accelerator double-buffers into SRAM [@chen2017]. The host link enters the critical path only when inputs stream from the host or when the model exceeds device memory.

Convolutional layers, the core of ResNet-50, place their memory pressure on activations rather than weights. Small filters sliding across feature maps supply three forms of reuse\index{CNN!spatial data reuse}: neighboring windows share input activations, each filter is applied at every spatial position, and each input channel feeds every output filter. Early layers therefore carry compact parameter tensors but large activation maps that exceed on-chip SRAM, and unoptimized layer-by-layer execution spills those maps to device DRAM. Spatial tiling keeps activation tiles, with their overlapping boundary pixels, in on-chip buffers so adjacent convolutions consume them without refetching [@chen2017].

Transformers such as GPT-2 stress both capacity and bandwidth, differently in each phase\index{Attention Mechanism!global token interaction}\index{Attention mechanism!memory pressure}. During training and prefill, standard attention materializes an $\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength$ score matrix for sequence length $\SequenceLength$ and moves $\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)$ bytes through HBM; IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention [@dao2022] keep those tiles in on-chip SRAM instead (@sec-model-training-flash-attention-ioaware-attention-optimization-3da0). During autoregressive decode, each generated token reads the weights and the accumulated key-value (KV) cache from HBM for a vector-matrix product, which binds generation speed to memory bandwidth.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ How much memory one request's KV cache claims as its sequence grows is established in @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1.
:::

Two other lighthouses stress memory in other ways. DLRM's sparse embedding lookups stress random-access bandwidth rather than dense compute, and MobileNetV2's depthwise convolutions trade arithmetic intensity for a smaller parameter footprint, so both reappear as memory-bound rows in the roofline operations table (@tbl-roofline-operations). Accelerators answer these divergent demands with the tiered hierarchy\index{Accelerator!design, workload-specific memory}. On-chip SRAM captures high-reuse activations and tiled matrix blocks at tens of terabytes per second, HBM stages large weight tensors and sequence state, and NVLink-class links carry tensors between accelerators when a model exceeds one device, avoiding the narrower host PCIe bus. @Tbl-mapping-strategies later pairs each family's memory profile with the mapping that answers it. A reference off-chip DRAM access costs far more energy per event than arithmetic (@fig-energy-hierarchy), so reducing repeated external accesses improves efficiency. Deciding whether a given kernel is limited by compute throughput or by memory bandwidth, however, requires an analytical boundary. The roofline model supplies that boundary by comparing operational intensity against hardware performance limits, so that optimization effort targets the resource that actually binds.

## Performance Bounds {#sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hw_acceleration_roofline_elbow.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Roofline elbow: a blue memory-bound slope rises left to right to a short orange compute-bound ceiling, with a dashed vertical ridge line at the bend and one workload dot sitting low on the blue slope, far below the ridge in the memory-bound region."}

*Low arithmetic intensity places the modeled throughput ceiling on the bandwidth slope.*
:::

The compute units fix how fast an accelerator can calculate, and the memory system fixes how fast it can be fed. A kernel's performance is bounded by whichever of the two runs out first. Putting numbers on that statement takes three pieces: the roofline's ceilings for each precision path, the ridge point at which they meet, and the hardware balance that moves the ridge from one generation to the next. The ResNet-50 INT8 workload meets its sharpest lesson in these bounds. The INT8 path doubles the H100's arithmetic ceiling without moving its bandwidth ceiling, so a layer that cleared the ridge at FP16 can fall below it at INT8.

### The roofline model {#sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-3e1a}

Quoting an accelerator's peak FLOP/s cannot explain why one kernel runs near the hardware ceiling while another stalls below 1 percent of peak on the same chip, because peak compute measures only what execution units can retire when operands are already in registers. With the compute units and memory systems that set the arithmetic and bandwidth ceilings now in place, the **roofline model**\index{Roofline model!definition}[^fn-roofline-performance-model] [@williams2009], which sorted training kernels in @sec-model-training-arithmetic-intensity-training-bottlenecks-4446, combines both limits on a single plot. It graphs attainable performance against arithmetic intensity and identifies the lower modeled ceiling, compute\index{Compute-Bound!roofline classification} or memory bandwidth\index{Memory-Bound!roofline classification}, for the chosen execution path before profiling establishes which physical resource limits execution.

[^fn-roofline-performance-model]: **Roofline model**\index{Roofline model!optimization diagnostic}: Introduced by @williams2009 at UC Berkeley, building on earlier I/O complexity work from the 1980s. Their specific contribution was making the compute vs. bandwidth trade-off visual and actionable: the characteristic roofline plot immediately reveals whether a kernel is compute bound (hitting the flat ceiling) or memory bound (hitting the sloped bandwidth line) and quantifies the gap to hardware limits. A kernel operating at only 50 percent of its ceiling has 2$\times$ theoretical headroom, but instruction mix, latency, and occupancy may prevent it from closing that gap.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: roofline-utilization-gap-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ROOFLINE UTILIZATION GAP CALCULATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: §Roofline Model and §Hardware ridge points prose; @fig-rising-ridge caption inputs
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate why newer accelerators are harder to saturate each generation.
# │ Show: Ridge points ~139 FLOP/byte (V100), ~153 (A100), ~296 (H100); rising gap.
# │ How: ridge_point() = peak_flops/memory_bw via Hardware Digital Twin; both in
# │      SI-compatible pint units so .to(flop/byte).magnitude extracts dimensionless ratio.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, check, fmt_arithmetic_intensity
from mlsysim import Hardware

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class RooflineGap:
    """
    Namespace for Roofline Utilization Gap.
    Scenario: Comparing Ridge Points across generations (V100 -> H100).
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Thresholds
    legacy_a100 = Scenarios.KernelAt200FlopPerByteA100  # a kernel tuned for the A100
    legacy_h100 = Scenarios.KernelAt200FlopPerByteH100  # the same kernel on the H100
    legacy_ai = legacy_a100.point_intensity.to(flop / byte).magnitude
    relu_ai = 0.125
    dense_matmul_dim = 1024
    dense_matmul_bytes_per_val = 2

    # Hardware Twins
    h_v100 = Hardware.Cloud.V100
    h_a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100
    h_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    h_b200 = Hardware.Cloud.B200

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Step 1: Ridge Points (FLOP/byte) directly from Twins
    v100_ridge = h_v100.ridge_point().to(flop / byte).magnitude
    a100_ridge = h_a100.ridge_point().to(flop / byte).magnitude
    h100_ridge = h_h100.ridge_point().to(flop / byte).magnitude
    b200_ridge = h_b200.ridge_point().to(flop / byte).magnitude

    # Step 2: FP32 Ridge for A100
    a100_ridge_fp32 = (h_a100.compute.precision_flops['fp32'] / h_a100.memory.bandwidth).to(flop / byte).magnitude

    # Step 3: Display specs for the ridge-point prose and fig-rising-ridge caption
    v100_flops = h_v100.compute.peak_flops
    v100_bandwidth = h_v100.memory.bandwidth
    a100_fp16_flops = h_a100.compute.peak_flops
    a100_bandwidth = h_a100.memory.bandwidth
    h100_fp16_flops = h_h100.compute.peak_flops
    h100_bandwidth = h_h100.memory.bandwidth

    # Step 4: Comparisons
    bw_growth = (h_h100.memory.bandwidth / h_a100.memory.bandwidth).to_base_units().magnitude
    flops_growth = (h_h100.compute.peak_flops / h_a100.compute.peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude
    relu_gap = h100_ridge / relu_ai
    # Idealized roofline gain for the legacy kernel: compute roof on the A100,
    # bandwidth slope on the H100 (both rates in FLOP/s).
    legacy_a100_rate = legacy_a100.attainable
    legacy_h100_rate = legacy_h100.attainable
    legacy_gain = (legacy_h100_rate / legacy_a100_rate).to_base_units().magnitude
    dense_matmul_flops = 2 * dense_matmul_dim**3
    dense_matmul_bytes = 3 * dense_matmul_dim**2 * dense_matmul_bytes_per_val
    dense_matmul_ai = dense_matmul_flops / dense_matmul_bytes

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    # Ridge points must climb: H100 > A100 > V100
    check(h100_ridge > a100_ridge > v100_ridge, f"Ridge points must climb. H100({h100_ridge:.0f}) > A100({a100_ridge:.0f}) > V100({v100_ridge:.0f}).")
    check(abs(b200_ridge / h100_ridge - 1) < 0.1, "Prose says the B200 ridge holds near the H100 level.")
    check(relu_gap >= 1000, f"ReLU gap ({relu_gap:.0f}x) is too small.")
    check(a100_ridge < legacy_ai < h100_ridge, "Prose says the legacy kernel sits above the A100 ridge and below the H100 ridge.")
    check(bw_growth < legacy_gain < flops_growth, f"Prose says the legacy gain lies between the bandwidth and compute ratios, got {legacy_gain:.2f}.")
    check(dense_matmul_ai > h100_ridge, f"Large matmul should clear the H100 ridge, got AI={dense_matmul_ai:.0f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    v100_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(v100_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    v100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(v100_bandwidth, unit=TB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(a100_fp16_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    a100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(a100_bandwidth, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_fp16_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bandwidth, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    h100_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(h_h100.ridge_point(), unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    v100_ridge_int_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(round(v100_ridge) * flop / byte, unit=flop / byte, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_ridge_int_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(round(h100_ridge) * flop / byte, unit=flop / byte, precision=0, commas=False)
    b200_ridge_int_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(round(b200_ridge) * flop / byte, unit=flop / byte, precision=0, commas=False)

    legacy_ai_str = fmt(legacy_ai, precision=0, commas=False)
    relu_ai_str = fmt(relu_ai, precision=3, commas=False)
    dense_matmul_dim_str = fmt(dense_matmul_dim, precision=0, commas=False)
    dense_matmul_ai_str = fmt(dense_matmul_ai, precision=1, commas=False)
    bandwidth_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bw_growth, precision=1, commas=False)
    flops_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(flops_growth, precision=1, commas=False)
    legacy_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(legacy_gain, precision=1, commas=False)
    full_util_pct_str = fmt_percent(1.0, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

Performance is bounded by two ceilings, as @eq-roofline formalizes; it writes the bound of the arithmetic intensity law (principle \ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}) as an idealized equality that ignores launch and synchronization overheads. Here, attainable performance $\AttainableComputeRate$ and peak compute $\PeakRate$ are in FLOP/s (often reported as TFLOP/s), peak bandwidth $\Bandwidth$ is in bytes/s (often TB/s), and arithmetic intensity $\ArithmeticIntensity$ is in FLOP/byte:
$$\AttainableComputeRate = \min(\PeakRate, \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity)$$ {#eq-roofline}

Arithmetic intensity $\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume$ is the ratio of operations to bytes moved across the memory interface being modeled (definition \ref{dfn-nn-computation-arithmetic-intensity}), and it depends on the implementation as well as the operation. Under the stated traffic models, a large well-tiled `{python} RooflineGap.dense_matmul_dim_str` $\times$ `{python} RooflineGap.dense_matmul_dim_str` multiply reaches about `{python} RooflineGap.dense_matmul_ai_str` FLOP/byte, while standalone ReLU is about `{python} RooflineGap.relu_ai_str` FLOP/byte, so the two meet different ceilings on the same hardware.

The roofline visualization shows performance (TFLOP/s) on the vertical axis and arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte) on the horizontal axis. At low arithmetic intensity, the upper bound increases linearly along the memory bandwidth slope ($\Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity$). Above the ridge point, the upper bound is peak compute ($\PeakRate$). A kernel approaching the slope is bandwidth limited, while one approaching the flat roof is compute limited on the specified path. Merely lying below either line does not establish the cause; profiling explains that remaining gap. @Sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-bottleneck-diagnostic-3fc9 maps each regime to the optimizations that pay off and the ones that waste effort, so classifying a kernel tells the engineer whether more bandwidth, less traffic, or more arithmetic throughput is the investment to test first.

### Hardware ridge points {#sec-hardware-acceleration-hardware-balance}

A kernel with `{python} RooflineGap.legacy_ai_str` FLOP/byte that was comfortably compute bound on a V100 or A100 falls below the compute ceiling when migrated unchanged to an H100, because different devices place the compute-bandwidth boundary at different intensities. The **ridge point**\index{Ridge point!definition}, the balance point between a machine's memory and compute limits previewed alongside the iron law, is a property of the device. Computer architects call the same ratio the **hardware balance $(\RooflineRidgePoint)$**\index{Hardware balance}, peak arithmetic throughput divided by peak memory bandwidth, the intensity at which the roofline's compute and bandwidth ceilings intersect:
$$ \RooflineRidgePoint = \frac{\PeakRate}{\Bandwidth} $$

The ratio sets a device-specific boundary. Depending on the chosen precision, the H100 requires about `{python} RooflineGap.h100_ridge_str` on its dense FP16 path (`{python} RooflineGap.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str`) to reach its arithmetic ceiling, and twice that on its INT8 path, whereas a microcontroller may have a much lower ridge point. The same kernel can therefore be bandwidth bound on a compute-dense accelerator and compute bound on an edge processor. Hardware balance does not label either device as universally efficient; it identifies how much reuse a workload needs on that device.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: compute-bandwidth-divergence-calc
# +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# | COMPUTE VS BANDWIDTH GROWTH, V100 THROUGH B200
# +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# | Context: the lead-in prose above @fig-rising-ridge.
# |
# | Goal: Quantify how much faster peak dense FP16 throughput grew than memory
# |       bandwidth across five NVIDIA datacenter generations.
# | Show: Growth multiples for compute, for bandwidth, and for the gap between
# |       them, which is the ridge-point rise @fig-rising-ridge then plots.
# | How:  Read peak_flops and memory.bandwidth per generation from the hardware
# |       registry and normalize both series to the V100 baseline.
# +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_multiple, MarkdownStr

class ComputeBandwidthDivergence:
    """Registry-sourced compute vs bandwidth growth, V100 through B200."""

    # +-- 1. LOAD (Constants) --------------------------------------------------
    gens = Scenarios.NvidiaGenerationsV100ToB200
    generations = gens.accelerators

    # +-- 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ---------------------------------------------
    # A comprehension body cannot see class-scope names, so the baselines are
    # divided out in plain expressions rather than inside a comprehension.
    years = [g.release_year for g in generations]
    compute = [g.compute.peak_flops.to(TFLOP / second).magnitude for g in generations]
    bandwidth = [g.memory.bandwidth.to(GB / second).magnitude for g in generations]
    compute_growth = gens.compute_growth
    bandwidth_growth = gens.bandwidth_growth
    gap_growth = gens.gap_growth

    # +-- 3. GUARD (Invariants) ------------------------------------------------
    check(compute_growth > bandwidth_growth, "Compute must outgrow bandwidth for the divergence to exist.")
    check(compute[3] == compute[2], "H200 should match H100 peak compute; the narrowing lesson depends on it.")
    check(bandwidth[3] > bandwidth[2], "H200 should exceed H100 bandwidth; the narrowing lesson depends on it.")

    # +-- 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) -----------------------------------------------
    span_str = MarkdownStr(f"{years[0]}--{years[-1]}")
    compute_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(compute_growth, precision=0, commas=False)
    bandwidth_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bandwidth_growth, precision=1, commas=False)
    gap_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(gap_growth, precision=1, commas=False)
```

Peak computational capability has expanded faster than memory bus performance across accelerator generations, and the size of that mismatch is what sets how much data reuse a kernel needs to stay fed. Across `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.span_str`, NVIDIA's data center generations multiplied dense FP16 compute by `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.compute_growth_mult_str` and memory bandwidth by only `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.bandwidth_growth_mult_str`, a `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.gap_growth_mult_str` rise in the reuse a kernel needs on B200 relative to V100.

That ratio measures how far the hardware ridge point\index{Ridge Point!hardware comparison}, the threshold a kernel must clear to become compute bound, has risen since the V100. @Fig-rising-ridge plots it generation by generation, leaving out the H200 exception. The doubling of the gap appears directly as the ridge point roughly doubling from V100 (`{python} RooflineGap.v100_ridge_int_str`) to H100 (`{python} RooflineGap.h100_ridge_int_str`) and then holding near that level on B200 (`{python} RooflineGap.b200_ridge_int_str`). A kernel that cleared the V100 ridge comfortably can fall below the H100 ridge without any change to its code, so newer hardware demands more operational reuse before execution reaches peak throughput.

::: {#fig-rising-ridge fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Rising Ridge**: Hardware arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte) over time computed as each chip's dense FP16 tensor peak divided by its memory bandwidth: `{python} RooflineGap.v100_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.v100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for V100, `{python} RooflineGap.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.a100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for A100, and `{python} RooflineGap.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for H100. This is the arithmetic intensity a kernel must reach before compute rather than bandwidth limits it. As compute capability grows faster than memory bandwidth, the ridge point rises from V100 through H100 and remains high on B200. This trend explains why architectures with high data reuse flourish while low-reuse workloads face a growing performance penalty." fig-alt="Line plot showing dense-FP16 arithmetic intensity ridge points: about 140 FLOP/byte for V100, 153 for A100, 295 for H100, and 281 for B200. Shaded regions indicate memory-rich and compute-dense zones."}


The generations in @fig-rising-ridge come from one vendor, but the divergence is industry-wide. @Fig-bandwidth-envelope tracks the best memory bandwidth and the best dense FP16/BF16 tensor throughput among `{python} BandwidthEnvelope.device_count_str` accelerators from every major vendor released since 2017 [@epochai2026hardware]. Measured from TPU v2, the best compute rate grew about `{python} BandwidthEnvelope.compute_growth_mult_str` while the best bandwidth grew about `{python} BandwidthEnvelope.bandwidth_growth_mult_str`, so the ridge point of the leading devices rose several-fold. The ratio is larger than the NVIDIA-only one above because TPU v2's 16-bit baseline was low. Since early 2025 the best bandwidth has held near `{python} BandwidthEnvelope.best_bandwidth_str`, and the best dense FP16 rate has leveled as well, because new devices put their added arithmetic into FP8 and FP4 paths rather than 16-bit ones. For a kernel whose reuse stays fixed, this rising ridge shows up as a ceiling on achievable utilization that falls with each generation.

::: {#fig-bandwidth-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Compute and Bandwidth Across Vendors**: Dense FP16/BF16 tensor throughput and memory bandwidth of machine learning accelerators from all major vendors with at least 16 GB of off-chip memory, each relative to TPU v2 (2017) on a logarithmic axis. Points are individual devices; step lines track the best device released to date. Compute pulls away from bandwidth, and both best-device envelopes level off in 2025 and 2026 as added arithmetic moves into lower-precision formats. Data from @epochai2026hardware." fig-alt="Scatter plot with two step lines on a logarithmic axis from 2017 to 2026, both starting at 1 for TPU v2. A red step line for best dense FP16 throughput climbs to about 55 by 2025 and stays flat. A blue step line for best memory bandwidth climbs more slowly to about 13 by early 2025 and stays flat. Faint red and blue points mark individual devices below each line."}

```{python}
_b0 = _E.baseline["memory_bandwidth_bytes_per_s"]
_f0 = _E.baseline["fp16_tensor_flops"]

ax.step(
    [_yr(d) for d, _ in _E.bw_env],
    [v / _b0 for _, v in _E.bw_env],
    where="post",
    color=COLORS["BlueLine"],
    lw=2,
    label="Memory bandwidth (best device to date)",
)
ax.step(
    [_yr(d) for d, _ in _E.fl_env],
    [v / _f0 for _, v in _E.fl_env],
    where="post",
    color=COLORS["RedLine"],
    lw=2,
    label="Dense FP16/BF16 throughput (best device to date)",
)
ax.set_yscale("log")
```
