## Hardware Mapping {#sec-hardware-acceleration-hardware-mapping-fundamentals-neural-networks-f9a9}

Consider one of ResNet-50's $3{\times}3$ convolutions running on an accelerator tile. The mathematical operation is fixed, but the execution plan is not. One schedule can keep a filter in local registers while many output pixels stream past it; another can advance pixel by pixel and reload the same filter values repeatedly from a slower memory tier. Both schedules compute the same tensor. Only one turns the reuse in the convolution into real bandwidth savings.

::: {#dfn-hw-acceleration-mapping-ai-acceleration .callout-definition title="Mapping in AI acceleration"}

***Mapping in AI acceleration***\index{Hardware Mapping!definition} is the accelerator-compiler process of binding the logical computation graph to the physical hardware topology by deciding which operations execute on which processing elements, which data resides in which memory tier, and in what temporal order.

1.  **Significance**: Within the D·A·M taxonomy, mapping is a machine-axis decision that helps determine how closely an operation approaches the roofline bound $\min(\PeakRate,\; \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity)$. A poor tiling choice that forces unnecessary DRAM accesses can reduce effective arithmetic intensity enough to move a nominally compute-bound operation into the bandwidth-bound regime.
2.  **Distinction**: Traditional compilation often emphasizes instruction selection, register allocation, and scheduling for general-purpose processors. Accelerator mapping gives equal prominence to spatial placement and explicit data movement across a dataflow architecture\index{Dataflow Architecture!definition}. The reason is physical: as quantified by the storage-tier energy ladder in @fig-energy-hierarchy, an off-chip DRAM access costs about `{python} EnergyGapAnchor.dram_vs_fp32_mult_str` the energy of an FP32 multiply, making operand placement as critical to efficiency as the execution unit that evaluates it.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that mapping is automatically handled by frameworks. For general GPU workloads, compilers such as Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA) can find strong mappings for common kernels. For specialized accelerators (systolic arrays, custom ASICs), compiler-generated mappings may still lag hand-tuned schedules because the compiler's search space is limited by the time budget at compilation.

:::

The convolution example exposes the three decisions that recur throughout accelerator compilation. Placement assigns the multiply-accumulate work to processing elements so parallelism does not turn into idle time or interconnect congestion. Allocation keeps weights, activations, and partial sums in the memory tier where their next use will occur, rather than letting reuse spill back to DRAM. Scheduling orders loops and kernels so the chosen placement and allocation remain valid over time. A poor choice in any one dimension can collapse a high-arithmetic-intensity operation back into a bandwidth-bound execution. In practice, these choices are too coupled for developers to manage by hand at model scale. Systems such as XLA\index{XLA!accelerator compilation}, TVM\index{Apache TVM!accelerator compilation}, and TensorRT\index{TensorRT!accelerator compilation} therefore lower high-level models and search or select execution plans within their compile-time and hardware budgets. @Sec-hardware-acceleration-compiler-support-172e examines that compiler support in detail.

### Placement and allocation {#sec-hardware-acceleration-computation-placement-23d2}

Spatial and storage mapping decisions pull against each other across the chip. Computation placement\index{Computation Placement!processing element assignment} spreads operations across processing elements to expose parallelism, but placing producer and consumer operations on distant units increases the interconnect bandwidth required to shuttle intermediate tensors between them. Memory allocation stages operands in fast on-chip buffers to cut access latency, but the small capacity of registers and SRAM limits how many processing elements can hold their working sets concurrently. Getting either side wrong leaves thousands of execution units idle or starved for data.

#### Computation placement {#sec-hardware-acceleration-computation-placement-e03f}

The scale of modern hardware magnifies any spatial imbalance: the NVIDIA H100 contains more than 16,000 CUDA cores\index{CUDA!cores, streaming processors} and more than 500 Tensor Cores [@choquette2023], TPUs organize thousands of multiply-accumulate units into systolic arrays [@jouppi2017], and wafer-scale processors such as Cerebras' CS-2 integrate more than 850,000 cores [@Cerebras2021]. Across arrays of that size, even a small fraction of idle processing elements or redundant cross-chip transfers wastes substantial time and energy.

The difficulty of placement depends on workload regularity. Convolutional networks and dense transformer operations possess regular access patterns that tile predictably, though transformer architectures mix operations with distinct tensor shapes and reuse profiles. Graph neural networks (GNNs)\index{Graph Neural Network!irregular computation} present greater difficulty: sparse, input-dependent neighborhood aggregations introduce load imbalance and non-uniform communication across processing elements. @Tbl-placement-challenges summarizes these core placement challenges and their operational impact.

| **Challenge**                                    | **Impact on execution**                                                                                            | **Key Considerations for Placement**                                                        |
|:-------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Workload imbalance**\index{Workload imbalance} | Some processing elements finish early while others remain overloaded, leading to idle compute resources.           | Distribute operations evenly to prevent stalls and ensure full utilization of PEs.          |
| **Irregular computation patterns**               | Sparse graphs, routing, and variable shapes can create nonuniform work that complicates static placement.          | Use adaptive placement when workload characteristics vary at run time.                      |
| **Excessive data movement**                      | Frequent memory transfers introduce latency and increase power consumption.                                        | Keep frequently used data close to the compute units and minimize off-chip memory accesses. |
| **Limited interconnect bandwidth**               | Poorly placed operations can create congestion, slowing data movement between PEs.                                 | Optimize spatial and temporal placement to reduce communication overhead.                   |
| **Model-specific execution needs**               | CNNs, transformers, and GNNs require different execution patterns, making a single placement strategy ineffective. | Tailor placement strategies to match the computational structure of each model type.        |

: **Computation Placement Challenges**: Effective neural network deployment requires strategic allocation of computations to processing elements, balancing workload distribution, data movement costs, and hardware constraints to maximize execution efficiency. These challenges guide the design of mapping strategies that optimize resource utilization and minimize communication overhead. {#tbl-placement-challenges tbl-colwidths="[20,45,35]"}

Static spatial mappings suffice for regular dense operations whose shapes and loop bounds are known ahead of time. Workloads with dynamic shapes, sparsity, or mixture-of-experts routing instead require runtime scheduling to balance execution across processing elements. Yet even an optimal computation placement stalls if the required operands are not staged in time: compute units can execute only as fast as operands arrive from the memory hierarchy.

#### Memory allocation {#sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-allocation-faec}

While computation placement determines where operations execute, memory allocation defines where data resides and how it flows through the hierarchy. The goal is to keep reused data near the processing elements without exceeding faster-tier capacity. GPUs expose global memory, shared memory, caches, and registers that kernels coordinate through tiling [@NVIDIA2020]. TPUs use on-chip SRAM buffers to stage the activations that flow horizontally through the 2D systolic-array dataflow [@jouppi2017] of @fig-systolic-array, with partial sums flowing vertically, while wafer-scale processors partition memory and computation to control interconnect traffic [@Cerebras2021]. General-purpose processors and accelerators both use memory hierarchies, but many accelerators expose more placement decisions to compilers and kernels. When allocation fails to exploit locality, processing elements stall waiting for operands, driving down utilization and dissipating energy across the memory bus.

The severity of these penalties varies by workload. Convolutional networks rely on structured, localized access patterns and benefit from well-defined memory layouts that support predictable reuse [@chen2016eyeriss]. Transformers require access to large parameter sets and intermediate activations, making them sensitive to capacity and bandwidth. Graph neural networks add irregular sparse structures that complicate allocation and prefetching.

Capacity is only the first allocation test. A tensor can fit in accelerator memory yet still dominate execution if each kernel rereads it from a distant tier; conversely, tiling can keep a larger working set efficient by preserving reuse locally. The allocation diagnostic is therefore traffic, not capacity alone: compilers must track how frequently values cross each memory boundary and keep high-reuse tensors in the fastest feasible tier. Systems combine static memory plans for known shapes with dynamic buffer management when shapes vary, while device capacity limits which models fit without partitioning or offload. @Tbl-memory-allocation summarizes these allocation challenges across the hierarchy.

| Challenge                            | Impact on Execution                                                                    | **Key Considerations for Allocation**                                                             |
|:-------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **High memory latency**              | Slow data access delays execution and reduces throughput.                              | Prioritize placing frequently accessed data in faster memory locations.                           |
| **Limited on-chip storage**          | Small local memory constrains the amount of data available near compute units.         | Allocate storage efficiently to maximize data availability without exceeding hardware limits.     |
| **High off-chip bandwidth demand**   | Frequent access to external memory increases delays and power consumption.             | Reduce unnecessary memory transfers by carefully managing when and how data is moved.             |
| **Irregular memory access patterns** | Some models require accessing data unpredictably, leading to inefficient memory usage. | Organize memory layout to align with access patterns and minimize unnecessary data movement.      |
| **Model-specific memory needs**      | Different models require different allocation strategies to optimize performance.      | Tailor allocation decisions based on the structure and execution characteristics of the workload. |

: **Memory Allocation Challenges**: Efficient memory management in AI accelerators balances data access speed with hardware constraints, mitigating performance bottlenecks caused by latency, bandwidth limitations, and irregular data patterns. Complex models such as transformers and graph networks impose variable and demanding memory requirements that amplify these challenges. {#tbl-memory-allocation tbl-colwidths="[17,40,43]"}

### Combinatorial complexity {#sec-hardware-acceleration-combinatorial-complexity-ea33}

The convolution that opened this section illustrates why hardware mapping becomes a combinatorial search problem\index{Hardware Mapping!combinatorial search space}. Keeping a filter resident in local storage improves reuse only if the assigned processing elements have sufficient storage and if the loop schedule revisits that filter before eviction. Similarly, parallelizing across more processing elements improves throughput only until synchronization overhead and interconnect contention erode the benefit. Because changing one decision alters the feasible and efficient choices for the others, compilers must evaluate placement, allocation, and scheduling jointly rather than independently. @Tbl-combinatorial-complexity summarizes these recurring trade-offs across the execution stack.

| Dimension                             | **Placement considerations**                                                                             | **Allocation and Scheduling Considerations**                                                         |
|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Computational granularity**         | Fine-grained placement enables greater parallelism but increases synchronization overhead.               | Coarse-grained scheduling reduces synchronization overhead but may limit flexibility.                |
| **Spatial vs. Temporal Mapping**      | Spatial placement enhances parallel execution but can lead to resource contention and memory congestion. | Temporal scheduling balances resource sharing but may reduce overall throughput.                     |
| **Memory and Data Locality**          | Placing data closer to compute units minimizes latency but may reduce overall memory availability.       | Allocating data across multiple memory levels increases capacity but introduces higher access costs. |
| **Communication and synchronization** | Co-locating compute units reduces communication latency but may introduce contention.                    | Scheduling synchronization mechanisms mitigates stalls but can introduce additional overhead.        |
| **Dataflow and Execution Ordering**   | Static placement simplifies execution but limits adaptability to workload variations.                    | Dynamic scheduling improves adaptability but adds scheduling complexity.                             |

: **Placement-Allocation-Scheduling Trade-Offs**: AI accelerator performance depends on mapping computations to hardware, allocating data to memory tiers, and scheduling execution over time. Careful consideration of these interdependent factors is essential for maximizing throughput and minimizing energy consumption. {#tbl-combinatorial-complexity tbl-colwidths="[25,38,37]"}

#### Counting the search space {#sec-hardware-acceleration-ordering-computation-execution-59e5}

Evaluating these trade-offs requires navigating an unconstrained search space governed by three structural decisions: loop execution order, spatial parallelization across processing elements, and memory placement across the hierarchy. Counting each dimension on its own shows why exhaustive search is impractical.

Machine learning workloads are expressed as nested loops over tensor dimensions, and the loop execution order\index{Loop Ordering!computational efficiency} dictates which tensor elements remain resident in registers or SRAM between iterations. Ignoring dependences and equivalent orderings, the number of ways to arrange $\LoopNestDepth$ loops has the toy upper bound:
$$
\LoopOrderCount= \LoopNestDepth!
$$
A convolutional layer with seven loop dimensions already has $7! = 5{,}040$ possible execution orders. If each memory level could choose an ordering independently, the toy upper bound would expand as:
$$
(\LoopNestDepth!)^{\MemoryHierarchyLevelCount}
$$
where $\MemoryHierarchyLevelCount$ is the number of memory hierarchy levels. A suboptimal ordering evicts values prematurely and multiplies DRAM traffic, whereas an optimized ordering maximizes reuse in local SRAM and caches [@sze2017].

Parallelization multiplies the count again. Parallelizing outer independent loops (such as batch or output feature channels) lets each core execute without interconnect traffic, whereas parallelizing an inner reduction loop requires cross-core synchronization and collective communication. Before legality and capacity constraints are applied, the number of ordered ways to select loops for parallel execution has the upper bound:
$$
\LoopParallelizationChoiceCount= \frac{\LoopNestDepth!}{(\LoopNestDepth-\ParallelLoopCount)!}
$$
where $\ParallelLoopCount$ is the number of loops selected for parallel execution; three of six loops already give $6!/3! = 120$ candidates, each with different demands on synchronization, interconnect bandwidth, and PE utilization. Memory placement is the third dimension, and physical capacity bounds it. In a toy model where five tensor structures can each be assigned to one of four storage handling choices at a single hierarchy level, a single level already yields $4^5 = 1{,}024$ placement combinations, and choosing independently across three memory levels expands the unconstrained count to $(4^5)^3 = 4^{15}$ placements. Because an off-chip DRAM fetch costs roughly 128$\times$ more energy than a read from an 8 KB SRAM array (@fig-energy-hierarchy), where each tensor resides directly dictates the achieved arithmetic intensity. Yet an operand tile can remain in on-chip SRAM only if its working set fits the allocated buffer. Larger resident tiles raise reuse but consume scarce capacity and register pressure, potentially reducing thread concurrency or forcing spills to slower tiers.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_hw_acceleration_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three gray bars on a log scale from 1, each counting choices at a single memory level using the section's separate toy examples: memory placement at 4 to the 5th, or 1,024; loop ordering at 7 factorial, or 5,040; and parallelization at 6 factorial over 3 factorial, or 120."}

*Per memory level, from the section's separate toy examples: $4^5 = 1{,}024$ placements, $7! = 5{,}040$ orders, $6!/3! = 120$ parallelizations. The product is raised to the number of levels, so three levels give $4^{15}$ placements alone.*
:::

These structural choices (loop ordering, spatial parallelization across processing elements, tile sizing, and memory placement) are deeply coupled. Choosing an output-stationary schedule, for example, pins accumulators in local registers and dictates which loops can be mapped spatially across processing elements without requiring inter-core reduction networks. Conversely, parallelizing across more execution units reduces the per-core SRAM budget available for operand staging, forcing smaller tile dimensions and increasing off-chip memory traffic.

While the unconstrained Cartesian product of these decisions suggests a very large combinatorial space, hardware capacity limits, data dependencies, and symmetry prune the vast majority of candidates as either physically illegal or strictly dominated. Exhaustive search across arbitrary loop permutations and placement choices is therefore both unnecessary and intractable. Production compilers and kernel developers manage this complexity by structuring their search around a small family of canonical dataflow patterns, spatial and temporal schedules engineered to exploit the specific reuse properties of neural network operators.

### Dataflow optimization {#sec-hardware-acceleration-dataflow-optimization-strategies-ce52}

Those canonical patterns exist because two mathematically identical loop schedules for the same convolution can differ by more than an order of magnitude in off-chip weight reads (example \ref{exmp-hw-acceleration-loop-ordering-small-convolution}), and every avoided read that would have reached DRAM saves the most expensive access on the energy ladder. While spatial and temporal mapping establish where operations execute and where operands reside, **dataflow optimization**\index{Dataflow optimization!data movement minimization} governs the exact trajectories and schedules of data moving through processing elements and the memory hierarchy to maximize operand reuse. In a systolic array or tiled vector unit, the temporal schedule and spatial routing of weights, inputs, and partial sums dictate how frequently operands must be fetched from energy-expensive DRAM rather than reused from local registers or scratchpads. By controlling off-chip traffic, the dataflow establishes the effective operational intensity of the kernel, determining whether execution achieves the compute-bound plateau or stalls in the bandwidth-bound regime of the roofline model. Optimizing compilers (@sec-hardware-acceleration-compiler-support-172e) and runtime systems (@sec-hardware-acceleration-runtime-support-f94f) therefore tailor dataflow patterns to match the reuse characteristics of each layer to the hardware constraints of the target accelerator.

Three recurring architectural decisions structure this design space, providing a compact vocabulary for navigating dataflow choices without exhaustive search across billions of candidate schedules:

1. **Locality**: Stationary operand selection\index{Data movement!optimization strategies} (weight-stationary, output-stationary, or input-stationary) dictates which tensor remains pinned in local registers or processing-element scratchpads, trading off memory traffic against register pressure.
2. **Organization**: Physical tensor layouts\index{Tensor layout!memory-aware} (such as channels-last `NHWC`\index{NHWC!channels-last layout} versus channels-first `NCHW`\index{NCHW!channels-first layout}) govern whether memory accesses match hardware memory controller burst sizes and SIMD vector widths, preventing uncoalesced memory transactions.
3. **Combination**: Kernel fusion\index{Kernel fusion!reducing memory writes} and loop tiling\index{Tiling!memory optimization} partition iteration spaces and merge adjacent operations to eliminate round-trips to off-chip memory for intermediate tensors.

### Stationary dataflows {#sec-hardware-acceleration-data-movement-patterns-3b06}

The first lever, locality, begins with the reuse already present in the inner loops of a tensor operator. Because fetching an operand from DRAM costs orders of magnitude more energy than the arithmetic operation that consumes it (@fig-energy-hierarchy) [@chen2016eyeriss], a data movement strategy\index{Data movement!energy dominance} must hold reused values in local registers or scratchpads rather than refetching them across the memory bus. @Lst-matmul_data_movement shows the canonical three-loop matrix multiplication, exposing the three distinct reuse streams across weights, inputs, and partial sums that a stationary schedule can pin on chip.

::: {#lst-matmul_data_movement lst-cap="**Naïve Matrix-Multiplication Dataflow**: The loop nest revisits weight rows, input columns, and output accumulators, exposing the reuse that a mapping must capture in local memory."}

```{.python}
# Matrix multiplication where:
# weights: [512x256] - model parameters
# input:   [256x32]  - batch of activations
# Z:       [512x32]  - output activations

# Computing each output element Z[i,j]:
for i in range(512):
    for j in range(32):
        for k in range(256):
            Z[i, j] += weights[i, k] * input[k, j]
```

:::

Every operand in this loop nest is reused, but along a different loop. Each weight `weights[i, k]` is used once for each of the 32 output columns, each input `input[k, j]` is used once for each of the 512 output rows, and each output `Z[i, j]` accumulates 256 products before it is final. A processing element's local storage holds only a small tile at a time, so the mapping cannot capture all three reuses at once. Fetching from DRAM whichever operand is not held locally, on every use, is what turns a compute-bound kernel into a memory-bound one [@han2016].

The central dataflow decision\index{Dataflow!optimization strategies}\index{Data reuse!accelerator optimization} is therefore which operand to keep local. The loop order answers it: whatever the innermost loops touch repeatedly without changing stays resident, and everything else streams. @Lst-stationary_dataflows reorders the same computation three ways, and the three orders are the three classic stationary dataflows.

::: {#lst-stationary_dataflows lst-cap="**Three Stationary Dataflows**: The same matrix multiplication as the naïve loop, reordered three ways; the operand held fixed across the innermost loop is the one fetched once and reused from local storage, while the other two stream."}

```{.python}
# Weight stationary: hold one weight, stream inputs and partial sums past it
for i in range(512):
    for k in range(256):
        w = weights[i, k]  # fetched once, reused 32 times
        for j in range(32):
            Z[i, j] += w * input[k, j]

# Output stationary: hold one partial sum, stream weights and inputs past it
for i in range(512):
    for j in range(32):
        acc = 0  # stays in a local accumulator
        for k in range(256):
            acc += weights[i, k] * input[k, j]
        Z[i, j] = acc  # written once

# Input stationary: hold one input, stream weights and partial sums past it
for k in range(256):
    for j in range(32):
        x = input[k, j]  # fetched once, reused 512 times
        for i in range(512):
            Z[i, j] += weights[i, k] * x
```

:::

A weight-stationary\index{Weight-stationary!CNN optimization} dataflow keeps parameters on chip, so each weight crosses the expensive memory boundary once no matter how many inputs it touches. That pays off wherever one filter or weight tile is applied to many inputs, as in convolutions and batched matrix multiplication, and it is the canonical TPU dataflow traced cycle by cycle in @sec-hardware-acceleration-tiling-principle. The saved traffic reappears on the other operands: inputs must arrive fast enough to keep the resident weights busy, and partial sums must move between processing elements as they accumulate. The resident tile is also bounded by on-chip capacity, so a layer whose weights far exceed it must cycle weight tiles through, reloading the inputs for each one.

An output-stationary\index{Output-stationary!partial sum accumulation} dataflow keeps each running sum in a local accumulator until all of its contributions have arrived, so every output is written to memory exactly once [@chen2016eyeriss]. It suits layers with wide fan-in, such as fully connected layers and attention projections, where writing a partial sum out after every step would cost far more than the reads it avoids. The cost is two operand streams at once, since both weights and inputs must now be delivered from memory. The naïve loop in @lst-matmul_data_movement already has this order, because its innermost loop runs over $\GemmReductionIndex$ while $\MatrixRowIndex$ and $\MatrixColumnIndex$ stay fixed.

An input-stationary\index{Input-stationary!dataflow strategy} dataflow keeps an activation tile local while weights stream past it. It pays off when one activation feeds several computations before eviction, as when a transformer token's activation feeds the query, key, and value projections. Its costs mirror weight stationary's, with weights now streaming from memory and partial sums still moving as they accumulate.

::: {#exmp-hw-acceleration-loop-ordering-small-convolution .callout-example title="Loop ordering in a small convolution"}

Consider a convolution applying 16 filters of size $3{\times}3$ to an $8{\times}8$ single-channel input. The computation can be expressed as five nested loops iterating over output rows ($\OutputFeatureMapHeight$), output columns ($\OutputFeatureMapWidth$), filter count ($\LayerOutputWidth$), filter height ($\KernelHeight$), and filter width ($\KernelWidth$). The $5! = 120$ permutations are an unconstrained upper bound: legal orderings preserve the mathematical result, although floating-point reduction order can change rounding, and they generate different memory traffic.

**Ordering A (weight-stationary)**: Place the filter loops ($\LayerOutputWidth$, $\KernelHeight$, $\KernelWidth$) outermost and the spatial loops ($\OutputFeatureMapHeight$, $\OutputFeatureMapWidth$) innermost. Each $3{\times}3$ filter is loaded into registers once and then applied across all 36 output positions before the next filter is loaded. Total weight loads: $16 \times 9 = 144$ values, each loaded exactly once.

**Ordering B (output-stationary, filters spilled)**: Place the spatial loops outermost and the filter loops innermost. For every output position, all 16 filters must be loaded, applied, and their partial sums accumulated before advancing to the next position. If the register file cannot hold all 16 filters simultaneously, filters are repeatedly fetched from cache or DRAM. In the worst case, each of the 36 output positions reloads all 144 filter weights, producing $36 \times 144 = 5{,}184$ weight reads.

**Systems insight**: Under these two limiting assumptions, Ordering A reduces modeled weight reads by 36$\times$ relative to the worst case for Ordering B. Real kernels also account for activation and partial-sum traffic, register capacity, cache behavior, and vectorization. The example nevertheless shows why two mathematically equivalent loop orders can place widely different demands on the memory system.

:::

The three strategies form a decision framework rather than a quality ranking. The right choice is the operand with the highest reuse relative to the on-chip storage it would occupy, which depends on layer dimensions and batch size, so compilers select among them per layer. Convolution-specific designs add a fourth label, row-stationary\index{Eyeriss!row-stationary dataflow}. The Eyeriss accelerator maps one-dimensional rows of filter weights and input activations to processing-element registers and accumulates rows of partial sums locally, a hybrid that captures more of a convolution's multidimensional reuse than fixing any single operand [@chen2016eyeriss].

### Tiling {#sec-hardware-acceleration-tiling-principle}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tiling-principle-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TILING PRINCIPLE: SRAM TO SYSTOLIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "The Tiling Principle" section
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate how large matrices are partitioned for hardware.
# │ Show: A 4096 GEMM has 1,024 output tiles and 32,768 tile products.
# │ How: Calculate tile count and memory reuse factors.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_flop_rate

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class TilingPrinciple:
    """
    Namespace for The Tiling Principle calculation.
    Scenario: Mapping a Transformer hidden layer to a Systolic Array.
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    tiling = Scenarios.Matmul4096Fp16Tile128  # a 4,096-square multiply on a 128-wide array's tiles
    layer_dim = tiling.m  # Standard Transformer layer width
    array_dim = tiling.tile_m  # 128

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Step 1: Number of tiles per dimension
    tiles_per_dim = tiling.tiles_m
    output_tiles = tiling.output_tiles
    tile_products = tiling.tile_products

    # Step 2: Each tile of weights is loaded once and used for 'layer_dim' MACs
    reuse_factor = array_dim

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(output_tiles == 1024, f"Output tiles for 4096/128 should be 1024. Got {output_tiles:.0f}")
    check(tile_products == 32768, f"Tile products for 4096/128 should be 32768. Got {tile_products:.0f}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    layer_dim_str = fmt(layer_dim, precision=0)
    array_dim_str = fmt(array_dim, precision=0, commas=False)
    output_tile_count_str = fmt_int(output_tiles)
    tile_product_count_str = fmt_int(tile_products)
    reuse_factor_mult_str = fmt_multiple(reuse_factor, precision=0, commas=False)
    tiles_per_dim_str = fmt_int(tiles_per_dim)
```

A stationary dataflow decides which operand stays local; tiling decides how large a block of it local storage can hold. A mismatch exists between the *computational graph* (which sees a single `{python} TilingPrinciple.layer_dim_str` $\times$ `{python} TilingPrinciple.layer_dim_str` matrix multiplication) and the *physical silicon* (which possesses a fixed `{python} TilingPrinciple.array_dim_str` $\times$ `{python} TilingPrinciple.array_dim_str` systolic array). Bridging this gap requires **tiling**\index{Tiling!definition}, which partitions a large tensor operation into tiles that fit exactly into the hardware's fast local memory (SRAM or scratchpad memory), so that each tile is reused many times before it is evicted.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tiling in its software form, the cache-aware blocking a framework applies to matrix multiplication, is established in @sec-ml-frameworks-basic-numerical-operations-5516.
:::

To process the `{python} TilingPrinciple.layer_dim_str`-wide worked-example layer on a `{python} TilingPrinciple.array_dim_str`-wide systolic array, the compiler decomposes the result into `{python} TilingPrinciple.output_tile_count_str` output tiles. Each output tile accumulates across `{python} TilingPrinciple.tiles_per_dim_str` reduction-dimension tiles, so the complete matrix multiplication executes `{python} TilingPrinciple.tile_product_count_str` $\GemmLeftOperand$-tile-by-$\GemmRightOperand$-tile products. This decomposition is a physical requirement imposed by memory hierarchy limits: operand tiles are fetched from high-capacity, high-latency HBM, staged in fast SRAM, and pulsed through the systolic array.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_hw_acceleration_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A utilization curve that climbs to full at a layer width of 128, then drops to about half at 129 where a fringe tile appears along one tiled dimension; the region past 129 is shaded red."}

*Exceeding the tile width along a single dimension tips utilization along that axis off a cliff.*
:::

Tile dimensions balance on-chip capacity against arithmetic intensity. A larger tile reuses each loaded byte across more multiply-accumulate operations, raising operational intensity toward the compute-bound regime of the roofline model. The capacity ceiling is how much of $\GemmLeftOperand$, $\GemmRightOperand$, and $\GemmOutputMatrix$ fits simultaneously in fast on-chip memory. Tiling sustains high hardware efficiency $(\EfficiencyHw)$ by ensuring that for every byte loaded from main memory, the data is reused `{python} TilingPrinciple.reuse_factor_mult_str` within the systolic grid. When a layer dimension is not an exact multiple of the hardware tile size, the accelerator pays a *fringe penalty* in idle silicon. Consider a layer where only one output dimension expands from 128 to 129 while the other dimensions remain perfectly aligned to the 128-element tile. Processing that single extra column requires scheduling a second 128-wide tile across the systolic array, leaving 127 execution units idle during the fringe pass. Two tiles execute where one nearly sufficed, so the utilization factor along that dimension falls to $129/256$, or approximately 50 percent, creating the efficiency cliff illustrated in the margin figure. When multiple dimensions misalign simultaneously, these padding losses multiply across the tiled axes: a $129 \times 129$ output block partitioned into four $128 \times 128$ physical tiles yields a useful-area efficiency of $(129/256)^2$, or barely 25 percent. @Algo-tiled-gemm formalizes the resulting loop nest emitted by the compiler to orchestrate this on-chip staging and accumulation.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-tiled-gemm
#| pdf-line-number: true
#| pdf-right-comment: false
#| html-comment-delimiter: "▷"
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Tiled (blocked) matrix multiply}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{M\times K}$, $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times N}$; tile sizes $M_{\text{tile}}, N_{\text{tile}}, K_{\text{tile}}$
\Ensure $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$
\For{each row tile $i_0$ (size $M_{\text{tile}}$)}
    \For{each column tile $j_0$ (size $N_{\text{tile}}$)}
        \State initialize the $\mathbf{C}$-tile accumulator to zero on chip
        \For{each $k_0$ over $K$ in steps of $K_{\text{tile}}$}
            \State load $\mathbf{A}$-tile $[i_0,k_0]$ and $\mathbf{B}$-tile $[k_0,j_0]$ on chip
            \State accumulate the tile product on chip \Comment{reuse $N_{\text{tile}}$/$M_{\text{tile}}$ per byte}
        \EndFor
        \State write the $\mathbf{C}$-tile back to memory
    \EndFor
\EndFor
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Once operand tiles reside in fast local SRAM, the hardware executes the tile product without further off-chip memory traffic. Systolic arrays achieve computational efficiency by routing operands through a structured 2D grid of processing elements (PEs) that communicate directly with adjacent neighbors across dedicated registers, bypassing shared-memory bus contention. In a weight-stationary design, the canonical TPU arrangement of @fig-systolic-array, weights from the $\GemmRightOperand$-tile are preloaded into local PE registers and held stationary. Input activations from the $\GemmLeftOperand$-tile stream horizontally across rows from left to right, while partial sums accumulate vertically down columns. On each clock cycle, every active PE multiplies its incoming activation by its stationary weight, adds the result to the incoming partial sum from above, and passes the activation rightward to its adjacent neighbor for the next cycle.

Because operands propagate one hop per cycle, synchronized execution requires an intentional time skew. Consider a minimal $2{\times}2$ tile product where output element $\GemmOutputElement_{ij} = \GemmLeftOperandElement_{i0}\GemmRightOperandElement_{0j} + \GemmLeftOperandElement_{i1}\GemmRightOperandElement_{1j}$ requires two products and one accumulation. The weight matrix $\GemmRightOperand$ is held stationary across four PEs: $\text{PE}_{00}$ stores $\GemmRightOperandElement_{00}$, $\text{PE}_{01}$ stores $\GemmRightOperandElement_{01}$, $\text{PE}_{10}$ stores $\GemmRightOperandElement_{10}$, and $\text{PE}_{11}$ stores $\GemmRightOperandElement_{11}$. Activation $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{i0}$ enters the top row and $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{i1}$ the second row, because each row holds the weights for one reduction index. If $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}$ enters the top row at $\text{PE}_{00}$ in cycle 0, its partial product $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\GemmRightOperandElement_{00}$ moves down to $\text{PE}_{10}$ in cycle 1. That PE holds $\GemmRightOperandElement_{10}$, so the activation it needs is $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{01}$, which must therefore enter the second row at $\text{PE}_{10}$ one cycle later than $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}$ entered the first. In cycle 1, $\text{PE}_{10}$ adds $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{01}\GemmRightOperandElement_{10}$ to the arriving partial sum and emits $\GemmOutputElement_{00}$. Meanwhile $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}$ has moved right to $\text{PE}_{01}$, and its product $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\GemmRightOperandElement_{01}$ reaches $\text{PE}_{11}$ in cycle 2, just as $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{01}$ arrives there from $\text{PE}_{10}$. As a result, $\GemmOutputElement_{01}$ emerges one cycle after $\GemmOutputElement_{00}$. Inputs along each successive row and column are staggered in the same way, so operands meeting at any physical coordinate represent identical reduction indices. Local reuse amortizes the initial fill and drain overhead: each loaded activation is reused across an entire row of $\GemmTileColumnDimension$ processing elements, while each stationary weight serves an entire sequence of input vectors before eviction. Sustained throughput, however, remains bounded by off-chip memory bandwidth whenever operand replenishment cannot keep pace with array retirement (@sec-hardware-acceleration-understanding-ai-memory-wall-3ea9).

#### Tiling across the memory hierarchy {#sec-hardware-acceleration-memoryefficient-tiling-strategies-9fce}

The systolic array is one instance of a general hierarchy rule. The same blocking that fits a graph-level matrix onto a fixed array, together with its fringe penalty and the loop structure of @algo-tiled-gemm, recurs across registers, L1/shared memory, and L2 caches [@lam1991]. At every tier of the memory hierarchy, tiling\index{Tiling!memory-efficient strategies}[^fn-tiling-cache-reuse] bounds the active working set so that each block is reused locally before eviction rather than refetched from a slower tier.

[^fn-tiling-cache-reuse]: **Tiling (loop blocking)**\index{Tiling!DRAM traffic reduction}: This restructuring partitions a computation into blocks sized for a fast local tier. A naive loop makes repeated references to the same elements; caches may capture some, while blocking deliberately concentrates reuse before eviction [@lam1991]. This reduction in lower-tier traffic is a primary source of the gap between naive matrix multiplication and optimized GEMM routines.

The naïve loop nest of @lst-matmul_data_movement shows the cost of leaving reuse to chance. Written as $\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand$, with the weights as $\GemmLeftOperand$ and the input batch as $\GemmRightOperand$, it references the same elements of both operands again and again. Without tiling, those repeated accesses consume unnecessary bandwidth. Some references can hit in cache, but large matrices and an unfavorable traversal order can still cause excessive lower-tier traffic. Tiling partitions this multiplication across its three principal dimensions ($\GemmRowDimension$, $\GemmInnerDimension$, and $\GemmColumnDimension$) (@fig-tiling-diagram). Each highlighted region represents the working set staged in fast memory at one moment. An $\GemmTileRowDimension{\times}\GemmTileInnerDimension$ block of $\GemmLeftOperand$ (within the green row band) multiplies a $\GemmTileInnerDimension{\times}\GemmTileColumnDimension$ block of $\GemmRightOperand$ (within the pink column band) to accumulate one $\GemmTileRowDimension{\times}\GemmTileColumnDimension$ output tile ($\text{Block}_{\TileRowIndex,n}$, shaded blue) of $\GemmOutputMatrix$. Processing all inner-product operations for an active tile before evicting it amortizes off-chip DRAM latency across $\GemmTileRowDimension\cdot \GemmTileColumnDimension\cdot \GemmTileInnerDimension$ arithmetic operations.

::: {#fig-tiling-diagram data-explore="original-v1-tiling-diagram" data-explore-key="vol1:fig-tiling-diagram" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Matrix Tiling Mechanics**: Partitioning large matrix multiplication ($\GemmOutputMatrix=\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand$) into $\GemmTileRowDimension\times \GemmTileInnerDimension$ and $\GemmTileInnerDimension\times \GemmTileColumnDimension$ blocks aligns memory footprints with fast on-chip SRAM/registers. Maximizing register reuse within each tile amortizes slow off-chip DRAM accesses and keeps compute engines operating at peak throughput." fig-alt="Three matrices A, B, C with highlighted tiles showing how matrix multiplication partitions into smaller blocks. Dimensions labeled M, N, K with corresponding tile sizes Mtile, Ntile, Ktile."}

##### Tiling fundamentals {#sec-hardware-acceleration-tiling-fundamentals-e9e6}

In the untiled loop of @lst-matmul_data_movement, each inner-loop step fetches $\GemmLeftOperandElement_{ik}$ and $\GemmRightOperandElement_{kj}$ across an entire row of $\GemmLeftOperand$ and column of $\GemmRightOperand$ to update $\GemmOutputElement_{ij}$ before advancing to the next column or row. Once $\SquareGemmDimension$ grows large enough that a full row or column evicts earlier entries from local storage, the processor reloads values it touched moments earlier and pays the lower-tier latency and energy penalty on every miss [@horowitz2014; @sze2017].

##### Performance benefits of tiling {#sec-hardware-acceleration-performance-benefits-tiling-e7bd}

Splitting the three loops into outer tile-stepping loops and inner within-tile loops confines the working set to three `TILE_SIZE` $\times$ `TILE_SIZE` submatrices at a time. @Lst-tiled_matmul shows this loop-blocking transformation in Python: the outer loops step in increments of `TILE_SIZE`, while the inner loops complete all $\text{TILE\_SIZE}^3$ multiply-accumulates for the active block before advancing.

::: {#lst-tiled_matmul lst-cap="**Cache-Blocked Matrix Multiplication**: This high-level loop blocking approach divides matrices into smaller index ranges so hardware caches can reuse data within each tile, improving computational efficiency without explicit scratchpad loads."}

```{.python}
TILE_SIZE = 32  # Choose a tile size based on hardware constraints

# Cache blocking: partition data via loop bounds.
# Loads are implicit through the hardware cache hierarchy.
for i in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
    for j in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
        for k in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
            # Each tile computed independently
            for ii in range(i, min(i + TILE_SIZE, N)):
                for jj in range(j, min(j + TILE_SIZE, N)):
                    for kk in range(k, min(k + TILE_SIZE, N)):
                        C[ii, jj] += A[ii, kk] * B[kk, jj]
```

:::

The restructuring produces a chain of effects. A small tile is revisited while it is still likely to be cached, so most operand references hit in L1/L2 or shared memory instead of DRAM. DRAM traffic falls as a result, and the processing units spend less time waiting for operands. When an untiled access pattern repeatedly fetches operands from lower memory tiers, that traffic can impose a bandwidth ceiling below the arithmetic ceiling.

##### Tiling methods {#sec-hardware-acceleration-tiling-methods-6257}

Tiling implementations differ along one axis, which is whether the hardware or the program decides what stays in fast memory. The two ends are implicit (cache) blocking and explicit (scratchpad) staging, and practical kernels often combine them.

Implicit (cache) blocking\index{Tiling!implicit cache blocking} restructures only the loop bounds. The tiled matrix multiplication in @lst-tiled_matmul issues no explicit loads; its tile-shaped access pattern lets hardware caches reuse nearby values before they are evicted. It suits CPUs and GPUs with capable caches and large tensors that exceed fast-memory capacity.

Explicit (scratchpad) staging\index{Tiling!explicit staging} copies each tile into shared memory, a scratchpad, or registers and reorganizes the computation around the staged copy. It is the only option on accelerators whose fast memory is software managed, and it guarantees reuse that a cache might lose to eviction. Convolution is the classic case, because staging a filter once lets it serve many input regions without being refetched. @Lst-loop_blocking loads blocks of $\GemmLeftOperand$ and $\GemmRightOperand$ into temporary fast storage and reuses them across the inner loops. It includes shortened boundary tiles when $\SquareGemmDimension$ is not divisible by `TILE_SIZE`, the software counterpart of the fringe penalty that a fixed-size array pays in idle processing elements.

::: {#lst-loop_blocking lst-cap="**Explicit Tile Staging Pseudocode**: A backend maps the temporary tile objects to fast storage and reuses them across inner-loop operations."}

```{.python}
# Explicit tile staging: load data into fast
# temporary storage before the inner loops.
for i in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
    for j in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
        for k in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
            # Pseudocode: map these tile objects to fast memory
            A_tile = A[i : i + TILE_SIZE, k : k + TILE_SIZE]
            B_tile = B[k : k + TILE_SIZE, j : j + TILE_SIZE]

            # Reuse loaded tiles for all inner iterations
            for ii in range(A_tile.shape[0]):
                for jj in range(B_tile.shape[1]):
                    for kk in range(A_tile.shape[1]):
                        C[i + ii, j + jj] += (
                            A_tile[ii, kk] * B_tile[kk, jj]
                        )
```

:::

##### Tiling challenges and trade-offs {#sec-hardware-acceleration-tiling-challenges-tradeoffs-e9c9}

Tiling improves performance only when the tile matches the locality budget of the hardware. If the tile is too small, memory fetches still dominate execution time because reuse is too limited. If the tile is too large, it exceeds fast memory and causes cache thrashing or scratchpad spills. Selecting the right tile size therefore directly determines computational efficiency and memory bandwidth usage.

The capacity test counts every buffer that is live at the same time. For the tile dimensions in @algo-tiled-gemm, the operand blocks contain $\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileInnerDimension$ and $\GemmTileInnerDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension$ elements, while the output accumulator contains $\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension$ elements. Suppose a hypothetical accelerator retains all three in one software-managed local store, uses FP16 operands and an FP32 accumulator, and loads only the current operand pair. Element storage size $\ElementStorageSize$ is then 2 bytes for each operand and 4 bytes for each accumulator entry. After reserving space for other live state, the tile must satisfy
$$
(2\text{ bytes})\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileInnerDimension+ (2\text{ bytes})\GemmTileInnerDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension+ (4\text{ bytes})\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension\le \text{available local bytes}.
$$ {#eq-hw-tile-capacity}
Keeping the output dimensions fixed while doubling the reduction tile doubles both operand buffers without changing the accumulator. Reject that larger candidate if the revised left-hand side of @eq-hw-tile-capacity exceeds the available capacity, even if its longer reduction amortizes accumulator handling over more products. Double buffering has the same operand-capacity effect at fixed tile dimensions: retaining the next $\GemmLeftOperand$ and $\GemmRightOperand$ tiles while computing the current pair requires a second copy of each operand buffer, while the running accumulator remains single buffered.

Actual storage tiers must be budgeted separately. A GPU kernel may stage operand tiles in shared memory while keeping output accumulators in thread registers; unused register capacity cannot make an oversized shared-memory allocation fit. Its shared-memory test counts the staged operand copies and any other shared state, while its register test counts accumulators, operand fragments, and temporary values across the participating threads. Passing both tests establishes capacity feasibility. It does not establish speed: alignment, bank conflicts, occupancy, synchronization, and measured traffic still determine whether the tile improves execution.

The tile choice also controls load balance. In architectures such as GPUs and TPUs, computations execute in parallel across thousands of processing units. If tiles are not evenly distributed, some units remain idle while others are overloaded, leading to suboptimal utilization of computational resources. Effective tile scheduling keeps parallel execution balanced and efficient.

Data movement remains a cost after tiling, even when another resource becomes the throughput limit. Although tiling reduces the number of slow memory accesses, transferring tiles between hierarchy levels still incurs latency and energy cost, especially when data falls from cache or scratchpad back to DRAM. Efficient memory prefetching and scheduling strategies minimize this residual movement and ensure that data is available when needed.

Hybrid tiling combines implicit blocking and explicit staging when neither alone captures the workload's reuse, for example relying on caches for an outer tier while staging convolution weights explicitly in a scratchpad. Register blocking, double buffering, and hierarchical tiling extend the same locality principle at smaller and larger memory tiers. AI compilers and runtime systems such as TensorFlow XLA, TVM, and MLIR automatically select these tiling strategies based on hardware constraints, enabling fine-tuned performance optimization without manual intervention. @Tbl-tiling-strategies compares implicit, explicit, and hybrid tiling.

| Aspect                | **Implicit (Cache) Blocking**                                            | **Explicit (Scratchpad) Staging**                                      | **Hybrid tiling**\index{Hybrid tiling}                         |
|:----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Who Decides Residency | Hardware cache replacement policy                                        | The program, through explicit copies into software-managed memory      | Caches for some tiers, explicit copies for others              |
| Optimization Focus    | Loop bounds shaped so accesses stay within cache-sized blocks            | Staging tiles and reordering computation around the staged copy        | Matching each memory tier to the mechanism it supports         |
| **Memory usage**      | Improves cache locality and reduces DRAM access                          | Keeps frequently used data in fast memory for multiple iterations      | Minimizes data movement while ensuring high reuse              |
| **Common use cases**  | Matrix multiplications, CNNs, self-attention in transformers             | Convolutions, recurrent neural networks (RNNs), iterative computations | AI accelerators with hierarchical memory, mixed workloads      |
| **Performance gains** | Reduced memory bandwidth requirements, better cache utilization          | Lower memory fetch latency, improved data locality                     | Maximized efficiency across multiple hardware types            |
| Challenges            | Reuse is not guaranteed; eviction can discard a tile before it is reused | Can increase register pressure, requires loop restructuring            | Complexity in tuning tile size and execution order dynamically |
| **Best when**         | Hardware caches are capable and the working set exceeds fast memory      | Fast memory is software managed or reuse must be guaranteed            | Different memory tiers favor different mechanisms              |

: **Tiling Strategies**: Implicit, explicit, and hybrid tiling optimize memory access patterns for improved performance. Implicit (cache) blocking shapes loop bounds and lets caches decide residency, explicit (scratchpad) staging copies tiles into software-managed memory to guarantee reuse, and hybrid tiling combines both across memory tiers. AI compilers and runtime systems use these techniques to automatically optimize model execution on diverse hardware. {#tbl-tiling-strategies tbl-colwidths="[16,31,27,26]"}

### Memory-efficient tensor layouts {#sec-hardware-acceleration-memoryefficient-tensor-layouts-e250}

Stationary dataflows (@sec-hardware-acceleration-data-movement-patterns-3b06) and tiling determine which operands stay close to compute units and in what blocks; tensor layouts\index{Tensor layout!hardware alignment} determine whether those operands can be accessed efficiently once they arrive. A well-chosen weight-stationary schedule still stalls if weights are laid out in a format that produces strided, non-coalesced memory fetches. Tensor layout is a kernel requirement. The physical ordering of multidimensional data in linear memory must match the memory access stride expected by the accelerator's execution units, or the processor pays in memory stalls, cache underutilization, and redundant bus transactions.

Hardware accelerators fetch data from device memory in fixed-size transactions, typically 32 to 128 bytes per transaction. When compute units request non-contiguous addresses, each transaction delivers only a fraction of useful payload, degrading effective memory bandwidth. Aligning tensor layout with the execution model lets concurrent threads or SIMD lanes access nearby aligned locations in fewer transactions; the count depends on access width and device granularity [@nvidia2021cudnn].

Machine learning frameworks and compilers often manage this layout selection automatically. Optimization tools such as cuDNN for NVIDIA GPUs, XLA for TensorFlow and JAX, and MLIR-based compiler stacks transform tensor layouts as they lower operations to backend-specific kernels [@nvidia2021cudnn; @GoogleXLA; @lattner2021]. In high-level frameworks, layout transformations are typically applied transparently, but developers authoring custom kernels or targeting low-level APIs such as CUDA, Metal, or OpenCL must manage tensor formats directly.

In PyTorch\index{PyTorch!tensor layout}, for example, view operations such as `tensor.permute()` adjust tensor strides without moving data in memory, requiring an explicit `tensor.contiguous()` call to materialize a packed buffer when a downstream kernel requires contiguous storage [@pytorch2026tensorviews]. Conversely, TensorFlow\index{TensorFlow!tensor layout} defaults to channels-last (NHWC) for convolutional models on NVIDIA GPUs, warning that NCHW inputs introduce automatic transpose overhead when lowered to GPU kernels [@tensorflow2024profiler]. Hardware-optimized libraries such as cuDNN on GPUs and oneDNN on CPUs implement tailored memory formats to maximize cache line utilization and SIMD throughput. The governing principle is to treat memory layout as an intrinsic property of the backend execution path: the fastest tensor format is the one that minimizes layout conversion overhead and makes memory accesses contiguous across hardware execution units.

#### Channels-last layout {#sec-hardware-acceleration-rowmajor-layout-741f}

In an NHWC channels-last layout, the channel index varies fastest in a contiguous tensor, placing the channel values for each spatial coordinate adjacent in memory. The label names the order in which dimensions are laid out in memory, from slowest-varying to fastest-varying, so NCHW and NHWC hold the same values in different linear orders.

Consider an RGB image tensor of shape $(\text{Height}, \text{Width}, \text{Channels}) = (3, 3, 3)$. The elements $\ImageTensorElement(\ImageRowIndex,\ImageColumnIndex,\ImageChannelIndex)$ are laid out in linear memory as follows:
\begin{gather*}
X(0,0,0), X(0,0,1), X(0,0,2), X(0,1,0), X(0,1,1), \\
X(0,1,2), X(0,2,0), X(0,2,1), X(0,2,2), \ldots
\end{gather*}

All channel values for a given pixel are adjacent, and memory addresses advance across width before advancing down height. This layout supports vectorized execution when a compute kernel processes multiple channels simultaneously: CPU SIMD registers and GPU Tensor Cores can load contiguous channel vectors directly without intra-register shuffling.

The advantage of channels-last storage depends on the target operator and hardware unit. TensorFlow uses NHWC\index{NHWC!channels-last layout} by default, whereas PyTorch provides a dedicated channels-last memory format that decouples logical dimension ordering from physical storage. Modern Tensor Core kernels in cuDNN favor NHWC because matrix-multiply units pack channel dimensions directly into accumulator tiles. When kernels require channel-contiguous inputs, passing an incompatible format forces the framework runtime to insert an explicit memory transpose, incurring a memory bandwidth penalty before computation begins.

#### Channels-first layout {#sec-hardware-acceleration-channelmajor-layout-d6a9}

In a contiguous NCHW channels-first layout, the spatial width index varies fastest, and all spatial values across an entire channel are stored contiguously before the next channel begins. Accelerators process data in parallel across thread warps or SIMD lanes; when consecutive threads in a warp access consecutive memory addresses, the memory controller coalesces those requests into fewer memory transactions (**memory coalescing**\index{Memory coalescing!GPU optimization}).[^fn-memory-coalescing-gpu]

[^fn-memory-coalescing-gpu]: **Memory coalescing**\index{Memory coalescing!tensor layout impact}: The GPU hardware mechanism that combines memory requests from threads in a warp into transactions according to address locality, alignment, access width, and device granularity. Tensor layout therefore decides how many transactions a warp's loads become, and whether a given layout helps depends on how the kernel assigns threads to tensor dimensions.

Consider the same RGB image tensor with dimensions reordered in channels-first order as $(\text{Channels}, \text{Height}, \text{Width}) = (3, 3, 3)$. Retaining $\ImageTensorElement(\ImageRowIndex,\ImageColumnIndex,\ImageChannelIndex)$ as semantic coordinate notation, the data are stored in channels-first order as follows:
\begin{gather*}
X(0,0,0), X(0,1,0), X(0,2,0), X(1,0,0), X(1,1,0), X(1,2,0), \ldots, \\
X(0,0,1), X(0,1,1), X(0,2,1), \ldots, X(0,0,2), X(0,1,2), X(0,2,2), \ldots
\end{gather*}

In this format, all red channel values for the entire image are stored first, followed by all green values, and then all blue values. This arrangement allows kernels that parallelize across spatial coordinates $(\ImageHeight, \ImageWidth)$ to issue coalesced reads along image rows, which suited earlier GPU convolution algorithms and SIMD execution pipelines [@chetlur2014cudnn].

The relative advantage of NCHW\index{NCHW!channels-first layout} versus NHWC depends on how the underlying kernel maps computation to hardware threads. Convolutional layers evaluate filters across spatial and channel dimensions simultaneously. In classic direct or FFT-based convolutions, channels-first ordering enabled efficient spatial sliding without stride jumps. However, modern GEMM-lowered convolutions and Tensor Core pipelines map channel reduction directly to matrix multiply accumulators, favoring channels-last structures. When a model operates in NCHW but invokes a Tensor Core-optimized backend, the runtime must either run an unoptimized fallback kernel or dynamically transpose the tensor into NHWC, burning memory bandwidth in both cases.[^fn-nhwc-nchw-layout]

[^fn-nhwc-nchw-layout]: **NHWC vs. NCHW**\index{NHWC vs. NCHW!performance impact}: NHWC lists dimensions as batch, height, width, channel; NCHW lists batch, channel, height, width. Physical memory format determines whether adjacent threads read adjacent addresses, so the performance effect is backend-specific. Layout-to-hardware mismatch is not a micro-optimization; it can create multi-fold performance gaps, especially when a conversion prevents Tensor Core convolution or fusion paths from being used.

#### Comparing channels-last and channels-first layouts {#sec-hardware-acceleration-comparing-rowmajor-channelmajor-layouts-e410}

Both channels-last (NHWC) and channels-first (NCHW) layouts address specific hardware access patterns, with their efficiency determined by whether a kernel parallelizes over spatial coordinates or vectorizes across channel dimensions. Layout choice directly governs cache line utilization, memory bus transaction count, and compute unit occupancy. @Tbl-major contrasts the performance trade-offs and hardware compatibility between these two approaches.

| Feature                     | **Channels-Last (NHWC)**                                       | **Channels-First (NCHW)**                                      |
|:----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Memory storage order**    | Pixels are stored row-by-row, channel interleaved              | All values for a given channel are stored together first       |
| Best for                    | CPU loops, element-wise operations, many channels-last kernels | Many legacy GPU convolution paths and channel-first model code |
| **Cache efficiency**        | High cache locality for sequential row/channel-last access     | Can improve coalescing for channel-first kernels               |
| **Convolution performance** | Often preferred by modern Tensor Core convolution/fusion paths | Efficient for older FP32 cuDNN paths and direct convolutions   |
| **Memory fetching**         | Good when kernels vectorize over adjacent channel data         | Good when kernels process channel-major tiles                  |
| **Default in frameworks**   | Common TensorFlow convention; PyTorch channels-last option     | Common PyTorch tensor shape convention                         |

: **Data Layout Strategies**: Channels-last (NHWC) and channels-first (NCHW) layouts optimize memory access patterns for different backend kernels. NHWC often suits CPU vectorization and modern Tensor Core convolution and fusion paths, while NCHW remains the default PyTorch tensor shape and suits older FP32 GPU kernel paths. Choosing the appropriate layout directly impacts performance by maximizing cache utilization and memory bandwidth efficiency. {#tbl-major}

While compilers such as XLA, TensorRT, and PyTorch Inductor automate layout propagation and insert layout conversions when beneficial, format conversions are not free. Transposing a tensor requires reading every element from memory and writing it back in a different order, which consumes memory bandwidth without executing useful arithmetic. In production deployments, matching the model's memory layout to the accelerator's native kernel format eliminates these layout transformations entirely. Even when tensor layout is perfectly aligned with the hardware, however, executing operations as isolated kernels introduces a separate bottleneck: intermediate values must be exposed through global-memory buffers between operations, even when caches absorb some physical traffic. Resolving that bottleneck requires changing how operations are scheduled rather than how tensors are laid out.

### Kernel fusion on the accelerator {#sec-hardware-acceleration-kernel-fusion-7faf}

At `{python} LayernormAnalysisCalc.ln_ai_str` FLOP/byte, the standalone LayerNorm kernel of notebook \ref{nbk-hw-acceleration-layernorm-analysis} can reach at most `{python} LayernormAnalysisCalc.ln_attainable_tflop_per_s_str`, about `{python} LayernormAnalysisCalc.ln_util_pct_str` of the H100's tensor peak, no matter how its internal arithmetic or tensor layout is scheduled. **Kernel fusion**\index{Kernel Fusion!hardware data movement}[^fn-kernel-fusion-memory] removes that bottleneck by combining successive operations into a single kernel so intermediate tensors stay in registers or on-chip SRAM instead of making round-trips through device memory. On an accelerator, the two engineering questions are which intermediate transfers fusion eliminates from the memory bus and what the combined kernel costs in register pressure and thread occupancy.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Kernel fusion (also called operator fusion), with its LayerNorm, dropout, and ReLU example and the traffic count for unfused versus fused chains, is established in @sec-ml-frameworks-execution-strategy-matters-memory-wall-1ce8.
:::

[^fn-kernel-fusion-memory]: **Kernel fusion**\index{Kernel fusion!memory traffic reduction}: Separate GPU kernels expose intermediate results through device memory, although caches can absorb some traffic. A fused kernel can keep intermediates in registers or local storage and avoid corresponding external write/read cycles. The resulting speedup depends on cache behavior, occupancy, launch overhead, and whether memory traffic was the bottleneck; it is not necessarily proportional to the byte reduction.

The case for fusion rests on a traffic count. Run as separate kernels, a chain of three elementwise operations writes each intermediate result to device memory and reads it back for the next operation. In contrast, a fused kernel reads the input once, keeps the intermediates in registers or on-chip SRAM, and writes only the final output, which cuts idealized external traffic by roughly 3$\times$. On an accelerator the saving matters most for elementwise operators, whose arithmetic intensity sits far below one FLOP per byte, so moving each intermediate across the memory bus takes longer than computing it [@Jia2019]. Fused execution\index{Fused execution}\index{Kernel fusion!memory efficiency} also shortens the lifetime of intermediate buffers, although an optimizing runtime can often reuse those buffers anyway. What fusion guarantees is the removed write and read for each eliminated intermediate, and how much of that removed traffic would have reached DRAM depends on cache behavior.

#### Performance benefits and constraints {#sec-hardware-acceleration-performance-benefits-constraints-1b74}

Because high-bandwidth memory is the scarce resource on GPUs and TPUs, eliminating redundant memory transactions translates directly into higher compute utilization [@NVIDIA2020]. Not all operations can be fused arbitrarily, however. Element-wise operations and frozen inference normalization are strong candidates because their computations do not require batch-wide reductions, whereas training-mode batch normalization computes batch statistics and is not purely element-wise. Matrix multiplications and convolutions constrain fusion further because they involve reductions and large data movement; compilers routinely fuse them with element-wise epilogues such as bias or activation, yet cannot freely merge them with unrelated global operations.

Even when two operators are algebraically compatible, register pressure bounds how aggressively they should be fused. Keeping intermediate values in registers eliminates redundant memory writes, but if a fused kernel exceeds the available registers per thread, the compiler spills excess values to per-thread local memory backed by device DRAM, adding latency that can negate the benefits of fusion. On GPUs, where thread occupancy (the number of threads active in parallel) is bounded by the register file, excessive fusion can also starve parallelism. Different accelerators and compilers therefore strike different balances. NVIDIA GPUs favor warp-level parallelism where element-wise epilogue fusion is straightforward [@NVIDIA2020]. TPUs prioritize systolic-array execution coupled to vector post-processing [@jouppi2017]. Compiler stacks such as TVM, XLA, TensorRT, and MLIR use graph rewrites and engine-building heuristics to weigh memory savings against register and occupancy limits [@chen2018tvm; @GoogleXLA; @nvidia2024tensorrt; @lattner2021]. When debugging performance regressions or modifying models frequently, frameworks also allow developers to disable fusion selectively so that memory savings, register usage, and hardware execution constraints can be evaluated independently.

::: {#chk-hw-acceleration-data-movement-kernel-fusion .callout-checkpoint title="Data movement and kernel fusion"}

The dataflow building blocks are now in place: data locality, tensor layout, and kernel fusion. These fusion decisions are ultimately about data locality, which ties together the chapter's core data movement strategies:

- [ ] **Locality choice**: given weight-stationary, output-stationary, and input-stationary dataflows, which tensor does each hold near the compute units, and how does that choice shift where the memory traffic lands?
- [ ] **Layout match**: a kernel runs on a backend expecting NHWC but receives an NCHW tensor. Predict what happens to its memory access pattern and to delivered throughput.
- [ ] **Fusion eligibility**: for a Conv2D, a BatchNorm, and a ReLU executed in sequence, decide which pairs are worth fusing and what determines whether fusing them pays off.
- [ ] **Remaining gap**: an operation still repeatedly fetches operands because its active blocks exceed fast-memory capacity. How could tiling from @sec-hardware-acceleration-tiling-principle change this access pattern, and what capacity and reuse evidence would justify that choice?

:::

### Applying mapping strategies to neural networks {#sec-hardware-acceleration-applying-mapping-strategies-neural-networks-3110}

Convolutional networks, transformers, and multilayer perceptrons stress the memory hierarchy in different places (@sec-hardware-acceleration-model-memory-pressure-f95e), so each model family requires a different combination of stationary dataflow, tiling, tensor layout, and kernel fusion. Mapping is a systematic search over loop permutations, tiling factors, and stationarity policies that maximizes data reuse under hard SRAM and register constraints. Because each family presents a distinct ratio of weights to activations and differing opportunities for temporal locality, optimal mapping policies diverge across workloads. Convolutional networks exploit 2D spatial weight reuse across receptive fields. Transformers split between compute-bound matrix multiplications during prefill and bandwidth-bound KV-cache streaming during autoregressive decoding. Dense MLPs demand blocked GEMM execution across batch dimensions. @Tbl-mapping-strategies consolidates how dataflow, memory layout, kernel fusion, and tiling align with these three architectural archetypes.

#### Convolutional neural networks (ResNet-50) {#sec-hardware-acceleration-convolutional-neural-networks-resnet50-3eb6}

For ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50!weight reuse mapping} and similar CNNs, a key mapping opportunity is spatial weight reuse\index{Weight Reuse!spatial}. A small filter is applied across many spatial locations, so its weights participate in many multiply-accumulate operations. Weight-stationary mappings can capture that reuse by retaining filter tiles locally, while row-stationary or output-stationary mappings may better balance activation and partial-sum traffic on other architectures. Favorable convolution shapes can achieve high arithmetic intensity, which makes them well suited to matrix and systolic execution paths. The model family does not determine one universal dataflow: layer shape, batch size, local-storage capacity, and the target's supported kernels decide which reuse pattern is worth retaining.

| **Property or technique**                                          | CNNs                                                                             | Transformers                                            | MLPs                           | Rationale                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Weight size**                                                    | Small, reused                                                                    | Large, usually dense; sparse in MoE or pruned variants  | Large, dense                   | Sets whether weights can stay on chip or must stream from HBM on every use.                                                                                                                                           |
| **Activation reuse**                                               | High                                                                             | Low to medium                                           | Low                            | Sets how much each loaded activation is worth keeping in local storage.                                                                                                                                               |
| **Memory access pattern**                                          | Spatial locality                                                                 | Mostly regular GEMM plus KV-cache and attention traffic | Regular, sequential (streamed) | Regular patterns tile and prefetch well; KV-cache reads grow with context length.                                                                                                                                     |
| **Potential memory pressure**                                      | Feature-map movement                                                             | Memory capacity and bandwidth                           | Bandwidth at low batch         | Starting hypotheses that execution phase, batch size, and data movement can change, not fixed bottleneck classifications.                                                                                             |
| **Dataflow strategy**\index{Dataflow strategy}                     | Weight, row, or output stationary                                                | Phase- and kernel-dependent                             | Weight or output stationary    | CNNs expose filter and spatial reuse; transformer attention and MLP blocks impose different traffic; dense MLPs reuse weights across a batch and accumulate outputs.                                                  |
| **Memory-aware tensor layouts**\index{Memory-aware tensor layouts} | Backend-dependent (channels-last on Tensor Core paths, NCHW on older FP32 paths) | Backend-dependent (row-major activations typical)       | Row-major typical              | Layout choice depends on backend kernel path and precision mode (@sec-hardware-acceleration-memoryefficient-tensor-layouts-e250 compares the layouts); the entries name common defaults, not universal prescriptions. |
| Kernel Fusion                                                      | Convolution + Activation                                                         | Fused Attention                                         | GEMM Fusion                    | CNNs optimize convolution+activation fusion; Transformers fuse attention mechanisms; MLPs benefit from fused matrix multiplications.                                                                                  |
