| **Tiling for Memory Efficiency**                                   | Explicit staging of feature-map tiles                                            | Explicit staging of attention blocks                    | Blocked GEMM                   | CNNs stage feature-map subregions in on-chip SRAM; transformers stage query and key/value blocks in fused attention; MLPs block large matrix multiplications, implicitly or explicitly.                               |

: **Memory Pressure and Mapping by Model Family**: The first four rows profile each family's memory demands, and the remaining rows give the mapping that answers them. Standard dense transformers demand bandwidth and capacity because large weights, KV caches, and attention traffic dominate their traffic, while CNNs benefit from spatial locality and high activation reuse. {#tbl-mapping-strategies tbl-colwidths="[13,21,14,10,42]"}

This spatial regularity also enables aggressive fusion and tiling. For inference with frozen BatchNorm statistics, compilers can fold or fuse convolution, normalization, and activation to avoid unnecessary intermediate writes. Training-mode BatchNorm requires reductions over batch statistics and does not have the same element-wise structure that permits fusion. Spatial tiling partitions the feature map into subregions sized to fit within on-chip SRAM, so the fused kernel processes each tile from fast memory before moving to the next.

#### Transformer architectures (GPT-2/Llama) {#sec-hardware-acceleration-transformer-architectures-gpt2llama-dd9a}

Transformer\index{Transformer!KV-cache memory pressure} mapping depends on execution phase. During training and prefill, attention creates large intermediate matrices unless a tiled implementation avoids materializing them; during autoregressive decoding, attention reads the growing key-value (KV) cache\index{KV cache!transformer memory pressure}. Each new query vector must access the stored key and value pairs across the preceding sequence. As sequences grow, the full KV cache usually lives in HBM or device DRAM, while attention kernels tile active blocks through SRAM, registers, or shared memory. This access pattern motivates staging active K/V tiles in SRAM so attention consumes them from fast local storage. During training and prefill, the memory traffic created by standard attention implementations similarly explains why fused attention kernels, such as FlashAttention\index{FlashAttention!tiled attention implementation} [@dao2022], can deliver large performance gains. They tile the query-key product, softmax, and value summation through on-chip SRAM so the full attention matrix never reaches HBM. The $\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)$ computation is preserved (@sec-model-training-flash-attention-ioaware-attention-optimization-3da0 develops the algorithm).

#### Multilayer perceptrons and DLRM {#sec-hardware-acceleration-multilayer-perceptrons-dlrm-7c0d}

MLPs\index{MLP!GEMM-dominated computation} present the most straightforward mapping problem because their computation reduces largely to dense GEMM.[^fn-gemm-ml-primitive] Each fully connected layer multiplies an activation matrix by a weight matrix. The weight matrix is fixed across samples, so batching reuses each loaded weight across more activations and raises arithmetic intensity. A batch size of one provides little cross-sample weight reuse and often leaves wide matrix engines underused, while larger batches can move execution toward the compute-bound regime.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How GEMM arithmetic intensity scales with matrix dimension is collected for reference in @sec-appdx-algorithm-foundations-general-matrix-multiply-gemm-b55d.
:::

[^fn-gemm-ml-primitive]: **GEMM**\index{GEMM!ML performance predictor}: The operation $\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmProductScale\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+ \GemmAccumulatorScale\GemmOutputMatrix$, with scalars $\GemmProductScale$ and $\GemmAccumulatorScale$, is the dense linear-algebra primitive that many deep-learning layers lower to. Optimized GEMM libraries such as cuBLAS and oneDNN use register blocking, vectorization, and hierarchical tiling to approach hardware limits on favorable shapes [@nvidia_cublas; @oneDNN2021]. Modern AI accelerators are heavily specialized for GEMM-like tiles: Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, and matrix extensions all exist to accelerate this primitive, which is why GEMM performance is an important predictor of end-to-end throughput across architectures.

Because MLP layers are typically followed by activation functions and bias additions, GEMM fusion combines these steps into a single kernel, avoiding intermediate memory writes. Blocked tiling partitions the large matrix multiplications into sub-blocks sized for the accelerator's shared memory, ensuring high cache utilization throughout computation. The simplicity of the MLP mapping, dominated by a single primitive with predictable access patterns, is precisely why hardware vendors optimize GEMM libraries so aggressively: gains in GEMM performance translate directly to MLP throughput. DLRM is not purely an MLP workload, however. Its large sparse embedding tables and feature-interaction stage can dominate capacity and memory traffic, so the dense mapping described here applies to its bottom and top MLP towers rather than to the entire model [@naumov2019deep].

### Hybrid mapping strategies {#sec-hardware-acceleration-hybrid-mapping-strategies-3e8c}

Production models rarely consist of a single layer type. A vision transformer, for example, combines a convolutional patch-embedding stage, self-attention layers, and dense MLP blocks within a single forward pass [@dosovitskiy2021image]. Those layers create different reuse patterns: the embedding stage can benefit from weight-stationary mapping, attention emphasizes activation movement and tiling, and MLP blocks demand blocked GEMM tiling and fusion. Because no single dataflow strategy is optimal across all three stages, hardware mapping in practice is hybrid and layer-specific\index{Hardware mapping!hybrid, layer-specific strategy}.

Hybrid mapping addresses this heterogeneity by allowing the accelerator to switch strategies at layer boundaries. Each layer presents a different balance of compute intensity, data reuse, and memory access pattern, and the optimal mapping must shift accordingly [@sze2017]. Rather than committing to one dataflow for the entire model, hybrid approaches consider weight stationary execution when weights can be reused locally, input-stationary execution when activation reuse justifies its storage, and output stationary execution when partial-sum traffic is costly. Layer dimensions and available local memory determine which candidate pays off.

TPU-style systolic arrays, NVIDIA GPUs, and tile-based accelerator designs expose different combinations of local memory, tensor layouts, fusion, and scheduling controls. Compilers and runtimes can therefore choose layer-specific strategies rather than one global dataflow for the whole model [@jouppi2023; @NVIDIA2020; @chen2018tvm]. These implementations depend on programmable memory hierarchies, efficient interconnects, and specialized execution pipelines. However, hybrid mapping remains a design-time optimization: in production workloads, execution conditions change dynamically due to varying input sizes, memory contention, and hardware resource availability. Machine learning compilers and runtime systems extend these static mapping choices by introducing dynamic scheduling, memory optimizations, and automatic tuning, ensuring that deep learning workloads operate efficiently across diverse accelerators and deployment environments.

## Compilers and Runtimes {#sec-hardware-acceleration-compiler-support-172e}

The roofline gives each ResNet-50 layer a ceiling, and hardware mapping showed which schedules can approach it, but neither reaches the silicon by itself. Every layer needs a tiling, a stationary operand, a tensor layout, a precision for the activations it reads and writes, and a fusion boundary. The resulting plan must then run on a device whose input shapes, free memory, and clock rate change while it serves. Across a whole model these choices number in the thousands, which is why compilers and runtimes, not engineers, make them. Graph capture and dispatch overhead, which decide how a model reaches a compiler, belong to @sec-ml-frameworks, and the choice of a deployment runtime for a service belongs to @sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef. What remains here is lowering, the path from a captured graph to the accelerator's units, and the runtime that executes the result. The decode floors this chapter quotes for GPT-2 XL assume that the step is launched as a captured graph (@sec-ml-frameworks-hybrid-approaches-jit-compilation-8954); executed one eager kernel at a time, launch overhead rather than memory bandwidth would set the floor.

A single convolution can be implemented with dozens of valid tiling strategies, kernel variants, and memory layouts, most of which perform poorly on a given target. **Machine learning compilers**\index{ML compiler!definition} navigate this space by translating high-level dataflow representations into target-specific executable code, making the mapping and dataflow decisions of the preceding sections automatically. Compiling ResNet-50 for GPU inference illustrates the core compiler stages:

1. **Graph optimization**\index{Graph optimization!definition} fuses repeated Conv2D-BatchNorm-ReLU patterns into single compound kernels, eliminating intermediate round-trips to HBM.
2. **Kernel selection**\index{Kernel selection!definition} chooses specialized Tensor Core implementations for compatible matrix multiplications, exploiting the high arithmetic intensity of dense convolutions.
3. **Memory planning**\index{Memory planning!definition} determines activation lifetimes to safely overlap and reuse intermediate buffer allocations.
4. **Computation scheduling**\index{Computation scheduling!definition} pipelines memory copies with execution across independent hardware queues to hide data transfer latencies.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Graph compilation, kernel fusion, and framework dispatch overhead are established in @sec-ml-frameworks-execution-problem-e1e1.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: compiler-speedup-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ML COMPILER OPTIMIZATION SPEEDUP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-hardware-acceleration-compiler-support-172e introduction
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the practical impact of ML compiler optimizations.
# │ Show: Batch-one ResNet-50 on the reference H100, eager framework vs compiled engine.
# │ How: The shared serving profile (mlsysim.engine.serving_profile), the same
# │      model the serving chapter's runtime comparison uses.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.engine.serving_profile import resnet50_h100_profile
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class CompilerSpeedupCalc:
    """ResNet-50 batch-one latency, eager FP16 vs compiled FP16 engine, on the reference H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    profile = resnet50_h100_profile()

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    naive_inference = profile.eager_fp16(batch=1)
    optimized_inference = profile.tensorrt("fp16", batch=1)
    compiler_speedup = (naive_inference / optimized_inference).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(compiler_speedup > 5, "compiling the batch-one graph should remove most of its fixed cost")
    check(profile.fused_kernels < profile.eager_kernels, "fusion must reduce the kernel count")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    naive_inference_ms_str = fmt_time(naive_inference, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    optimized_inference_ms_str = fmt_time(optimized_inference, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    compiler_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(compiler_speedup, precision=1, commas=False)
    eager_kernels_str = fmt_count(profile.eager_kernels, commas=False)
    fused_kernels_str = fmt_count(profile.fused_kernels, commas=False)
```

On the reference H100, the modeled batch-one forward pass falls from `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.naive_inference_ms_str` in an eager framework to `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.optimized_inference_ms_str` as a compiled FP16 engine, a `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.compiler_speedup_mult_str` improvement without altering the model's mathematical output. The arithmetic per image is unchanged. The gain comes from fusing the network's `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.eager_kernels_str` framework kernels into `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.fused_kernels_str` and launching them as one graph instead of one Python dispatch at a time, which removes the fixed cost that dominates a single image. That answers the question the chapter opened with. The INT8 arithmetic for one image takes about `{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.floor_int8_us_str` on the H100 (`{python} ResnetArithmeticFloor.floor_fp16_us_str` at FP16), so even the compiled pass spends almost all of its time on launch and overhead. Batch-one latency sits on the overhead floor rather than on either roofline ceiling, which is why halving the arithmetic barely moves it. The latencies are modeled rather than measured, and @sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef separates the same gap into the contribution of each runtime, but the mechanism is general. Graph rewrites, kernel selection, memory planning, and scheduling systematically apply kernel fusion (@sec-hardware-acceleration-kernel-fusion-7faf) and memory-efficient tiling (@sec-hardware-acceleration-memoryefficient-tiling-strategies-9fce) to convert theoretical hardware FLOP/s into delivered throughput [@chen2018tvm; @nvidia2024tensorrt].

### ML compiler design {#sec-hardware-acceleration-compiler-design-differences-ml-workloads-0698}

A conventional C++ compiler such as `gcc` or `clang` cannot collapse ResNet-50's `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.eager_kernels_str` framework dispatches into `{python} CompilerSpeedupCalc.fused_kernels_str` fused kernels on its own, because by the time operators lower to scalar loops and pointer arithmetic, the high-level tensor algebra is gone. Machine learning compilers\index{ML compiler!vs. traditional compiler} preserve that domain structure by operating on tensor graphs and operator libraries before lowering to machine code. Whereas general-purpose compilers optimize scalar control flow, vector instructions, register allocation, and cache locality, ML compiler stacks optimize graph topology, tensor memory layouts, shape specialization, accelerator kernel dispatch, and inter-device execution planning [@li2021]. @Tbl-ml-vs-traditional-compilers contrasts the emphasis of these two compiler layers. The boundary is complementary rather than disjoint: an ML compiler stack lowers high-level tensor operations into intermediate representations that feed into an LLVM, GPU, or vendor-specific backend.

| Aspect                      | **Traditional compiler**\index{Traditional compiler}             | **Machine learning compiler**\index{Machine learning compiler}        |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Input representation**    | Source or intermediate-representation program                    | Tensor graph or tensor-level intermediate representation              |
| Execution Model             | Control flow, loops, threads, vectors, and tasks                 | Tensor operators, kernels, graphs, and accelerator streams            |
| **Optimization priorities** | Instruction selection, loop transforms, vectorization, registers | Graph rewrites, fusion, layouts, shapes, and kernel selection         |
| **Memory management**       | Objects, stack/heap, caches, locality, and prefetching           | Tensor lifetimes, buffer reuse, layouts, tiling, and device transfers |
| Target Hardware             | CPUs, GPUs, and other programmable targets                       | CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, and custom accelerators                             |
| **Compilation output**      | Machine code or lower-level intermediate representation          | Kernels plus a hardware-specific graph or execution plan              |

: **Compiler Optimization Priorities**: ML compiler stacks add tensor- and graph-level decisions to conventional instruction- and loop-level compilation. In a production toolchain, the two layers commonly cooperate rather than replace one another. {#tbl-ml-vs-traditional-compilers tbl-colwidths="[21,40,39]"}

The distinction in @tbl-ml-vs-traditional-compilers explains why compiler configuration dictates delivered performance even when the underlying neural network code remains unmodified. ML compilers manage the translation layer between high-level tensor operations and hardware execution units; when this mapping fails to expose reuse or efficient access, execution can be limited by memory traffic, latency, or insufficient parallel work.

### ML compilation pipeline {#sec-hardware-acceleration-ml-compilation-pipeline-7676}

Bridging those two compiler layers requires a staged **ML compilation pipeline**\index{ML compiler!compilation pipeline} that progressively lowers a framework's dataflow graph into executable code for CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, or custom ASICs [@chen2018tvm; @GoogleXLA; @lattner2021]. A full production pipeline adds a fifth stage, code generation, to the four stages previewed on ResNet-50 (graph optimization, kernel selection, memory planning, and computation scheduling), emitting target-specific machine instructions, assembly, or interpreted bytecode. Across these five stages, the compiler applies the dataflow strategies developed in @sec-hardware-acceleration-dataflow-optimization-strategies-ce52: kernel fusion, memory tiling, and compute placement. Hardware acceleration delivers its theoretical throughput only when these compiler-driven transformations expose sufficient arithmetic intensity and align memory access with the hardware hierarchy.

#### Graph optimization {#sec-hardware-acceleration-graph-optimization-f888}

Machine learning frameworks represent models as high-level computation graphs\index{Graph optimization!computation graph restructuring}, where nodes represent mathematical operators (such as convolutions, matrix multiplications, and activations) and directed edges represent tensor data dependencies. Executing each operator as a separate kernel can incur intermediate-buffer traffic and repeated launches. An edge denotes a dependency, not necessarily a new allocation or an off-chip transfer, and asynchronous dependencies need not synchronize the host. When intermediate materialization and dispatch dominate execution, graph transformations can remove substantial overhead.

Graph optimization transforms this computation graph into an efficient execution plan before hardware code generation [@chen2018tvm; @Jia2019]. Working primarily at a target-independent intermediate representation (IR) level before lowering (@sec-hardware-acceleration-code-generation-85c8), graph passes apply four core transformations. Kernel fusion merges adjacent operations into a single compound kernel to eliminate off-chip memory round-trips and launch overheads. In convolutional networks, fusing Conv2D, batch normalization with frozen inference statistics, and ReLU keeps activations in local registers or shared SRAM throughout the sequence (@sec-hardware-acceleration-kernel-fusion-7faf). In transformers, pattern matchers replace multi-operator self-attention subgraphs (score matrix multiplication, scaling, masking, softmax, and multiplication by the value matrix) with IO-aware attention kernels that keep active tiles and running reduction statistics in fast on-chip memory [@dao2022]. Redundant computation elimination and constant folding remove work that need not happen at runtime at all. A typical case is folding frozen normalization parameters into the weights and biases of the preceding linear or convolutional layer (@sec-model-compression-operator-fusion-ac1d). These passes also prune dead subgraphs and merge identical parallel paths through common subexpression elimination.

The remaining two passes reduce data movement and live memory footprint without changing the operator set. Algebraic simplification and layout adjustments reorder mathematically equivalent operations to avoid runtime reshape traffic, for example by pushing transpositions through elementwise ops or canceling them against inverse permutations. Memory-aware node reordering evaluates topological sorts of the dependency graph. It schedules independent operations so intermediate activations are consumed and deallocated promptly before memory pressure forces spills to host DRAM. Production compilers execute these rewrites through pattern-matching rules, producing a coarse-grained execution graph aligned with the accelerator's bandwidth constraints before binding each node to a concrete hardware routine.

#### Kernel selection {#sec-hardware-acceleration-kernel-selection-df01}

Kernel selection\index{Kernel selection!hardware-specific implementation} binds each node in the optimized graph to a concrete hardware implementation. Accelerators provide dozens of valid kernel implementations for a single tensor operation, each parameterized by tile dimensions, thread block configurations, memory staging patterns, and target precision. Choosing the optimal kernel determines whether the execution engine achieves high compute utilization or stalls on uncoalesced memory accesses and pipeline bubbles [@chen2018tvm; @zheng2020ansor].

In most production pipelines, compilers draw from vendor-optimized kernel libraries (NVIDIA's cuDNN\index{cuDNN!NVIDIA deep learning library} and cuBLAS\index{cuBLAS!NVIDIA linear algebra} for GPUs, Intel's oneDNN\index{oneDNN!Intel optimization library} for x86) rather than synthesizing kernels from scratch. These libraries encode microarchitectural details such as register file capacity, cache latency, and vector lane width, so the compiler can invoke pre-tuned implementations.

AI compilers trade compilation time against execution speed across three strategies when choosing among candidate kernels, with numerical precision constraining all three. Rule-based selection is the fastest at compile time. It relies on static heuristics\index{Heuristic!kernel selection trade-off} over tensor shapes, alignment, data types, and target support to pick implementations such as a Tensor Core GEMM without benchmarking a large candidate set, at the risk of missing faster configurations on irregular shapes. Cost-model selection refines that choice without running hardware benchmarks by estimating kernel latency, register pressure, cache hit rates, and arithmetic intensity with analytical models that prune unpromising candidates [@lattner2021]. When compilation budgets allow hardware measurement, profile-guided selection benchmarks candidates directly on the target device. Autotuners such as TVM's AutoTVM and Ansor search over tile sizes, unrolling factors, and thread configurations to converge on the fastest implementation [@chen2018tvm; @zheng2020ansor], and TensorRT similarly times candidate tactics against the target batch sizes. Across all three strategies, precision-aware constraints govern which candidates are legal: inference can use lower-precision paths after quality validation, but selecting INT8 without appropriate range handling degrades accuracy, whereas selecting a wider path unnecessarily forgoes available throughput.

#### Memory planning {#sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-planning-fb9f}

Memory planning\index{Memory planning!compiler phase} assigns physical storage locations, buffer offsets, and tensor lifetimes across the accelerator's memory hierarchy [@roesch2018; @chen2018tvm]. High-performance execution plans fail if memory management introduces uncoalesced memory transactions, bank conflicts, or unnecessary memory allocations that exhaust accelerator memory, so the compiler coordinates three core memory management mechanisms.

Tensor layout optimization chooses the physical arrangement of tensor dimensions that each kernel needs for coalesced access and vectorization, such as channels-last `NHWC` for Tensor Core convolutions (@sec-hardware-acceleration-memoryefficient-tensor-layouts-e250) [@nvidia2021cudnn; @GoogleXLA]. Compilers perform layout assignment globally across the graph to prevent back-to-back layout transformation kernels that consume memory bandwidth.

Liveness analysis and buffer reuse prevent out-of-memory errors by sharing physical memory across non-overlapping tensors. Deep neural networks generate dozens of intermediate activation tensors during forward propagation. Allocating a unique memory buffer for every tensor would quickly exceed the capacity of device memory (such as 16 to 80 GB on typical accelerator GPUs). The compiler analyzes the graph to compute the liveness interval of each tensor, from its generation to the completion of its last consumer. By modeling memory allocation as an interval graph coloring or 2D bin-packing problem, the compiler assigns multiple non-overlapping intermediate tensors to the same physical memory offsets [@roesch2018]. This static reuse reduces peak device memory requirements to the working set size of concurrently active tensors, avoiding runtime allocation overhead and fragmentation.

Memory hierarchy placement optimizes the staging of data between external memory (HBM or GDDR) and on-chip scratchpad memories (SRAM or shared memory). External memory bandwidth is a scarce resource; moving intermediate tiles back and forth across the memory bus creates memory-bound stalls. Compilers synthesize tiling parameters that guarantee intermediate blocks remain resident in on-chip SRAM until all local compute operations complete, minimizing round-trip traffic across the memory bus. With memory layouts fixed and buffer addresses assigned, the compiler schedules operation execution across hardware compute resources.

#### Computation scheduling {#sec-hardware-acceleration-computation-scheduling-7ccd}

Computation scheduling\index{Computation scheduling!parallel execution} determines the execution timeline and hardware resource binding for operations in the compiled graph [@zheng2020ansor]. Modern accelerators feature deep hardware pipelines, multiple independent compute engines, and dedicated DMA copy engines. Effective scheduling coordinates these resources across three distinct architectural dimensions to maximize hardware occupancy, preserve data dependencies, and prevent pipeline stalls [@chen2018tvm].

Task partitioning maps computational subgraphs onto the target's physical execution units. On GPUs, computations are partitioned into grids of thread blocks dispatched across Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). On TPUs, matrix multiplications are partitioned into tile sequences matched to the physical dimensions of systolic arrays (e.g., $128 \times 128$ or $256 \times 256$ processing elements) [@norrie2021]. On CPUs, tasks are split into thread pools matching physical cores and vectorized to fill SIMD registers.

Execution ordering resolves dependencies while minimizing live memory pressure. Operations that depend on prior results must wait for producer kernels to complete, but independent branches (such as multi-head attention projections or parallel residual paths) can execute concurrently or interleave to maintain uniform compute utilization. Compilers analyze the dependency graph to schedule operations in an order that keeps compute pipelines full while keeping activation lifetimes short, preventing buffer bloat.

Asynchronous overlap hides memory latency by executing data transfers concurrently with compute kernels. Accelerators feature dedicated DMA engines that operate independently of arithmetic pipelines. Compilers exploit this architectural separation by scheduling memory transfers (such as host-to-device weights or inter-accelerator halo exchanges) in separate hardware queues or CUDA streams, overlapping transfer latency behind long-running compute operations [@chen2018tvm; @nvidia2024tensorrt]. When compute and transfer overlap completely, data movement costs are hidden behind arithmetic execution. Poor scheduling instead introduces execution bubbles where arithmetic units sit idle waiting for kernel dispatches or serialized data copies, so synchronizing kernels via explicit compiler-generated events and stream schedules ensures the hardware sustains continuous execution without CPU driver intervention [@nvidia2024tensorrt; @zheng2020ansor].

#### Code generation {#sec-hardware-acceleration-code-generation-85c8}

With scheduling complete, the final compilation stage translates the scheduled execution plan into target-specific machine instructions. Code generation\index{Code generation!hardware-specific instructions} applies traditional backend compiler passes (instruction selection, register allocation, instruction scheduling, and peephole optimization) tailored to accelerator architectures.

Instruction selection for ML targets must emit instructions that directly engage specialized matrix ISA extensions. On NVIDIA GPUs, code generators emit PTX instructions such as `mma.sync.aligned` to invoke Tensor Cores directly, as shown in @lst-tensor_core_op. On Intel CPUs with Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), the backend targets tile-multiply instructions operating on 2D register tiles. On Arm architectures with the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME), the target is outer-product accumulation across scalable vector tiles. A backend that emits generic floating-point vector instructions instead of these matrix extensions leaves the primary compute engines idle, reducing effective throughput by an order of magnitude. For CPUs and GPUs, compilers emit machine code or optimized assembly; for TPUs, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs),[^fn-fpga-reconfigurable-logic] and proprietary NPUs, the output is often an optimized bytecode or binary execution package executed by a specialized hardware runtime.

[^fn-fpga-reconfigurable-logic]: **Field-programmable gate array**\index{FPGA!reconfigurability trade-off}: "Field-programmable" means the logic fabric is configurable after manufacturing, contrasting with fixed-function ASICs. FPGAs can improve performance for latency-sensitive data center services by implementing custom pipelines matched to a particular workload [@putnam2014]. This reconfigurability makes FPGAs attractive for rapidly evolving ML architectures where committing to an ASIC risks obsolescence, but the requirement for hardware description languages (Verilog/VHDL) and compilation times measured in hours creates a productivity barrier that limits adoption to deployments where the efficiency benefit justifies the engineering cost.

### Runtime support {#sec-hardware-acceleration-runtime-support-f94f}

A compiler transforms a high-level model into an execution plan tailored to target hardware, but that plan embeds static assumptions about runtime conditions: tensor shapes, workspace allocation limits, device capabilities, and execution concurrency. Ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation optimizes graph structures, fusion boundaries, and memory layouts for fixed shapes and known hardware configurations. While just-in-time (JIT) compilation can compile specialized variants dynamically as new shapes arrive, each compiled kernel still executes a fixed execution plan. Production serving breaks those assumptions: request arrival rates fluctuate, batch sizes vary, several inference workloads compete for shared accelerator memory, and thermal throttling can pull clock frequencies below their rated values. Request batching and admission control belong to the serving layer (@sec-model-serving); the concern here is how the accelerator runtime dispatches compiled execution plans once a batch reaches the hardware.

An AI runtime\index{AI runtime!dynamic execution management} bridges static graph compilation and the dynamic realities of accelerator execution. Compilers optimize and lower computational graphs under fixed structural assumptions, but production systems encounter variable batch sizes, fluctuating sequence lengths, and constrained memory budgets. The runtime executes compiled engines while managing input-dependent tensor shapes, device-memory buffers and workspace, asynchronous hardware streams, and precompiled execution profiles. In production inference stacks such as NVIDIA TensorRT, the offline builder optimizes the network and benchmarks candidate tactics to construct an execution engine, while the runtime engine binds input buffers, selects valid optimization profiles, and dispatches kernels to the accelerator [@nvidia2026tensorrtarchitecture; @nvidia2026tensorrtdynamicshapes].

This execution lifecycle spans three core responsibilities. First, the runtime selects and dispatches precompiled kernel variants matched to runtime tensor dimensions and hardware capabilities. Second, it manages device memory through arena allocators and static buffer reuse, reducing repeated allocation and associated host-device synchronization overhead. Third, in distributed environments, framework runtimes coordinate cross-device execution boundaries, as demonstrated in pipeline-parallel frameworks such as GPipe [@huang2019gpipe] and automated device-placement systems [@mirhoseini_device_placement_2017]. While serving schedulers oversee request batching and admission control across clusters, the accelerator runtime governs local execution on the device.

#### ML runtime architecture {#sec-hardware-acceleration-runtime-architecture-differences-ml-systems-932e}

General-purpose runtimes manage threads, preemptive tasks, heap allocations, and asynchronous I/O across arbitrary control-flow paths. In contrast, an AI runtime\index{AI runtime!vs. traditional runtime} operates over dataflow graphs composed of multidimensional tensors, pre-scheduled kernel grids, device memory arenas, and hardware command queues, as contrasted in @tbl-runtime-comparison.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

| Aspect                  | **Traditional runtime**\index{Traditional runtime}         | **AI runtime**\index{AI runtime}                              |
|:------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Execution Model         | Functions, threads, tasks, events, and asynchronous I/O    | Tensor graphs, kernels, streams, and device events            |
| **Task scheduling**     | Threads and tasks across processor resources               | Dependency-aware kernel and transfer dispatch                 |
| Memory Management       | Objects, stacks, heaps, pools, and virtual memory          | Tensor buffers, workspaces, device memory, and buffer reuse   |
| Optimization Priorities | Responsiveness, throughput, locality, and resource sharing | Shape compatibility, transfer overlap, reuse, and utilization |
| **Adaptability**        | Dynamic scheduling and allocation within program semantics | Runtime choices within compiled graphs and available kernels  |
| Target Hardware         | CPUs and heterogeneous devices                             | CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, and custom accelerators                     |

: **Runtime Execution Models**: AI runtimes add tensor-, graph-, and accelerator-aware resource management to conventional runtime services. The exact boundary among framework, compiler runtime, device library, and serving scheduler varies by stack. {#tbl-runtime-comparison tbl-colwidths="[22,35,43]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

Tensor memory management represents a primary architectural divergence. In traditional systems, general-purpose allocators manage variable-sized heap objects using runtime metadata. Traditional device allocation calls such as `cudaMalloc` can introduce costly driver work and synchronization. AI runtimes reduce repeated allocation overhead by combining lifetime analysis with pooled or arena allocation. For fixed-shape graphs, the compiler computes static memory offsets, mapping non-overlapping intermediate tensors to shared physical buffers. For variable-shape tensors, the runtime can carve device-memory buffers from preallocated pools, avoiding repeated driver allocation calls within the reserved capacity.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: runtime-production-tdp
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ A100 FORM-FACTOR TDP COMPARISON
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Production and benchmark hardware may use different form factors
# │
# │ Goal: Show one hardware reason production performance can differ.
# │ Show: The gap in Thermal Design Power (TDP) between SXM and PCIe variants.
# │ How: List TDP wattage constants for different A100 form factors.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt

class RuntimeProductionTdp:
    """A100 SXM maximum Thermal Design Power for form-factor comparison."""

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    # (constant lookup, no derivation)

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    a100_tdp_w_str = fmt_power(Hardware.Cloud.A100.tdp, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Production environments introduce physical constraints that differ from offline benchmarks. For example, an NVIDIA A100 SXM accelerator operates with a maximum TDP of `{python} RuntimeProductionTdp.a100_tdp_w_str`, whereas the A100 PCIe variant is constrained to a 300 W TDP envelope. Because sustained clock frequencies scale with available power and thermal dissipation, a compiled kernel tuned for an SXM module may experience thermal throttling or fail to meet latency bounds on a PCIe card. The runtime cannot re-synthesize loop structures or change thread-block dimensions dynamically in response to thermal constraints; it must execute within precompiled profiles while the serving system handles request batching and admission control.

#### Dynamic kernel execution {#sec-hardware-acceleration-dynamic-kernel-execution-33fc}

While static compilation generates high-performance machine code for fixed shapes, production inference requires executing requests with dynamic dimensions\index{Dynamic kernel execution!runtime adaptation}. In language models, input sequence length $\SequenceLength$ and batch size $\BatchSize$ vary across requests. Recompiling an execution plan for each unexpected shape can violate a request deadline: exploring loop unrolling, shared-memory tiling, and register allocation requires seconds or minutes, while serving deadlines operate on millisecond timescales.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How serving runtimes form batches of varying size under latency deadlines is developed in @sec-model-serving-static-vs-dynamic-batching-fd0a.
:::

Profile-based inference stacks address this mismatch with precompiled shape ranges. The engine is built for a declared range of each dynamic dimension (the minimum, typical, and maximum shapes), with device-memory workspace reserved for that range. A request inside the range binds its tensors to preallocated buffers and launches precompiled kernels without compilation overhead. A request outside it must be padded, split, or routed to a slower general-purpose kernel, because the runtime cannot synthesize new tiling strategies on the fly. TensorRT's optimization profiles are the common example, and choosing and configuring such a runtime for a service is developed in @sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef.

Variable requests also keep the host link busy, and the runtime hides those transfers with the asynchronous streams and double buffering\index{Double buffering!latency hiding} of @sec-hardware-acceleration-transfer-optimization-85a8, copying batch $\BatchIndex{+}1$ while batch $\BatchIndex$ executes. The overlap holds only while compute duration exceeds transfer duration.

#### Runtime kernel selection {#sec-hardware-acceleration-runtime-kernel-selection-1ffe}

An operation may have multiple kernel implementations, termed tactics in TensorRT. The builder selects tactics while constructing an engine; other stacks may retain variants for runtime dispatch. The available choice depends on tensor dimensions, the compiled plan, and permitted device-memory workspace.

Operational batch size changes the available reuse and parallelism. At $\BatchSize=1$ in weight-streaming autoregressive decoding, GEMV kernels often target memory throughput. Larger prompt-processing batches can favor GEMM kernels using Tensor Core paths, register tiles, and shared memory. The transition depends on dimensions, precision, traffic, and hardware balance; no fixed batch threshold establishes compute-bound execution.

Device-memory workspace availability further constrains tactic selection. In a standard output-tiled GEMM, each thread block computes one $(\GemmRowDimension, \GemmColumnDimension)$ output tile and loops sequentially over the entire inner reduction dimension $\GemmInnerDimension$, accumulating partial sums in on-chip registers before writing the final output tile once. When the output matrix is small but the reduction dimension $\GemmInnerDimension$ is long, the output grid spawns too few thread blocks to occupy every streaming multiprocessor. A split-$\GemmInnerDimension$ tactic exposes extra parallelism by partitioning the $\GemmInnerDimension$ reduction loop across multiple thread blocks running on different multiprocessors. Because separate multiprocessors do not share registers or local scratchpad memory, each split-$\GemmInnerDimension$ block must write its partial tile sum to a temporary buffer in global device memory so a subsequent reduction step can sum the slices into the final result. A runtime execution plan built under a tight workspace memory limit may therefore disallow split-$\GemmInnerDimension$ tactics and accept lower multiprocessor occupancy instead.

Runtime selection remains strictly bounded by the numerical formats established during compilation. In mixed-precision training and inference systems such as Megatron-LM, executing matrix multiplications in FP16 or BF16 on Tensor Cores with FP32 accumulation is a numerical requirement of the chosen recipe, validated prior to deployment [@shoeybi2019megatron]. The runtime does not monitor loss values or dynamically alter precision; it only chooses among the validated tactics that implement the specified numerical precision.

#### Kernel scheduling and utilization {#sec-hardware-acceleration-kernel-scheduling-utilization-99d6}

Kernel dispatch\index{Kernel scheduling!hardware utilization} represents the final stage of runtime execution, coordinating host-side task queues with device-side execution. The software runtime manages host-side command queues (such as CUDA streams or TPU command rings) and records hardware events or semaphores to enforce dataflow dependencies asynchronously. When independent operations (such as parallel multi-head attention projections) have no mutual data dependencies, the runtime dispatches them onto separate streams to enable concurrent execution on the accelerator. Once submitted to the device queue, however, execution control transfers entirely to hardware schedulers. On a GPU, the hardware warp scheduler and work distribution engine assign thread blocks to SMs based on register file availability, shared memory capacity, and maximum warp occupancy. The software runtime cannot schedule individual threads or dictate L1/L2 cache replacement policies. Similarly, TPU runtimes submit macro-instructions to on-chip command queues, while hardware sequencers feed systolic matrix units and vector units [@jouppi2017].

A low achieved rate alone cannot distinguish runtime gaps from a memory bottleneck. Consider three supplied illustrative profiles of low-intensity kernels, not measurements from a particular device. In the first, the timeline shows continuous kernel execution and HBM traffic close to the sustainable bandwidth ceiling. Reducing transferred bytes or increasing reuse addresses that observed limit. In the second, kernels remain active but dependent loads produce long stalls while HBM traffic stays well below its ceiling. More bandwidth alone need not help: independent requests or a different access schedule must expose enough concurrency to hide the latency. In the third, short kernels alternate with device-idle gaps while the host submits work. Reducing dispatch and synchronization overhead addresses those gaps; changing the arithmetic instruction rate does not.

The discriminating evidence is the timeline together with traffic and stall observations. If added independent requests raise bandwidth and shorten load stalls, they support the latency hypothesis; if bandwidth is already sustained near its ceiling, traffic reduction is the more direct lever. The roofline bounds the resource opportunity, while the profile identifies which mechanism leaves the kernel below it. Even with aggressive kernel fusion, optimal tactic selection, and zero-allocation memory reuse, the execution capacity of a single accelerator is physically bounded by its silicon area, thermal dissipation limit, and high-bandwidth memory capacity. Scaling beyond these physical boundaries therefore requires distributing computation across multiple accelerators.

## Beyond One Accelerator {#sec-hardware-acceleration-multichip-scaling-c649}

A single accelerator holds the chapter's ResNet-50 workload and GPT-2 XL decoding comfortably in on-package memory, but larger workloads outgrow one device either because their arithmetic would take too long on it or because their weights and runtime state do not fit in its HBM. Multi-chip scaling\index{Multi-chip scaling!beyond single accelerator} still depends on an efficient per-device dataflow, since each accelerator must feed its own execution units, but communication adds further boundaries to the memory hierarchy. Moving data through on-chip storage, HBM, an intra-node link, and a network fabric generally increases latency and energy at each step, so scaling is not merely a question of adding chips.

Each step outward moves the communication boundary and changes the dominant trade-off. Inside the package, chiplet-based architectures\index{Chiplet!modular die interconnect} partition a large design into smaller dies joined at relatively low latency, bypassing the manufacturing limits of a monolithic chip. Wafer-scale integration takes the opposite approach and keeps more computation on one device. At the node, a multi-accelerator server joins several chips, each with its own memory, through board- or server-level interconnects such as NVLink. A workload then splits through data parallelism\index{Data parallelism!multi-accelerator scaling} (each accelerator processes different batches) or model parallelism\index{Model parallelism!multi-accelerator scaling} (different accelerators hold different layers, or individual matrix multiplications are sliced across devices). When a model's weights and runtime state exceed one device's HBM, that split becomes a placement requirement rather than a speed choice. How training uses the accelerators of one machine, including how they synchronize gradients, is developed in @sec-model-training-singlenode-multigpu-training-c87f. Within a server, the engineering test compares the computation or device-memory capacity that partitioning saves with the communication it exposes, accounting for overlap and the actual directional link bandwidth.

Beyond the node, the network interface card\index{Network interface card!node interconnect} links each machine to the others over Ethernet or InfiniBand\index{InfiniBand!node-to-node link}. It is the narrowest, highest-latency step of the bandwidth taper measured in @sec-hardware-acceleration-nodelevel-interconnect-topology-b45b, and traffic that must cross it leaves single-node reasoning behind. Work that spans several machines lies beyond this book's one-machine scope. Scaling out across identical data-center accelerators is one way a system combines multiple engines; at the opposite end of the power spectrum, mobile and embedded systems integrate several *different* engines onto a single silicon die.

## Heterogeneous SoC Design {#sec-hardware-acceleration-heterogeneous-soc-ai-acceleration-b1bb}

Edge, mobile, and automotive deployments operate under strict physical constraints: sealed enclosures without active fans limit thermal dissipation to a few watts, while battery capacity caps total energy consumption. To deliver machine learning capabilities within these boundaries, heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC)\index{System-on-chip!heterogeneous AI acceleration} architectures integrate general-purpose CPU cores, GPU shader arrays, digital signal processors (DSPs), and specialized neural processing units (NPUs) onto a single silicon die sharing a unified memory subsystem. The workload mapping problem introduced for discrete accelerators persists, but it expands to include hardware operator coverage, cross-engine transfer overheads, real-time deadlines, and dynamic thermal throttling. Two of the book's lighthouses take over from ResNet-50 here. MobileNetV2, compute-bound in its efficient regime and built for phone cameras, runs its convolutions on a phone's NPU within a few watts. KWS, the power-bound lighthouse, listens continuously on a DSP or microcontroller within milliwatts. Both run on silicon that shares one memory system among every engine on the chip.

### Mobile SoC architecture evolution {#sec-hardware-acceleration-mobile-soc-architecture-evolution-6ca8}

That single-die integration evolved as mobile workloads outgrew what a CPU and graphics pipeline could sustain within a battery budget. Mobile system-on-chip architectures\index{Mobile SoC!architecture evolution} implement heterogeneous computing\index{Heterogeneous computing!mobile SoC} by connecting each specialized block, namely CPU clusters, wide SIMD GPU shaders, fixed-point DSPs, and dedicated neural processing units (NPUs)\index{NPU!mobile SoC}\index{NPU!efficiency trade-off}, over an on-chip network to shared low-power DRAM (LPDDR) so sensory and perceptual tasks can run on the engine best aligned with their arithmetic structure. Continuous audio feature extraction and keyword spotting run on low-power DSPs, dense convolution and matrix-multiplication layers execute on systolic or tensor-array NPUs, parallel graphics and image postprocessing map to GPUs, and sequential control flow runs on the CPU. Meeting real-time frame deadlines without triggering aggressive thermal throttling requires scheduling execution across these engines while respecting their differing power profiles.

::: {#exmp-hw-acceleration-heterogeneous-microcontrollers .callout-example title="Heterogeneous microcontrollers"}

**Scenario**: An embedded smart doorbell must run periodic person detection within a tight memory, energy, and latency budget.

**Diagnosis**: On a supported deployment, a general-purpose Cortex-M path misses the measured energy or latency target. A micro-NPU such as Arm Ethos-U can offload compatible convolution operators, while the CPU retains control flow and unsupported operations.

**Systems lesson**: Micro-NPU specialization can improve the energy and latency of supported operators, but feasibility must be measured for the whole pipeline, including fallbacks and sensor processing.

:::

Modern mobile SoCs use unified memory architectures\index{Unified memory!mobile SoC} where all processing units share a common physical address space in LPDDR. Unlike discrete accelerator architectures that incur explicit PCIe transfer latencies, unified memory allows zero-copy buffer passing between the image signal processor (ISP), CPU, GPU, and NPU. Sharing physical DRAM does not guarantee zero software overhead, however. Non-coherent engines need explicit cache maintenance (@sec-hardware-acceleration-software-stack-challenges-255c), and specialized NPUs often require hardware-specific tensor layouts (such as channels-last (NHWC) with 16- or 32-byte channel alignment to feed vector register lanes), forcing memory-bound transpositions when interfacing with CPU layers structured in channels-first (NCHW) formats.

SoC architects customize these compute blocks according to domain-specific physical constraints. High-end smartphone SoCs emphasize peak burst performance and low idle leakage for interactive tasks such as real-time computational photography and on-device text generation. In contrast, embedded and automotive SoCs prioritize deterministic memory access, hardware fault detection, and bounded worst-case latency to satisfy real-time control constraints.

### Strategies for dynamic workload distribution {#sec-hardware-acceleration-strategies-dynamic-workload-distribution-a421}

Consider a real-time object detection pipeline executing on a mobile SoC with an integrated CPU, GPU, and NPU. The pipeline comprises three consecutive stages: a MobileNetV2 backbone for feature extraction, nonmaximum suppression\index{Non-maximum suppression!irregular memory access} (NMS) for postprocessing candidate bounding boxes, and a display overlay\index{Display overlay!GPU mapping} to render final detections onto a camera feed. Partitioning neural network workloads\index{Workload distribution!heterogeneous processor} across those heterogeneous cores requires matching the arithmetic intensity and memory regularity of each stage to the microarchitecture built for it. The convolutional backbone has regular, deterministic memory access and dense arithmetic suited to the NPU's fixed-function tensor engine, even though depthwise separable layers have lower arithmetic intensity than standard convolutions. NMS, by contrast, relies on score-based sorting and conditional intersection-over-union loops evaluated across variable-length candidate lists. This irregular, branch-heavy control flow maps poorly to an NPU's spatial array but executes efficiently on out-of-order CPU cores with branch prediction and hardware caching. Finally, the display overlay requires per-pixel rasterization and alpha blending across a high-resolution frame (an embarrassingly parallel, memory-bandwidth-bound task that maps directly to the GPU's rasterizers and texture units). Splitting the pipeline across the three engines, with the NPU for feature extraction, the CPU for NMS, and the GPU for display compositing, is a candidate mapping. Its compute savings must exceed transfer, layout, and synchronization costs before it improves end-to-end latency or energy over a single-engine implementation.

This pipeline partitioning reflects the broader relationship between algorithmic structures and machine architectures. Regular matrix contractions and convolutions map cleanly to systolic or vectorized NPU datapaths, whereas data-dependent control flow maps to CPU execution resources. Transformer attention layers span both paradigms: the projection GEMMs ($\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix, \AttentionOutputMatrix$) and attention score contractions ($\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T$, and the product of the attention weights with $\AttentionValuesMatrix$) execute efficiently on NPU matrix units. Intermediate softmax reductions, causal masking, and layer normalizations, however, involve elementwise operations. If the NPU runtime cannot fuse these elementwise operations into on-chip SRAM scratchpads, intermediate tensors must spill to LPDDR, eroding the accelerator's throughput advantage.

Optimal processor assignment is dynamic rather than static. As device thermal conditions deteriorate or battery reserves drop, the runtime must adapt its scheduling policy. However, migrating an executing model across processor backends carries non-trivial overhead: weights must be re-bound in memory, intermediate buffers may require layout reformatting, and device drivers incur kernel dispatch latency. If the overhead of synchronizing state across processors exceeds the compute savings of offloading, retaining execution on a single suboptimal engine can yield lower total latency and energy than continuous cross-engine migration.

Shared memory subsystems introduce cross-engine interference during simultaneous execution. Because the CPU, GPU, NPU, camera ISP, and display engine share a single LPDDR memory bus, the SoC memory controller enforces Quality of Service (QoS) priorities to satisfy real-time hardware deadlines. The display engine and camera ISP must receive guaranteed memory bandwidth and bounded latency to prevent display flicker and sensor FIFO overflow; the memory controller consequently prioritizes display and camera transactions over NPU and GPU traffic. During memory-intensive phases (such as autoregressive language model decoding where model weights must be read from DRAM for every generated token) high-priority ISP or display traffic reduces effective NPU memory bandwidth, increasing token generation latency.

Automotive computing platforms\index{Automotive AI!real-time safety requirements} expose a stricter form of the same interference. A perception pipeline with a hard deadline may share the SoC and memory system with a cabin assistant or infotainment model. If the convenience workload streams weights from DRAM without a bandwidth limit, it can delay the perception pipeline even when the two use different compute engines. Such deployments require resource isolation and validation under concurrent load; average inference throughput alone cannot establish deadline compliance. The hardware lesson is the interference boundary: assigning work to separate engines does not isolate workloads that still share memory bandwidth.

### Power and thermal management {#sec-hardware-acceleration-power-thermal-management-6c00}

Fanless mobile devices operate within strict continuous power budgets\index{Power management!mobile AI} and thermal envelopes\index{Thermal management!mobile constraints}, typically dissipating no more than 3 to 5 watts sustained across the entire chassis before touch temperatures exceed safety thresholds. Although transient bursts can draw 10 to 15 watts, continuous inference rapidly saturates the thermal capacitance of the device, heating the silicon junction and requiring active power management across the SoC.

Heterogeneous SoCs manage power across distinct silicon partitions using **dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)**\index{DVFS!power-performance envelope}, which exploits the cubic dependence of dynamic power on frequency behind the power wall (@eq-power-scaling). Total power in complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) digital circuits is the sum of dynamic switching power and static leakage power:
$$\TotalChipPower= \DynamicPower+ \LeakagePower= \SwitchingActivityFactor \SwitchedCapacitance \SupplyVoltage^2 \ClockFrequency+ \LeakageCurrent \SupplyVoltage$$
where $\SwitchingActivityFactor$ is the gate switching activity factor, $\SwitchedCapacitance$ is physical load capacitance, $\SupplyVoltage$ is supply voltage, $\ClockFrequency$ is clock frequency, and $\LeakageCurrent$ is temperature-dependent leakage current. Over an operating range where increasing clock frequency $\ClockFrequency$ requires supply voltage $\SupplyVoltage$ to rise approximately proportionally, fixed activity and capacitance give the cubic approximation for dynamic power dissipation\index{Scaling!frequency, cubic power relationship}:
$$\DynamicPower\propto \ClockFrequency^3$$
Under that approximation, doubling clock frequency can incur an eightfold penalty in dynamic power [@le2010dynamic]. The same relation run in reverse is what DVFS exploits: dropping the clock lets the core voltage fall, and dynamic power falls faster than throughput. The cubic penalty also explains why ML accelerators favor large parallel arrays of simple execution units clocked at moderate frequencies over narrow pipelines clocked at extreme frequencies.

On a heterogeneous SoC, CPU clusters, GPU shader cores, and NPU engines occupy separate power and voltage domains. Increasing the voltage and frequency of the NPU to meet a tight latency deadline consumes electrical current and thermal headroom that would otherwise be available to the CPU or GPU. System power governors continuously adjust these operating points based on workload queues, temperature sensor readings, and frame deadline targets.

When sustained computation exceeds the chassis dissipation rate, the platform initiates thermal throttling\index{Thermal throttling!intelligent migration}. Because specialized NPUs achieve higher energy efficiency (TOPS/W) for tensor math than general-purpose cores, offloading matrix workloads to a CPU or GPU during a thermal event often increases total energy dissipation, exacerbating thermal accumulation. Instead, runtimes manage thermal limits by capping clock frequencies, reducing inference duty cycles (such as throttling a perception model from 30 frames per second to 15 frames per second), or dynamically switching to a smaller, pruned model checkpoint. Task migration is applied selectively to move non-tensor preprocessing away from localized silicon hot spots on the die. Battery state further shapes runtime scheduling. When battery charge drops below critical thresholds or the device enters a low-power mode, the system scheduler trades inferencing fidelity for battery life. It does so by selecting prevalidated lower-precision or sparse model variants, or by batching asynchronous inference requests to maximize the time cores spend in deep low-power sleep states.

### Software stack challenges {#sec-hardware-acceleration-software-stack-challenges-255c}

When a model deployed on an SoC contains even a single operator unsupported by the NPU delegate (such as a custom activation, dynamic tensor shape, or non-standard reduction), the inference runtime must split the computation graph into subgraphs and insert fallback paths to the CPU or GPU. Each boundary crossing requires synchronizing execution and translating data representations, transforming a single algorithmic graph into a fragmented sequence of hardware dispatches. Standard programming models like OpenCL\index{OpenCL!cross-processor execution} and Vulkan provide portable low-level execution abstractions across compute devices, but they do not eliminate this delegation overhead or the need for microarchitecture-specific kernel tuning.

Shared memory subsystems require explicit cache and memory management across non-coherent execution domains. While CPUs maintain cache coherence across their own cores via hardware snooping protocols, mobile NPUs and DSPs frequently interface with system memory as non-coherent DMA bus masters. When the CPU writes input tensors to cached DRAM and hands control to an NPU, software must explicitly flush the CPU's dirty cache lines to DRAM before NPU execution begins. Similarly, upon NPU completion, the CPU must invalidate its own cache lines over the destination memory range to prevent reading stale cached data. If unsupported operators cause an inference graph to ping-pong repeatedly between CPU and NPU, the latency of cache maintenance and intermediate DRAM round-trips can exceed the execution time of the operators themselves.

Runtimes navigate this scheduling complexity using ahead-of-time compilation, empirical profile databases, and dynamic dispatch heuristics. Device telemetry (monitoring frame completion times, core temperatures, and battery drain) informs runtime decisions to throttle clock frequencies or swap execution delegates. However, dynamic adaptation cannot replace deterministic graph lowering for latency-sensitive applications; deployment requires validating the compiled, lowered partition on physical target silicon under worst-case thermal and memory contention.

On an SoC, speed comes from keeping work and data on the right engine, not from how many engines the chip has. In the D·A·M taxonomy, an SoC represents a composite Machine layer whose components have different memory hierarchies, arithmetic strengths, and thermal envelopes. The iron law's data term and the energy-movement principle (\ref{pri-energy-movement}) together make data movement the governor of both runtime and energy. When software coordination fails to maintain tensor locality or induces frequent cross-engine fallbacks, energy dissipation is dominated by interconnect and DRAM traffic rather than arithmetic. Maximizing performance on heterogeneous SoCs requires minimizing data movement across domain boundaries while matching each algorithmic operation to the specialized datapath architected to accelerate it. From the microcontroller that runs keyword spotting to the data-center accelerator that serves GPT-2 XL, that matching ends in a choice of machine, which the next section makes explicit.

## Choosing an Accelerator {#sec-hardware-acceleration-choosing-accelerator-6b2d}

Every section of this chapter ends in the same question asked at a different level: which machine should run a given workload. The question cannot be answered from a datasheet, because the resource that binds belongs to the workload on a particular machine rather than to the machine alone. The book's five lighthouses make the point on a single reference machine. Their bytes and operations differ by orders of magnitude, and each one exhausts a different resource of an H100 first (@tbl-hw-acceleration-lighthouse-memory-compute).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lighthouse-memory-compute-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LIGHTHOUSE MEMORY AND COMPUTE ON THE REFERENCE ACCELERATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-hw-acceleration-lighthouse-memory-compute and the
# │          cost-performance prose in
# │          @sec-hardware-acceleration-choosing-accelerator-6b2d.
# │
# │ Goal:    Give compute and memory equal weight for every lighthouse before
# │          the chapter compares accelerators.
# │ Show:    Model bytes at FP16 and INT8, operations per inference (per token
# │          for GPT-2 XL), and whether the model fits one H100's memory.
# │ How:     Registry model sizes and FLOP counts; H100 memory capacity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, BYTES_FP16, BYTES_INT8
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_flops, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory_capacity

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class LighthouseMemoryCompute:
    """Per-lighthouse model bytes and operations against one H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    mobilenet = Models.Vision.MobileNetV2
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2
    dlrm = Models.Recommendation.DLRM
    kws = Models.Tiny.DS_CNN
    h100_mem = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity
    h100_bw = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_fp16 = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    resnet_int8 = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    mobilenet_fp16 = mobilenet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    mobilenet_int8 = mobilenet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    gpt2_fp16 = gpt2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    gpt2_int8 = gpt2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    gpt2_token_flops = (2 * flop / param) * gpt2.parameters
    kws_fp16 = kws.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    kws_int8 = kws.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    dlrm_bytes = dlrm.model_size

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(gpt2_fp16 < h100_mem, "GPT-2 XL must fit one H100 at FP16.")
    check(dlrm_bytes > h100_mem, "DLRM's embedding tables must exceed one H100's memory.")
    check(kws_int8 < 1 * MB, "KWS must fit in under a megabyte at INT8.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_fp16_str = fmt_memory(resnet_fp16, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_int8_str = fmt_memory(resnet_int8, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_ops_str = fmt_flops(resnet.inference_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_fp16_str = fmt_memory(mobilenet_fp16, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_int8_str = fmt_memory(mobilenet_int8, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_ops_str = fmt_flops(mobilenet.inference_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    gpt2_fp16_str = fmt_memory(gpt2_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt2_int8_str = fmt_memory(gpt2_int8, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    gpt2_ops_str = fmt_flops(gpt2_token_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=0, commas=False)
    dlrm_bytes_str = fmt_memory(dlrm_bytes, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_fp16_str = fmt_memory(kws_fp16, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_int8_str = fmt_memory(kws_int8, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_ops_str = fmt_flops(kws.inference_flops, unit=MFLOPs, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_mem_str = fmt_memory_capacity(h100_mem, unit=GiB, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=True)
```

| **Lighthouse**             | **Home regime** | **Model bytes (FP16)**                                      | **Model bytes (INT8)**                                | **Operations per inference**                              | **Binding resource on one H100**                                                            |
|:---------------------------|:----------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **ResNet-50**              | Compute bound   | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.resnet_fp16_str`          | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.resnet_int8_str`    | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.resnet_ops_str`         | Arithmetic, once batching amortizes the weights                                             |
| **MobileNetV2**            | Compute bound   | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.mobilenet_fp16_str`       | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.mobilenet_int8_str` | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.mobilenet_ops_str`      | Launch overhead and depthwise-layer bandwidth; built for a phone NPU                        |
| **GPT-2 XL (decode)**      | Bandwidth bound | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.gpt2_fp16_str`            | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.gpt2_int8_str`      | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.gpt2_ops_str` per token | HBM bandwidth: every token rereads every weight                                             |
| **DLRM**                   | Capacity bound  | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.dlrm_bytes_str` of tables | Tables dominate either way                            | Few per lookup                                            | Memory capacity: tables exceed one device's `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.h100_mem_str` |
| **Keyword spotting (KWS)** | Power bound     | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.kws_fp16_str`             | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.kws_int8_str`       | `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.kws_ops_str`            | None on an H100; built for a microcontroller's milliwatt budget                             |

: **Lighthouse Memory and Compute**: Model bytes and operations for the book's five lighthouses from the model registry, with the resource each exhausts first on one H100. The operation counts are per inference, and per generated token for GPT-2 XL decode; DLRM's bytes are dominated by its embedding tables, whose lookups perform little arithmetic. {#tbl-hw-acceleration-lighthouse-memory-compute tbl-colwidths="[16,13,14,14,16,27]"}

The table turns the chapter's diagnosis into a selection rule. ResNet-50 rewards arithmetic throughput on a supported INT8 path, GPT-2 XL decode rewards memory bandwidth, DLRM rewards memory capacity, and MobileNetV2 and KWS reward energy per inference on chips that never see a data center. The rest of the section applies that rule at three levels: the configurations accelerator families adopt for their target deployments, the cost of delivered throughput, and the energy each request consumes.

### Processor configurations across deployment targets {#sec-hardware-acceleration-interconnects}

Across data-center, server-CPU, and mobile targets, architects assemble SIMD lanes, Tensor Cores, and systolic arrays into markedly different full-chip organizations depending on which resource binds first. Training-optimized accelerators such as the NVIDIA A100 pack 108 Streaming Multiprocessors with wide SIMD units and FP16 Tensor Cores because training throughput scales with aggregate multiply-accumulate capacity across general kernels [@NVIDIA2020]. Google's TPU v4, by contrast, concentrates each chip into two cores built around large $128{\times}128$ BF16 systolic arrays, trading per-thread flexibility for area and energy efficiency on dense matrix multiplications [@jouppi2023]. Inference and edge targets shift the balance again. Intel's Sapphire Rapids dedicates Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) tile engines to INT8 and BF16 because server inference models tolerate reduced precision [@intel2021amx], while mobile neural engines shrink those matrix datapaths into low-power SoC blocks that prioritize energy per operation over peak throughput. @Tbl-execution-units compares these architectural configurations.

| Processor                                       | **Vector execution**\index{Vector execution} |   **Matrix engine**\index{Matrix engine}   |  Processing Elements  | **Primary workloads** |
|:------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------:|:------------------------------------------:|:---------------------:|:----------------------|
| **NVIDIA A100**\index{NVIDIA A100}              |              CUDA FP/INT lanes               |       Tensor Core instruction tiles        |        108 SMs        | Training, HPC         |
| **Google TPU v4**\index{Google TPUv4}           |                 Vector unit                  |   $128{\times}128$ BF16 systolic arrays    |      2 cores/chip     | Training              |
| **Intel Sapphire**\index{Intel!Sapphire Rapids} |               512-bit AVX-512                | AMX tiles (up to 16 rows by 64 bytes each) |     Up to 60 cores    | Inference             |
| Mobile NPU                                      |             CPU/GPU/DSP vectors              |            Small matrix engines            | Integrated NPU blocks | Mobile inference      |

: **AI Processor Configurations**: Modern AI processors prioritize different execution unit characteristics for specific workloads: NVIDIA A100 uses wide SIMD and Tensor Cores for training, Google TPU v4 emphasizes high-throughput BF16 matrix multiplication, Intel Sapphire Rapids focuses on INT8-optimized inference, and mobile NPUs prioritize low-power execution. These variations in SIMD width, Tensor Core size, and processing element count reflect the growing diversity in AI hardware architectures. {#tbl-execution-units tbl-colwidths="[15,23,20,23,19]"}

The pattern across these configurations reveals a consistent engineering principle: each design sacrifices generality to optimize for its target workload's dominant operation and precision. Training chips invest silicon in wide floating-point datapaths; inference chips trade precision for throughput; mobile chips trade throughput for energy efficiency. No single design dominates across all workloads, which is precisely why hardware selection depends on workload analysis rather than headline specifications.

### Cost-performance analysis {#sec-hardware-acceleration-costperformance-analysis-e925}

Consider an engineering team choosing between deploying a larger cluster of older accelerators or a smaller cluster of newer units. Architectural specifications define computational potential, but procurement decisions require **cost-performance analysis**\index{Cost-Performance Analysis!accelerator economics} grounded in delivered throughput rather than datasheet peaks. Because memory access costs dominate computation (@sec-hardware-acceleration-machine-learning-hardware-specialization-09c5), accelerators achieve only a fraction of their advertised FLOP/s on memory-bound kernels while sustaining high utilization on dense matrix multiplications that amortize each fetch across many operations.

Peak FLOP/s figures therefore mislead whenever dominant kernels are memory-bandwidth or communication bound. In a large model pipeline, dense feed-forward and attention projection layers may remain compute bound, whereas embedding lookups, layer normalization, residual additions, and small-batch autoregressive decoding often have low arithmetic intensity. Their measured bottlenecks can include memory bandwidth, dependent access latency, reductions, and launch overhead; the operator name alone does not identify the limiting resource. The decisive metric is delivered workload throughput per dollar under realistic cluster utilization, memory capacity constraints, available memory bandwidth, and scale-out interconnect efficiency.

These architectural and economic constraints explain the rapid industry adoption of newer accelerators despite substantial increases in nominal unit price. For bandwidth-bound workloads, generational improvements in memory bandwidth and compiler code generation dominate end-to-end execution time. Cloud deployments introduce additional trade-offs: hourly rental rates, dynamic instance utilization, and infrastructure overhead continuously shift the economic break-even point between purchasing on-premises hardware and leasing cloud capacity.

Price-per-peak worksheets for named products age quickly. List prices vary with vendor, region, contract terms, and procurement volume, and each product's headline peak uses a different precision, so the ratio of price to peak is meaningful for one device but not as a comparison across devices. A dated worksheet for several accelerator generations is kept with the other specifications in @sec-appdx-system-assumptions. The durable rule is the one the lighthouse table states: divide cost by the throughput the workload delivers on its binding resource, not by the advertised peak.

No worksheet reduces accelerator selection to a single headline specification. A bandwidth-bound kernel benefits more from the H100's `{python} LighthouseMemoryCompute.h100_bw_gb_per_s_str` memory subsystem than from an incremental gain in peak arithmetic, whereas a compute-bound GEMM shows the opposite sensitivity.
