Device memory capacity dictates whether working sets fit on-chip without spilling or partitioning, while compiler and driver maturity determines whether the application can actually reach the advertised datapath.

### Energy per request {#sec-hardware-acceleration-hardware-sustainability-e902}

At fleet scale, energy per useful inference becomes an important hardware-selection criterion\index{Hardware sustainability!carbon footprint}. Operational emissions depend on workload throughput, measured system power, utilization, cooling overhead, and the electricity mix; embodied emissions add another lifecycle cost. Peak performance per watt\index{Performance per watt!efficiency metric}\index{Energy efficiency!TFLOPS per watt} is therefore a screening metric, not a substitute for end-to-end energy per request. The following scenario shows how useful throughput and a common power boundary determine the fleet needed for the same inference service.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: carbon-roi-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CARBON ROI OF SPECIALIZED SILICON
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "An illustrative operational-energy comparison" callout
# │
# │ Goal: Compare operational energy for the same inference service.
# │ Show: Fleet counts, joules per served request, and annual emissions.
# │ How: Size fleets from useful throughput with capacity headroom, then
# │      apply matched whole-server wall power and a common grid factor.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Infrastructure, BILLION, HOURS_PER_DAY, DAYS_PER_YEAR
from mlsysim.core.units import watt, second, hour, joule, kWh, kg, metric_ton
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_rate, fmt_percent, fmt_time, fmt_power, fmt_energy, fmt_carbon_intensity, fmt_emissions

class CarbonRoiCalc:
    """Hypothetical matched-service comparison; no product measurements."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    cpu_power = 100 * watt  # hypothetical whole CPU-server wall power
    npu_power = 200 * watt  # hypothetical whole NPU-equipped-server wall power
    cpu_rate = 100 / second  # supplied useful requests/s at the latency target
    npu_rate = 1000 / second  # same model, inputs, quality, and latency target
    operating_fraction = 0.8  # scenario policy: reserve capacity for variation
    inferences_per_day = 1 * BILLION  # hypothetical daily service target
    duration = HOURS_PER_DAY * hour
    carbon_intensity = Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg.carbon_intensity_kg_kwh * kg / kWh

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    cpu_daily_capacity = (cpu_rate * operating_fraction * duration).to_base_units().magnitude
    npu_daily_capacity = (npu_rate * operating_fraction * duration).to_base_units().magnitude
    cpu_servers = math.ceil(inferences_per_day / cpu_daily_capacity)
    npu_servers = math.ceil(inferences_per_day / npu_daily_capacity)
    cpu_energy_day = (cpu_servers * cpu_power * duration).to(kWh)
    npu_energy_day = (npu_servers * npu_power * duration).to(kWh)
    cpu_energy_request = (cpu_energy_day / inferences_per_day).to(joule)
    npu_energy_request = (npu_energy_day / inferences_per_day).to(joule)
    energy_savings_day = cpu_energy_day - npu_energy_day
    cpu_co2_year = (cpu_energy_day * DAYS_PER_YEAR * carbon_intensity).to(metric_ton)
    co2_saved_year = (energy_savings_day * DAYS_PER_YEAR * carbon_intensity).to(metric_ton)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        (cpu_servers - 1) * cpu_daily_capacity < inferences_per_day <= cpu_servers * cpu_daily_capacity,
        "CPU fleet must be the smallest meeting reserved-capacity target.",
    )
    check(
        (npu_servers - 1) * npu_daily_capacity < inferences_per_day <= npu_servers * npu_daily_capacity,
        "NPU fleet must be the smallest meeting reserved-capacity target.",
    )
    check(cpu_servers == 145 and npu_servers == 15, "Unexpected fleet sizing for this scenario.")
    check(abs(cpu_energy_request.to(joule).magnitude - 1.2528) < 1e-9, "CPU joules/request must include the complete provisioned fleet.")
    check(abs(npu_energy_request.to(joule).magnitude - 0.2592) < 1e-9, "NPU joules/request must include the complete provisioned fleet.")
    check(0 * metric_ton < co2_saved_year < cpu_co2_year, "Savings must be positive and below baseline emissions.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    cpu_power_w_str = fmt_power(cpu_power, unit=watt, precision=0)
    npu_power_w_str = fmt_power(npu_power, unit=watt, precision=0)
    cpu_rate_str = fmt_rate(cpu_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "requests/s", precision=0)
    npu_rate_str = fmt_rate(npu_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "requests/s", precision=0)
    operating_fraction_str = fmt_percent(operating_fraction, precision=0, style='prose')
    duration_h_str = fmt_time(duration, unit=hour, precision=0)
    cpu_daily_capacity_str = fmt_count(cpu_daily_capacity, precision=0)
    npu_daily_capacity_str = fmt_count(npu_daily_capacity, precision=0)
    cpu_servers_str = fmt_count(cpu_servers, precision=0)
    npu_servers_str = fmt_count(npu_servers, precision=0)
    workload_str = fmt_count(inferences_per_day, scale="billion", commas=False, scale_style="word")
    cpu_energy_day_kwh_str = fmt_energy(cpu_energy_day, unit=kWh, precision=0)
    npu_energy_day_kwh_str = fmt_energy(npu_energy_day, unit=kWh, precision=0)
    cpu_energy_request_j_str = fmt_energy(cpu_energy_request, unit=joule, precision=4)
    npu_energy_request_j_str = fmt_energy(npu_energy_request, unit=joule, precision=4)
    carbon_intensity_str = fmt_carbon_intensity(carbon_intensity, unit=kg / kWh, precision=3)
    co2_saved_str = fmt_emissions(co2_saved_year, unit=metric_ton, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-hw-acceleration-carbon-roi-specialized-silicon .callout-notebook title="An illustrative operational-energy comparison"}

**Problem**: An inference service must complete `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.workload_str` requests per day. Which of two hypothetical server platforms uses less operational energy for that service?

**Supplied observations**: For the same model, input distribution, accuracy, and latency target, a CPU server sustains `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.cpu_rate_str`, and an NPU-equipped server sustains `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.npu_rate_str`. Their whole-server wall powers are `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.cpu_power_w_str` and `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.npu_power_w_str`, respectively, including hosts and attached accelerators. These are hypothetical observations for this exercise, not product benchmarks. Assume requests arrive steadily through the day. Both fleets operate at no more than `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.operating_fraction_str` of the supplied throughput to reserve capacity for arrival-rate variation. Assume the listed wall power throughout the `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.duration_h_str` day, including spare capacity. Facility cooling and embodied emissions are outside this operational boundary.

**Calculation**:

1. **Size the fleets from useful work.** Multiplying useful throughput by the operating fraction and the day length gives `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.cpu_daily_capacity_str` requests per CPU server per day and `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.npu_daily_capacity_str` per NPU-equipped server. Divide the daily target by each capacity and round up to whole servers. The service requires `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.cpu_servers_str` CPU servers or `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.npu_servers_str` NPU-equipped servers.
2. **Account for the provisioned fleet.** Server count multiplied by wall power and day length yields `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.cpu_energy_day_kwh_str` per day for CPUs and `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.npu_energy_day_kwh_str` for NPUs. Dividing each fleet's energy by the same completed-request target gives `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.cpu_energy_request_j_str` per request and `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.npu_energy_request_j_str` per request. These values include capacity headroom and integer fleet rounding.
3. **Translate the energy difference.** At a common grid factor of `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.carbon_intensity_str`, the NPU-equipped fleet avoids approximately `{python} CarbonRoiCalc.co2_saved_str` of operational CO~2~ emissions per year at the stated system boundary.

**Decision**: Choose the NPU-equipped fleet if the objective is to minimize operational energy under these supplied conditions. Each server draws more power, but its greater useful throughput reduces the required fleet enough to lower joules per completed request. This conclusion depends on meeting the same quality and latency targets; a faster peak arithmetic rate alone would not establish the advantage. A procurement decision must additionally compare acquisition costs, software support, and embodied emissions.

:::

Energy per request completes the selection rule that the lighthouse table began. Hardware selection is not determined by peak speed alone. Energy per useful result, carbon intensity, embodied impact, and total cost of ownership belong beside latency, throughput, and memory capacity, and each is measured against the resource the workload actually exhausts. The misconceptions that follow are the ways teams skip that measurement and choose the wrong hardware path.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-hardware-acceleration-fallacies-pitfalls-dc1f}

Hardware acceleration often defies intuition because headline specifications mask workload-specific bottlenecks. The fallacies and pitfalls here capture selection, scaling, and optimization errors that leave expensive compute resources underused. Sound system evaluation follows one diagnostic habit instead: characterize the workload arithmetic intensity, identify the physical bottleneck metric, match execution to the appropriate datapath, and account for interconnect, scaling, and portability costs.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-workload-fit-recap
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, check, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_percent

class FpWorkloadFitRecap:
    """A100 roofline recap for the hardware-specialization fallacy."""

    # LOAD
    a100_peak_flops = Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.peak_flops
    a100_bandwidth = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.bandwidth
    softmax_ai_low = 2 * (flop / byte)  # scenario assumption: attention-softmax AI lower bound
    softmax_ai_high = 5 * (flop / byte)  # scenario assumption: attention-softmax AI upper bound
    cpu_ridge_low = 10 * (flop / byte)  # scenario assumption: CPU ridge lower bound
    cpu_ridge_high = 20 * (flop / byte)  # scenario assumption: CPU ridge upper bound

    # EXECUTE
    a100_ridge = (a100_peak_flops / a100_bandwidth).to(flop / byte)
    softmax_flops_low = (softmax_ai_low * a100_bandwidth).to(TFLOP / second)
    softmax_flops_high = (softmax_ai_high * a100_bandwidth).to(TFLOP / second)
    softmax_util_high = (softmax_flops_high / a100_peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude
    cpu_softmax_util_low = (softmax_ai_low / cpu_ridge_high).to_base_units().magnitude
    cpu_softmax_util_high = (softmax_ai_high / cpu_ridge_low).to_base_units().magnitude

    # GUARD
    check(150 * (flop / byte) <= a100_ridge <= 160 * (flop / byte), f"Unexpected A100 ridge: {a100_ridge.to(flop / byte).magnitude:.1f}")
    check(
        4 * (TFLOP / second) <= softmax_flops_low <= 5 * (TFLOP / second),
        f"Unexpected softmax low throughput: {softmax_flops_low.to(TFLOP / second).magnitude:.1f} TFLOP/s",
    )
    check(
        10 * (TFLOP / second) <= softmax_flops_high <= 11 * (TFLOP / second),
        f"Unexpected softmax high throughput: {softmax_flops_high.to(TFLOP / second).magnitude:.1f} TFLOP/s",
    )

    # OUTPUT
    a100_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(a100_ridge, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(a100_peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    softmax_ai_low_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(softmax_ai_low, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    softmax_ai_high_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(softmax_ai_high, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    softmax_low_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(softmax_flops_low, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    softmax_high_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(softmax_flops_high, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    softmax_util_high_str = fmt_percent(softmax_util_high, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    cpu_ridge_low_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(cpu_ridge_low, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    cpu_ridge_high_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(cpu_ridge_high, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    cpu_softmax_util_low_str = fmt_percent(cpu_softmax_util_low, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    cpu_softmax_util_high_str = fmt_percent(cpu_softmax_util_high, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *More specialized hardware always provides better performance than general-purpose alternatives.*

Specialized accelerators achieve high efficiency only when workload access patterns match underlying execution datapaths: the core tenet of algorithm-machine co-design. On the roofline (@sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff), the A100 reference tensor path has a ridge point of `{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.a100_ridge_str`; below that ridge, increasing its `{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` arithmetic peak does not raise the modeled bandwidth ceiling. A transformer attention softmax with $\ArithmeticIntensity$ = `{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.softmax_ai_low_str`--`{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.softmax_ai_high_str` is capped at `{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.softmax_low_tflop_per_s_str`--`{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.softmax_high_tflop_per_s_str` (`{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.softmax_util_high_str` of tensor peak) on an A100. On a CPU, whose ridge point sits around `{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.cpu_ridge_low_str`--`{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.cpu_ridge_high_str`, the same traffic model places the kernel below the reference ridge, and its bandwidth ceiling represents `{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.cpu_softmax_util_low_str`--`{python} FpWorkloadFitRecap.cpu_softmax_util_high_str` of the CPU's compute capacity. These fractions are modeled bandwidth bounds, not measured utilization. When workloads have irregular memory access, tiny batch sizes, or dynamic control flow, highly parallel execution pipelines stall on memory latency and thread divergence. General-purpose CPUs with large cache hierarchies, out-of-order execution, and branch predictors often deliver superior latency and resource efficiency under these conditions. Hardware selection\index{Hardware selection!workload matching} requires matching workload arithmetic intensity and dataflow regularity to architectural ridge points rather than assuming specialization guarantees speed.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-memory-energy-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ F&P: MEMORY BANDWIDTH ENERGY COSTS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Pitfall about ignoring memory bandwidth limitations
# │
# │ Goal: Quantifies the energy penalty of DRAM vs on-chip memory and shows
# │      how low-AI operations like LayerNorm achieve <1% utilization on
# │      high-compute accelerators.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_energy, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_percent

class FpMemoryEnergyCalc:
    """Energy cost disparity and ridge-point pitfall for memory-bandwidth-limited ops."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Energy values sourced from the mlsysim registry (Hardware.Tech.Memory).
    ENERGY_DRAM_ACCESS_PJ = Hardware.Tech.Memory.DRAM.energy_per_access
    ENERGY_SRAM_L1_PJ = Hardware.Tech.Memory.L1.energy_per_access
    dram_pj = ENERGY_DRAM_ACCESS_PJ.to(pJ).magnitude
    sram_pj = ENERGY_SRAM_L1_PJ.to(pJ).magnitude

    layernorm_ai = 1.5
    peak_flops = 300 * (TFLOP / second)  # hypothetical accelerator
    peak_bw = 2 * (TB / second)  # hypothetical accelerator

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    energy_ratio = int(dram_pj / sram_pj)
    fp_ridge_example = (peak_flops / peak_bw).to(flop / byte).magnitude

    layernorm_flops = (layernorm_ai * flop / byte * peak_bw).to(TFLOP / second)
    layernorm_util = (layernorm_flops / peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(round(fp_ridge_example) == 150, f"Ridge point mismatch: {fp_ridge_example}")
    check(round(layernorm_util, 1) == 1.0, f"LayerNorm utilization mismatch: {layernorm_util}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    fp_ridge_example_str = fmt(fp_ridge_example, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_layernorm_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(round(layernorm_flops), unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_layernorm_util_str = fmt_percent(round(layernorm_util / 100, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    fp_dram_pj_str = fmt_energy(ENERGY_DRAM_ACCESS_PJ, unit=pJ, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_sram_pj_str = fmt_energy(ENERGY_SRAM_L1_PJ, unit=pJ, precision=1, commas=False)
    fp_peak_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_peak_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(peak_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_layernorm_ai_str = fmt(layernorm_ai, precision=1, commas=False)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Ignoring memory bandwidth limitations when selecting acceleration strategies.*

Procurement decisions frequently target peak arithmetic throughput while overlooking memory interface constraints. Off-chip data movement imposes severe performance and energy penalties: fetching an operand from DRAM consumes roughly `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_dram_pj_str` compared to `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_sram_pj_str` for a small, register-adjacent L1 SRAM access, the cheapest tier noted in the caption of @fig-energy-hierarchy. Consider an accelerator providing `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_peak_tflop_per_s_str` of compute alongside `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_peak_bw_tb_per_s_str` of memory bandwidth, setting a ridge point of `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_ridge_example_str` FLOP/byte. A normalization kernel such as LayerNorm with an arithmetic intensity of `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_layernorm_ai_str` FLOP/byte has a bandwidth ceiling of `{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_layernorm_tflop_per_s_str` (`{python} FpMemoryEnergyCalc.fp_layernorm_util_str` of compute peak). Under the stated HBM streaming assumption, memory bandwidth supplies this upper bound, and adding compute units alone does not raise it.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-multigpu-scaling-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ F&P: MULTI-GPU SCALING OVERHEAD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Fallacy about linear multi-GPU scaling
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate why multi-GPU scaling is sublinear.
# │ Show: The communication overhead of gradient synchronization.
# │ How: Contrast local compute throughput with NVLink bandwidth for an 8-GPU node.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

class FpMultigpuScalingCalc:
    """NVLink gradient-sync overhead quantifying sublinear multi-GPU scaling."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    nvlink_bw = Hardware.Cloud.A100.nvlink.bandwidth  # datasheet bidirectional total (for display)
    nvlink_bw_beta = Hardware.Cloud.A100.nvlink.bandwidth_per_direction  # one-way rate for transfer math
    gradient_size = 1.0 * GB  # scenario assumption
    step_time = 50 * millisecond  # scenario assumption
    gpu_count = Systems.Nodes.DGX_A100.accelerators_per_node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    ring_transfer_multiplier = 2 * (gpu_count - 1) / gpu_count
    transfer_volume = gradient_size * ring_transfer_multiplier
    sync_time = (transfer_volume / nvlink_bw_beta).to(millisecond)
    sync_overhead_pct = (sync_time / step_time).to_base_units().magnitude * 100
    no_overlap_speedup = (gpu_count * step_time / (step_time + sync_time)).to_base_units().magnitude
    no_overlap_efficiency_pct = no_overlap_speedup / gpu_count * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(round(sync_time.magnitude, 2) == 5.83, f"Sync time mismatch: {sync_time}")
    check(round(sync_overhead_pct, 1) == 11.7, f"Sync overhead mismatch: {sync_overhead_pct}")
    check(round(no_overlap_efficiency_pct, 1) == 89.6, f"Efficiency mismatch: {no_overlap_efficiency_pct}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    fp_nvlink_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_ring_transfer_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ring_transfer_multiplier, precision=2, commas=False)
    fp_sync_time_ms_str = fmt_time(sync_time, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    fp_sync_overhead_str = fmt_percent(sync_overhead_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    fp_no_overlap_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(no_overlap_speedup, precision=1, commas=False)
    fp_no_overlap_efficiency_str = fmt_percent(no_overlap_efficiency_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Hardware acceleration benefits scale linearly with additional accelerators.*

Distributed training need not deliver $8\times$ throughput on eight accelerators because exposed inter-chip communication can reduce parallel efficiency. Synchronizing gradients across ranks via ring AllReduce makes each rank send and receive about twice the gradient payload (@eq-training-ring-allreduce), or `{python} FpMultigpuScalingCalc.fp_ring_transfer_mult_str` payloads across eight devices. With an interconnect such as NVLink providing `{python} FpMultigpuScalingCalc.fp_nvlink_bw_gb_per_s_str` bidirectional bandwidth (half that per direction), transmitting a 1 GB gradient payload consumes `{python} FpMultigpuScalingCalc.fp_sync_time_ms_str`. For a model with a 50 ms compute step, this data exchange adds `{python} FpMultigpuScalingCalc.fp_sync_overhead_str` communication overhead before counting software collective latency. Without compute-communication pipelining, an eight-accelerator node reaches only `{python} FpMultigpuScalingCalc.fp_no_overlap_speedup_mult_str` speedup (`{python} FpMultigpuScalingCalc.fp_no_overlap_efficiency_str` parallel efficiency). Stragglers, barrier synchronizations, and collective protocol overhead widen the gap between linear expectations and physical cluster scaling.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-peak-vs-sustained-recap
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple

class FpPeakVsSustainedRecap:
    """A100 peak and sustained ranges for the peak-FLOP/s fallacy."""

    # LOAD
    a100_peak_flops = Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.peak_flops
    h100_fp16_flops = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.peak_flops
    h100_fp32_flops = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["fp32"]
    transformer_flops_low = 120 * (TFLOP / second)  # scenario assumption: sustained transformer lower bound
    transformer_flops_high = 180 * (TFLOP / second)  # scenario assumption: sustained transformer upper bound
    recsys_flops_low = 10 * (TFLOP / second)  # scenario assumption: sustained recommender lower bound
    recsys_flops_high = 30 * (TFLOP / second)  # scenario assumption: sustained recommender upper bound

    # EXECUTE
    transformer_util_low = (transformer_flops_low / a100_peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude
    transformer_util_high = (transformer_flops_high / a100_peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude
    recsys_util_low = (recsys_flops_low / a100_peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude
    recsys_util_high = (recsys_flops_high / a100_peak_flops).to_base_units().magnitude

    transformer_util_low_rounded = round(transformer_util_low * 10) / 10
    transformer_util_high_rounded = round(transformer_util_high * 10) / 10
    h100_prec_gap = (h100_fp16_flops / h100_fp32_flops).to("").magnitude

    # GUARD
    check(
        300 * (TFLOP / second) <= a100_peak_flops <= 320 * (TFLOP / second),
        f"Unexpected A100 peak: {a100_peak_flops.to(TFLOP / second).magnitude:.0f}",
    )
    check(0.35 <= transformer_util_low <= 0.45, f"Unexpected transformer low utilization: {transformer_util_low:.3f}")
    check(0.55 <= transformer_util_high <= 0.65, f"Unexpected transformer high utilization: {transformer_util_high:.3f}")
    check(0.03 <= recsys_util_low <= 0.04, f"Unexpected recsys low utilization: {recsys_util_low:.3f}")
    check(0.09 <= recsys_util_high <= 0.10, f"Unexpected recsys high utilization: {recsys_util_high:.3f}")

    # OUTPUT
    a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(a100_peak_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_fp16_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=True)
    h100_fp32_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_fp32_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_prec_gap_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(h100_prec_gap), precision=0, commas=False)
    transformer_low_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(transformer_flops_low, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    transformer_high_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(transformer_flops_high, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    transformer_util_low_str = fmt_percent(transformer_util_low_rounded, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    transformer_util_high_str = fmt_percent(transformer_util_high_rounded, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    recsys_low_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(recsys_flops_low, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    recsys_high_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(recsys_flops_high, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    recsys_util_low_str = fmt_percent(recsys_util_low, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    recsys_util_high_str = fmt_percent(recsys_util_high, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Planning accelerator capacity from peak FLOP/s specifications.*

Peak FLOP/s\index{Peak FLOPS!misleading metric} measures arithmetic unit capacity under ideal instruction mixes and continuous operand availability, not delivered application throughput. Realized performance depends on kernel arithmetic intensity, matrix dimensions, memory coalescing, and runtime launch overhead. The roofline model (@sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff) bounds the gap between peak compute and bandwidth-limited execution. On an A100 GPU with a `{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` peak, an illustrative dense-transformer scenario supplies a sustained range of `{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.transformer_low_tflop_per_s_str`--`{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.transformer_high_tflop_per_s_str` (`{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.transformer_util_low_str`--`{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.transformer_util_high_str` model FLOPs utilization). This supplied range is illustrative, not a measurement or a prediction for every model. Sizing cluster capacity from peak FLOP/s creates severe under-provisioning; capacity planning must rely on measured sustained throughput or roofline-bounded kernel projections.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *One peak FLOP/s rating describes a workload at every precision.*

Accelerators have separate datapaths for different precisions, and the peak throughput varies dramatically across them. An H100 delivers roughly `{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` in FP16 tensor operations but only about `{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.h100_fp32_tflop_per_s_str` in FP32 CUDA-core operations: a roughly `{python} FpPeakVsSustainedRecap.h100_prec_gap_mult_str` gap within the same chip [@choquette2023]. Dividing achieved BF16 model FLOP/s by the smaller FP32 peak inflates the reported utilization, while using that FP32 peak to estimate ideal training time overestimates the time. Matching against the wrong roofline misclassifies kernels as compute-bound when they are memory-bound (or vice versa). Useful model FLOP utilization divides the model's useful operations per elapsed second by the matching supported precision and execution-path peak. Hardware busy time is a different metric: an active device can spend time on transfers, redundant work, or fallback execution. Quote the denominator and precision explicitly.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-small-batch-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ F&P: SMALL-BATCH INFERENCE ECONOMICS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Pitfall about deploying small-batch inference on high-compute GPUs
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the economics of small-batch inference.
# │ Show: At batch=1 the T4/A100 gap is the bandwidth ratio, not the compute ratio.
# │ How: Contrast arithmetic intensity and utilization across GPU tiers.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_multiple, check

class FpSmallBatchCalc:
    """Small-batch arithmetic intensity and T4 ridge point for inference economics."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    M = 2048
    N = 2048
    B = 256

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    # Batch=1
    flops_b1 = 2 * M * N
    bytes_b1 = (M * N + M + N) * 2
    ai_b1 = flops_b1 / bytes_b1

    # Batch=256
    flops_b256 = 2 * B * M * N
    bytes_b256 = (M * N + B * M + B * N) * 2
    ai_b256 = flops_b256 / bytes_b256

    # T4 ridge point
    t4_flops = Hardware.Cloud.T4.compute.peak_flops
    t4_bw = Hardware.Cloud.T4.memory.bandwidth
    a100_bw = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.bandwidth
    t4_ridge = (t4_flops / t4_bw).to(flop / byte).magnitude
    a100_roof_b1 = (a100_bw * ai_b1 * flop / byte).to(TFLOP / second)
    t4_roof_b1 = (t4_bw * ai_b1 * flop / byte).to(TFLOP / second)
    a100_flops = Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.peak_flops
    roof_ratio_b1 = (a100_roof_b1 / t4_roof_b1).to_base_units().magnitude
    peak_ratio = (a100_flops / t4_flops).to_base_units().magnitude
    cost_ratio = (Hardware.Cloud.A100.unit_cost / Hardware.Cloud.T4.unit_cost).to_base_units().magnitude
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(roof_ratio_b1 - (a100_bw / t4_bw).to_base_units().magnitude) < 1e-9, "B=1 roof ratio must equal bandwidth ratio")
    check(0.8 < roof_ratio_b1 / cost_ratio < 1.25, "prose claims batch-1 throughput per dollar is roughly equal")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    fp_ai_b1_flops_per_byte_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ai_b1 * flop / byte, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    fp_ai_b256_flops_per_byte_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ai_b256 * flop / byte, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    fp_t4_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(Hardware.Cloud.T4.ridge_point(), unit=flop / byte, precision=1, commas=False)
    fp_t4_flops_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(t4_flops, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_t4_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(t4_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fp_a100_roof_b1_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(a100_roof_b1, unit=TFLOP / second, commas=False)
    fp_t4_roof_b1_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(t4_roof_b1, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    fp_roof_ratio_b1_mult_str = fmt_multiple(roof_ratio_b1, precision=1)
    fp_peak_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(peak_ratio, precision=1)
    fp_cost_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cost_ratio)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Deploying small-batch inference workloads on high-compute accelerators.*

Small-batch dense inference can use only a small fraction of arithmetic peak because single-sample execution lacks cross-sample parameter reuse. For a dense linear projection with widths $\LayerInputWidth=\LayerOutputWidth=2048$, a single request ($\BatchSize=1$) is modeled as streaming the entire weight tensor from device memory to execute a matrix-vector product, yielding an arithmetic intensity of only `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_ai_b1_flops_per_byte_str`. At batch size $\BatchSize=256$, weight reuse amortizes memory transfers across tokens, elevating arithmetic intensity to `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_ai_b256_flops_per_byte_str`. At $\BatchSize=1$, memory bandwidth bounds performance at `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_a100_roof_b1_tflop_per_s_str` on an A100 and `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_t4_roof_b1_tflop_per_s_str` on a T4. Although the T4 provides a lower peak of `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_t4_flops_tflop_per_s_str` with a ridge point of `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_t4_ridge_str`, the two batch-1 ceilings differ by `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_roof_ratio_b1_mult_str`, which is exactly their memory-bandwidth ratio. The A100's `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_peak_ratio_mult_str` advantage in peak compute contributes nothing. The A100 costs `{python} FpSmallBatchCalc.fp_cost_ratio_mult_str` as much as the T4, so their modeled batch-1 throughput ceilings per dollar are nearly the same. Actual procurement requires measured latency, throughput, memory fit, and the intended request mix.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Vendor-specific optimizations have no long-term portability cost.*

Optimizing exclusively for a single vendor runtime captures immediate kernel efficiency but introduces severe architectural lock-in\index{Vendor lock-in!portability trade-off} (@sec-hardware-acceleration-compiler-support-172e). Codebases saturated with proprietary device intrinsics, vendor-specific assembly, and non-standard memory layouts require months of engineering labor to port when newer, more cost-effective accelerators emerge. This technical debt delays hardware transitions and prevents multi-vendor procurement. To preserve flexibility, systems must isolate vendor-tuned micro-kernels behind hardware abstraction layers\index{Hardware abstraction layer!portability} or target intermediate compiler representations (such as Triton or MLIR).

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: feasibility-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HARDWARE FEASIBILITY ASSESSMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "Feasibility Assessment: Can You Run It?"
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify three deployment feasibility checks.
# │ Show: Memory headroom, bandwidth-limited latency, and real-time frame budget.
# │ How: Three independent checks using model_memory() formula.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, check
from mlsysim.physics import model_memory

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class FeasibilityAssessment:
    """
    Namespace for Hardware Feasibility Assessment.
    Check 1: Memory--7-billion-parameter model (FP16) on 16 GB GPU.
    Check 2: Bandwidth--70-billion-parameter model on 1 TB/s GPU.
    Check 3: Compute—30 FPS video processing.
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Memory check: 7-billion-parameter Llama model on 16 GB GPU
    llama_7b = Models.Language.Llama2_7B
    params_7b = llama_7b.parameters
    gpu_memory = 16 * GB  # scenario assumption

    # Bandwidth check: 70-billion-parameter model on 1 TB/s GPU
    llama_70b = Models.Language.Llama2_70B
    mem_bw = 1 * (TB / second)  # scenario assumption

    # Compute check: video at 30 FPS
    fps_target = 30
    latency_target = 50 * millisecond  # scenario assumption
    roofline_peak = 2 * (TFLOP / second)  # scenario assumption
    roofline_bandwidth = 200 * (GB / second)  # scenario assumption
    roofline_kernel_ai = 10 * (flop / byte)  # scenario assumption

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Step 1: Memory: does the model fit?
    model_7b_memory = llama_7b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16).to(GB)
    headroom = gpu_memory - model_7b_memory

    # Step 2: Bandwidth: how fast can we generate tokens?
    model_70b_memory = llama_70b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16).to(GB)
    token_latency = (model_70b_memory / mem_bw).to(millisecond)

    # Step 3: Compute: real-time frame budget
    frame_budget = (1 / fps_target) * second
    roofline_ridge = roofline_peak / roofline_bandwidth

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(headroom >= 2 * GB, f"Expected >= 2 GB VRAM headroom, got {headroom}")
    check(abs(token_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 140.0) < 1.0, f"Expected ~140 ms token latency, got {token_latency}")
    check(abs(roofline_ridge.to(flop / byte).magnitude - 10) < 1e-9, "Roofline checkpoint should put a 10 FLOP/byte kernel at the ridge point.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    model_7b_gb_str = fmt_memory(model_7b_memory, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    model_70b_gb_str = fmt_memory(model_70b_memory, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    mem_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(mem_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    latency_target_ms_str = fmt_time(latency_target, 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=False)
    frame_budget_ms_str = fmt_time(frame_budget, 'millisecond', precision=1, commas=False)
    params_7b_billion_str = fmt_params(params_7b, scale="billion", precision=0, commas=False, scale_style="word", attributive=True)
    gpu_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory(gpu_memory, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    roofline_peak_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(roofline_peak, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    roofline_bandwidth_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(roofline_bandwidth, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    roofline_kernel_ai_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(roofline_kernel_ai, unit=flop / byte, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#chk-hw-acceleration-feasibility-assessment-can-you-run-it .callout-checkpoint title="Feasibility assessment: Can you run it?"}

Before procuring hardware, validate each physical constraint. These failure modes translate into a concrete feasibility test:

- [ ] **Memory capacity**: use $\TotalMemoryFootprint = \WeightMemory + \KvCacheMemory + \ActivationMemory$ (weights, KV cache, and activation buffers) to list the inputs needed to test $\TotalMemoryFootprint < \DeviceMemoryCapacity$ for a `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.params_7b_billion_str`-parameter Llama model with `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.model_7b_gb_str` FP16 weights on a `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.gpu_mem_gb_str` GPU. What sequence length, concurrency, model dimensions, and runtime workspace information is missing before a complete fit decision?
- [ ] **Bandwidth**: compute the weight-streaming lower bound $\DecodeTokenTimeFloor= \DataVolume / \Bandwidth$ for a 70-billion-parameter model (`{python} FeasibilityAssessment.model_70b_gb_str`) on `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.mem_bw_tb_per_s_str` memory bandwidth, then compare the result with a `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.latency_target_ms_str` latency target. Assume one dense FP16 weight read per generated token; what additional traffic and overhead would a measured latency include?
- [ ] **Compute**: identify the operation count, numerical path, and measured efficiency needed to use $\IronLawComputeTime = \Operations / (\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$. With serialized frame processing, 30 FPS leaves `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.frame_budget_ms_str` per frame for the whole pipeline. How does overlapped processing change the distinction between frame latency and sustained throughput?
- [ ] **Roofline placement**: for an accelerator at roughly `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.roofline_peak_tflop_per_s_str` peak and `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.roofline_bandwidth_gb_per_s_str` bandwidth, estimate the ridge-point arithmetic intensity, then place a `{python} FeasibilityAssessment.roofline_kernel_ai_str` kernel against it: how do the two ceilings compare, and would increasing only the compute clock raise the overall bound? What measurements would test the actual bottleneck?

:::

## Summary {#sec-hardware-acceleration-summary-a5f8}

Hardware acceleration co-designs compute engines, memory hierarchies, numerical formats, and dataflows. For a chosen memory interface, the iron law compares compute time $\Operations/(\PeakRate\EfficiencyHw)$ with movement time $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$; the roofline restates that competition as $\min(\PeakRate, \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity)$. End-to-end latency also includes launch, synchronization, communication, and fixed overheads. Accelerators improve efficiency only when supported paths capture reuse locally. Hardware selection therefore begins with the workload's measured or modeled bottleneck, not a vendor peak. For ResNet-50, INT8 multiplies large-batch throughput because large batches sit near the arithmetic ceiling, while batch-one latency sits on the overhead floor and moves only when compilation removes launch cost.

The chapter map (@tbl-hw-acceleration-chapter-spine) can now be read row by row for the INT8 ResNet-50 workload that opened the chapter. Its convolutions lower onto matrix units. Its INT8 path doubles the H100's arithmetic ceiling without moving the bandwidth ceiling. Its activation tiles stay on chip only when the mapping and the tile sizes allow it. Whether a given layer gains from INT8 depends on whether its activations travel at INT8, a choice the compiler and runtime make. GPT-2 XL decode, the single contrast, gains from none of the arithmetic and from every byte saved.

The bounds developed across the chapter fit in one table (@tbl-hw-acceleration-key-equations). Together they let an engineer estimate, before profiling, whether a kernel on a given accelerator is limited by arithmetic, by memory bandwidth, by on-chip capacity, or by work the accelerator never touches.

| **Quantity**                       | **Formula**                                                                                                                                                                                                         | **Where derived**                                                   |
|:-----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Amdahl bound**                   | $\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1 - \ParallelFraction) + \ParallelFraction/\AcceleratorGain}$                                                                                                                           | @eq-amdahl                                                          |
| **Memory and compute time**        | $\IronLawMemoryTime = \DataVolume/\Bandwidth$; $\IronLawComputeTime = \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$                                                                                                  | @sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-access-patterns-ml-workloads-a960 |
| **Arithmetic intensity**           | $\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume$                                                                                                                                                                    | definition \ref{dfn-nn-computation-arithmetic-intensity}            |
| **Ridge point (hardware balance)** | $\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth$, per precision path                                                                                                                                                    | @sec-hardware-acceleration-hardware-balance                         |
| **Roofline bound**                 | $\AttainableComputeRate = \min(\PeakRate, \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity)$                                                                                                                                  | @eq-roofline                                                        |
| **Required bandwidth**             | $\RequiredMemoryBandwidth = \TargetComputeRate/\ArithmeticIntensity$                                                                                                                                                | @eq-required-bandwidth                                              |
| **Dense-layer intensity**          | $\ArithmeticIntensity \approx \BatchSize$ when weight traffic dominates                                                                                                                                             | @eq-batch-ai                                                        |
| **Decode floor**                   | $\DecodeTokenTimeFloor = \DataVolume/\Bandwidth$, with $\DataVolume$ the weight bytes read per token                                                                                                                | Notebook \ref{nbk-hw-acceleration-throughput-ceiling}               |
| **Tile capacity**                  | $(2\text{ bytes})\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileInnerDimension + (2\text{ bytes})\GemmTileInnerDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension + (4\text{ bytes})\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension \le$ local bytes | @eq-hw-tile-capacity                                                |
| **Transfer overlap**               | Hidden when $\IronLawComputeTime \ge \BatchTransferTime$                                                                                                                                                            | @sec-hardware-acceleration-transfer-optimization-85a8               |

: **Key Equations**: The chapter's bounds in the notation of the sections that derive them. Each ceiling is specific to one precision path and one memory interface; the tile-capacity form assumes FP16 operands and an FP32 accumulator held in one software-managed local store. {#tbl-hw-acceleration-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[22,56,22]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: summary-roofline-recap
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, check

class SummaryRooflineRecap:
    """H100 FP16 and INT8 ridge-point recap for the final takeaways."""

    # LOAD
    h100_fp16 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    h100_int8 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.precision_flops["int8"]
    h100_bandwidth = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth

    # EXECUTE
    h100_ridge = (h100_fp16 / h100_bandwidth).to(flop / byte)
    h100_ridge_int8 = (h100_int8 / h100_bandwidth).to(flop / byte)

    # GUARD
    check(290 * (flop / byte) <= h100_ridge <= 300 * (flop / byte), f"Unexpected H100 summary ridge: {h100_ridge.to(flop / byte).magnitude:.1f}")
    check(h100_ridge_int8 > h100_ridge, "The INT8 ridge must exceed the FP16 ridge.")

    # OUTPUT
    h100_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(h100_ridge, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
    h100_ridge_int8_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(h100_ridge_int8, unit=flop / byte, commas=False)
```

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Moving data costs more than computing it"}

* **The roofline model bounds attainable performance**: Compare a kernel's arithmetic intensity with the ridge for its memory interface and supported execution path (`{python} SummaryRooflineRecap.h100_ridge_str` for the H100's dense FP16 tensor path and `{python} SummaryRooflineRecap.h100_ridge_int8_str` for its INT8 path). Below it, bandwidth supplies the tighter modeled ceiling; above it, compute does. Profiling establishes whether the kernel approaches that ceiling or is limited by dependencies, dispatch, or another execution resource.
* **Memory bandwidth constrains performance**: GPU compute capacity has grown faster than memory bandwidth. Many inference phases are memory bound, especially low-batch decoding and embedding lookup, while large-batch GEMMs can remain compute bound.
* **Hardware-software co-design compounds performance**: Matching algorithm patterns to architectural capabilities, such as dense GEMM on systolic or tensor units and supported sparsity on sparse paths, can produce large improvements.
* **Tensor Cores require a compatible path**: Precision, dimensions, layouts, and library support must match the architecture. Batch and shape affect reuse and utilization, but no single batch threshold guarantees peak performance.
* **End-to-end speedup stops at the next bottleneck**: Accelerating one kernel leaves launch, transfer, synchronization, communication, and unsupported work unchanged. Use Amdahl's law (principle \ref{pri-amdahl}) and profiling to decide whether further silicon, better mapping, or less movement will improve the complete workload.

:::

An accelerator is not a uniformly faster computer. It provides efficient paths for particular operations and dataflows, and each of those paths is a way of moving fewer bytes per useful operation. Tiling, fusion, stationary dataflows, and systolic execution pay off only when the workload, numerical format, and software path can use them. The diagnostic habit the chapter leaves is therefore an ordering. Place the kernel on the relevant roofline to bound its performance, bound the end-to-end gain with Amdahl's law, and only then choose among more silicon, a better mapping, or less movement. Each step is a prediction that measurement must confirm. The same habit is what keeps the bitter lesson affordable. Scale keeps winning only while each additional operation gets cheaper in time and energy, and on modern accelerators the operation is rarely the expensive part. The bytes that feed it are.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From optimization to validation"}

Data selection, model compression, and hardware acceleration each end with a favorable local number. Data selection reaches target accuracy on fewer examples, compression produces a smaller artifact, and the roofline places a kernel below a ceiling that the vendor's peak overstates. Each number is a prediction made for one stage in isolation, and the stages interact once they run together on a real device under real load. @Sec-benchmarking takes up that test, beginning with this chapter's ResNet-50 workload, whose predicted roofline position becomes the first claim a measurement must confirm. It asks which local gains survive deployment-representative conditions, and it supplies the measurement scope, standardized suites, and statistical protocols that let different systems be compared on the same terms.

:::

::: { .quiz-end }
